The grief that swells the Christian's heart is the bud of a new beauty bursting into flower. If you Would learn self-mastery, begin by yielding your- se lif to the one Great Master .—Lobstein. It is the habitual thought that frames itself into our life. It affects us even more than our intimate social relations do. Our confidential friends have not so much to do in shaping our lives as the thoughts have which we harbour. —.T. W.Teale.

Christianity in its divine service to a troubled world does not break a twig, bruise a flower, crush an insect, or dis- turb a-honey bee in the garden of life. As it goes from sacrifice to duty, from teaching to burden-bearing, the echo of its angelic song is everywhere heard: "On earth peace, good-will to men." - - A gentleman who had taken the right of shooting over a moor in Ayrshire at a high rent, bagged only two brace the first day. After counting the pace he grumblingly re- marked to the tenant of the moor that the birds had cost him two guineas the brace. The tenant very innocently replied, "Awed, air, ye may be thankfu' ye line gotten sae few o' them; they're far too dear." - A celebrated singer, Madame Le Rochois, was giving a younger companion in art some instruction in the tragic character of Medea, which she was about to sustain. "In- spire yourself with the situation," said she. "Fancy your- self in the poor woman's place. If you were deserted by a lover whom you adored, what would you do ?" The reply was as unexpected as it was ingentious—" I would look out tor another.' _

THE BRUTAL MAN AND THE NOBLE BRIITE.—" Donald," the first of the poems in Mr. Brovrning's new volume, is concerned with the subject of sport, which is just now re- ceiving some legislative attention with us. It is a tradi- tion that the bosom of the sportsman is the receptacle of every human virtue but Mr. Browning shows, by a das- tardly incident which actually occurred some years ago, that this is far from being necessarily the case, though, of course, there are many noble-mined sportsmen. We are introduced in the poem to a number of Oxford undergradu- ates, who in a Scotch bothy are holding merry carousal and telling rare stories of sporting feat& The usual things are said, that "good sportsman means good fellow," and a man "sound-hearted to the centre," dm., when one -of the com- pany interrupts and tells a very different tale of a sports- man whom he calls Donald. This Donald was once skirting the sides of Ben—, in Ross-shire, when on the edge of a lefty but narrow ledge of rock he came suddenly face to face with a great gold-red stag, which "stood and stared, gigan- tic and mag,nific." The wonder and the peril struck the whilom fierce and untamed creature, "intelligent and paci- fic." Neither man nor beast could turn back or go forward. The happy thought struck Donald that by lying fiat down, breast upwards, the stag might pass over him. The stag understood, and lifted gently over the prostrate man first one foot and then another. Now comes the diabolical act a the sportsman :- - The last of the legs as tenderly Follows the rest or never Or now is the time! His knife in reach, And his right hand loose—how clever 1 Fur this can stab up the stomach's soft, While the left hand lotrasps the pastern. Arise on the elbow, and—now's the time Or never: this turn's the last turn! • I shall dare to place myself by God Who scanned—for He does—each feature Of the face thrown up in appeal to Him By the agonising creature. Nay, I hear pltVn wordi : "Thy gift brings this 1" Up he sprang, back he staggere,t, Over he fell, and with him our friend At following game no laggard. Yet he was not dead when they picked next day From the gully's depth the wreck of him; His fall had been stayed by the stag beneath, Who cushioned and saved the neck of him. But the rest of his body—why, doctors said, Whatever could break was broken; • Legs, arms, ribs, all of him looked like a toast. In a tumbler of port wine soaken. "That your life is left you, thank the stag!" Said they when—the slow cure ended— They opened the hospital door, and thence --trapped, spliced, main fractures mended, Ant minor damage left wisely atone.— Like an old shoe clouted and cobbled Out—what went in a Goliath well-nigh— Some half of a David hobbled. The miserable wretch. a hopeless cripple for life, was driven to roam about the country, showing the head of the stag, and telling his story to other sportsmen. Many applauded him, but the narrator of the incident exclaims, "Rightly rewarded—ingrate." . .

EARLY CONSPIRACIES AGAINST LINCOLN.-The rebel Government was virtaully established when, on the 11th of bruary, 1861, Mr. Lincoln left Springfield, Illinois, for Washington, accompanied by some of his friends. At vari- ous points speeeir. were delivered, 'according to American custom; and everywhere the President-elect expressed him- self in favour of maintaining peace, uul. war were forced urn him in self-defence. Advocates of the Southern have alleged that his conduct on the road was that of a buffoon; and it may be that, considering the dignity of his office and the gravity of the time, he was too free with his Jokes and his familiarities. But on many. occasions his utterances were grave and even solemn. At Philadelphia. on the anniversary of Washington's birthday (the 2nd of February), and in the old State limte where the Declara- tion of Independence had been signed, he made use of the remarkable expression that he would "rather be assassi- nated" on the spot than surrender the principle of liberty on which the Union was based; that he had said nothing but what he was willing to live by, and, if it so pleased God, to die by. This might almost seem like a prophecy of his actual end; but it was in truth prompted bya know- ledge of the fact that a plot to assassinate him on his jour- ney to the Federal capital had really been formed. The details of this conspiracy have been only obscurely revealed but it appears certain that Mr. Lincoln was warned by the detective police that a plot against his life had been hatched at Baltimore, and was to be carried out at the railway sta- tion on his arrival there. Lincoln himself always believed in the reality of this scheme, and not without reason, for, on the first day of his journey, an attempt was made to up- set the railway train, and at Cincinnati a hand-grenade was discovered in the carriage in which he was to travel. The Baltimore attempt was baffled by the President-elect alter- ing his hoar of arrival; and on the 23rd of February he got safely to Washington.—ausell's Illustrated History of the United States.

THR ORIGIN OF TILE STORY OF ROBIN HOOD.—In the lifetime of Robert Henryson the art of printing first came into use in England, and among the pleasure books produced by one of the earliest printers, Wynkyn de Worde, was the story of Robin Hood, in ballad verse. Wynkyn de 'Worde, a native of Lorraine, had been assistant to William Caxton, the introducer of the art of printing into England. After Caxton's death, in 1491, he carried on his work, and after- wards removed the business to Fleet-street, where it watt continued until his own death in the year 1534. The first printing-press was not set up in Scotland before 1507, when James IV. granted a patent to Walter Chepman, a merchant, and Andrew Millar, a workman, for a press in Edinburgh. "A Lytell Geste of Robin Hode" was printed in London by Wynkyn•cle Worde, in thirty-two leaves of black letter, be- fore the reappearance of it as one of the first pieces printed at Edinburgh. It came from the press of Chepman and Millar in 1508. Here, therefore, the story of Robin Hood is to be read as it was actually read in rhyme by our fore- fathers at the end of the fifteenth and beginning of the six- teenth centuries. As the hero of old _popular tales and ballads, R,obin.Hood is supposed to have been formed by the gathering of later traditions about the memory of Robert Fitzooth, reputed Earl of Huntingdon, who was born at Loxley Chase, near Sheffield, in Yorkshire (by the river Loxley), perhaps at the close of the reign of Henry IL, but more probably in the reign of Henry 111., towards the year 1230. He was outlawed and lived in war against authority; eating the king's deer, defying the oppressive game laws, and all those of the king's officers who represented the hard hand of power that was used often oppressively against the poor. He scorned bishops and archbishops, who grew fat Re on the goods of the people. was generous to the poor, and he was religious in the poor man's fashion, by devotion to the Virgin; for in her the mistaught and oppressed of the Middle Ages—forced to fear power in this world and in the zolzt—found the lost spirit of love within an image of mild, womanly tenderness, and to her, therefore, they prayed for shelter from the wrath of God and man. Robin Hood personified to thousands in England the spirit of liberty in arms against the cruel forest laws, against all tyrannies of toe strong in Church and State, against all luxury fed on the spoils of labour. From the old clays when Hereward the Saxon held the woods in defiance of the Norman kings, there had been stories of bold outlaws who through songs and tales of the country side became heroes to the labour- ing men with more freedom in their souls than in their lives. They were heroes full of wild energy, with rough- ness of the times in much of the adventure set down to them ; but they epresented not an aspiration only, for there was also the vigour of a shrewd practical humour that would in good time refine and raise, and realise all that was best in the ideal of the men who wrote such ballads as that of Robin Hood.—Cassell's Library of English Literature. 0111.0110-LINSSED COUGH LOZENGES, a medicated linseed extract, 6d; postage, 2d. The late Henry Giles, formerly of Liverpool, and one of the lecturers in the famous Unitarian Controversy at Liver- pool, left behind him a number of unpublished essays and lectures. A volume of them is in preparation. A memoir and portrait will preface these papers. We take the following from the Italian Times :—" The 'Academy of Science sends us a note on the discovery in the Vatican Library of a codex of tie ninth century heretofore believed not to exist. It cqntains fragments of the writings of M. T. Cicero, and we are promised an early translation for the readers of the Italian Times." A.marble tablet, placed by the Municipality of Rome on the house, No. 17, Via dei Prefetti, in commemoration of theresidence in it of Samuel Morse, the telegraph inventor, from February, 1825, till January,lB26, has been uncovered in the presence of the authorities, of Mr. Astor, United States minister at Rome, and many American residents and visitors. At the last meeting of the Royal Swedish Geographical Society, says Nature, on the proposal of Baron Nordensk- jold, the greatest honour at the disposal of the Society, the "Vega" gold medal, was conferred on Mr. Stanley. The medal, str,ack in commemoration of the Vega expedition, has been only twice conferred before. In 1881 it was awarded to Baron Nordenskjold, and in 1882 to Captain Palander. Mr. Henry Kerr, of Stacksteads, is preparing for publica- tion, by subscription, "The Birds of Northumberland and Durham." During the past five years Mr. Kerr contributed the articles which will form the work to the Newcastle Weekly Chronicle. Each bird; whether resident, migrant, or casual visitant, will be described, and many of the illus- trations are taken from the avi-fauna of Lancashire. It will form two volumes of about 500 pages each. The following is from Engineering:—" The centennial of the discovery of the balloon by Montgolfier is to be cele- brated in a special manner at Paris on June 5 next. A committee of scientific societies have requested the Muni- cipal Council of Paris to lend its assistance to this fete ; and subscriptions have been opened at Annonay, in Ardeche, to erect a monument to the memory of the brothers Mont- golfier. Already some 32,000 francs have been raised. We also hear that a balloon trip across the Mediterranean is about to be organised, but the details of the attempted voy- age, which will far outstrip the crossing of the Channel by Colonel Burnabp, have not reached us." THE ALLEGED SPEED OF SOLAR PROTUBERANCES.— Spectroscopists who have studied the solar protuberances affirm that the matter of these rises with the tremendous velocities of 80, 100, or 120 leagues per second. M. Faye, however, who has been lately expounding his theory of solar phenomena in the Paris Academy, explains the ap- pearances in the following way :—The protuberantial gas, expanding in space, is enormously cooled, and ceases to be visible; but presently the solar radiation, which amounts to 1,300 to I,so(lcalorius per square metre and per second, heats it again, and renders .it perceptible. The visibility commences at the lower side of the cloud of hydrogen, and progresses upwards to the top. M. Faye holds that it is this phenomena that is propagated with the high velocity just referred to, and not the gas itself. . Co.smicaL DIIST.—We find in the last number of the Izvestia of the Russian Geographical Society a note by Prof. Lenz on the costnical dust collected by M. Marx at the meteorological station at Yeniseisk. Aster having vainly searched for traces of comical matter, as he was ad- vised to do by Baron Nordenskjold, he discovered it finally on October 31, 1881. The wind was blowing in the even- ing with great force from the west, and durinc, the night it turned into a strong gale, with some snow anfrain. When M. Marx measured next morning the amount of water in his pluviometer he remarked that it had a considerable quantity of suspended matter of a brick-red colour. After careful . analysis this matter proved to consist of iron, nickel, and cobalt. Prof. Lenz does not doubt that the red dust found by M. Marx had a cosmical origin, and points out that it was observed on a day very near to the appear- ance of the November meteors.—Nature. _ _ _

A NEW CARTRIDGE.—An entirely novel cartridge has been tried in America. According to the inventor, the cart- ridge will not heat the gun, it is self-ejecting, has twice the propelling force of powder, and is much cheaper. It will also cost very much less than metallic cartridges of gunpow- der, and will not be injured by water. Its materials and mode of preparation are secrets, but in appearance it is like paper pulp soaked in some explosive material, and pressed into a hard roll. The ball is attached to the end of the roll, and the whole thing leaves the gun together, on the sky- rocket principle. It may be adapted to any gun, and is to revolutionise the ordnance departments "of the world. At the trial, the inventor fired one of the ball cartridges into a spruce log eight inches thick. The ball passed entirely through the log and a two inch plank behind it, and flattened against a stone wall. After firing 12 rounds out of the same gun, there was no apparent heat and no fouling. A more scientific and satisfactory test is shortly to be made by government experts.—lron. . MEDICINAL PiANTS.—The new number of the Journal of the Linnean Society, issued this week, contains an abstract of the paper by Captain Armit on certain plants of North- western Queensland possessing valuable medicinal qualities, and used by the aborigines for specific purposes. In many cases Captain Armit found, on experimenting in Queensland, that the reputation of many of the plants amongst the na- tives rested on faith alone; in some cases, however, it was well founded. The leaves of • Gretaia polyyama yielded a decoction which effected " traly_magical " cures in cases of ague and dysentery. Captain Armit has never foutfd it to fail, though he has tried it in scores of cases, and he justly remarks that the importance of possessing a specific against the most insidious disease to which Europeans are exposed in tropical countries cannot be exaggerated. The leaves of Careya arborea, reduced to a pulp, and applied to ulcers resulting from blood poisoning,-the poultice being renewed four times per diem, have proved equally efficacious. Ery- threa australis yields a useful tonic in febrile complaints; the dried bark of Pettilostigma guadriloculare administered in lOgr. doses three times per- diem is a useful remedy in low or intermittent fevers, and the ripe fruit is a valuable vermifuge in horses. Andropoyan cams makes a useful tea in fevers. Euphorbia paulifera is largely used in Queensland by all who suffer from asthma. The aborigines use several species of Malvaceous shrubs medicinally. Ant GAS.—An ingenious method of gas manufacture, resulting in a very good light, has recently been perfected by Colonel Chamberlain. The materials from which the gas is made is petroleum, water, and air, and the process is simple, cleanly, and apparently safe. The petroleum, which is of high quality, is stored in one compartment of a divided tank, the water being stored in the other compartment. The generator consists of a cast-iron retort, so fixed in the body of a furnace that the the heat is conducted both under and over it, the fuel being coke. The oil and water are 4-1-• • • - - ' -four drops of oil retort. Ldrou6. pipes by drops, being fed in to one drop of water. As the oil and water are decomposed the resulting gas is led away through a pipe to a washer. This consists of an iron close tank Con- taining water and fitted with vertical divided plates, so arranged that the gas passes alternately under and over them through the wtter on its way to the gas-holder, where it is stored for use. As soon as a sufficient quantity of gas has been made and stored the oil and water is turned'off, and a jet of air is forced into the retort by means of a small Root's blower. This air is also decomposed, and, following the course of the oil and water gas through the washer, finally joins it in the holder, having picked up on its way any gas remaining in the retort or in the washer. The air is added in the proportion of three of air to one of the gas already made. The resulting gas is stated to be of 21 candle power, and to possess the qualities of elasticity and perman- ence. Various trials have shown it to be a good travelling gas and free from humidity and deposit. It is reported to contain no sulphur and only a trace of carbonic acid, to deposit no soot or other impurity in use, and to cost only is. 6d. per 1,000 cubic feet to produce, all expenses included. These good points—save that of cost—are for the most part demonstrated by means of a gas-producer which has been fitted up at No. 10, Lower Belgrave-street, Eaton-square. The furnace is about Bit. square in plan and 4ft. high, and is stated to be capable of producing 100 cubic feet of gas per hour. The good quality_ of the light is shown by colour tests, and its innocuous chafracter by the healthiness of some plants and shrubs, which are unaffected by its daily manu- facture and use. It has already been adopted in the country mansion, and there is no apparent reason why, with care in manufacture, it should not do good service where coal gas or other source of- artificial light is either expensive or unobtainable.

CAMPING Our.—Any one who has travelled by small canoes on the sea must remember those happy camping times when, often wet, and always hungry and tired, the little party cautiously selected some sheltered nook, or spe- cially good beach, and then paddled with a will ashore. No lack of drift-wood or small trees on that coast, and no lord of the manor to interfere with one taking it. A -glorious fire is soon raised, and the cooking preparations commenced. Sometimes it is only the stereotyped tea—frying-pan bread (something like the Australian "damper," only baked before the fire), or "slap-jacks" (i.e., flour-and-water pancakes), fried bacon, and boiled Chili beans; but ofttimes it can be, varied by excellent fish, game, bear-meat, venison, or moose- meat, purchased from some passing Indians, or killed by themselves. It is absurd to suppose that "roughing it' need mean hardship and. semi-starvation all the time. Not a bit of it! On the northern coasts now being described one may often live magnificently, and most travellers learn instinctively to cook, and make the most of things. Nothing is finer in camp than a roast fish—say a salmon—split and gutted, and stuck on a stick before the fire, not over it. A few dozen turns, and you have a dish worthy of a prince. Or a composition stew—say of deer and bear-meat and beaver's tail well-seasoned, and with such vegetables as you may obtain there; potatoes from some sea-side farm—and there are such on that coast, where the settler is as brown as his Indian wife—or compressed vegetables, often taken on exploring expeditions. Or, again, venison dipped in a thick batter, and thrown into a pan of boiling-hot fat, making a kind of meat fritter, with not a drop of its juices wasted. Some of these explorers and miners are veritable chefs. They- can make good light bread in the woods from plain flour, water, and salt, and ask no oven but a frying- pan. They will make beans, of a kind only given to horses at home, into a delicious dish, by boiling them soft—along job, generally done at the night camp, and then frying them with bread-crumbs and pieces of bacon in the morning, till they are brown and crisp.—From The Sea: its Stirring Story of Adventure, Peril, and Heroism, for ilfarch.

• Cvntors RESULT OF THE WET SEASON.—WO are credibly informed (says the Dorset Chronicle) that last week the attention of Mr. Martin Small, the well-known farmer in the parish of Shapwick, -was called by IliS shepherd to one of the sheep, all along the back of which grass was springing up. It is conjectured that the animal, having been supplied with hay, had lain down on some of it, and the seeds, mixing with the wool, germinated through the sheep having been exposed to rain for a very long period. THE GROWTH OF GRASS IN TowNs.—Mr. G. E. Davis, one of her Majesty's inspectors of alkali works, in an in- teresting paper on the growth of grass in towns, read be- fore the Society of Chemical Industry, says :—"Amongst the products of combustion is found sulphurous acid. This in time becomes sulphuric acid, and is carried down in the rain, making it almost impossible for vegetation of any kind to live in a large town. It does not seem to be gene- rally knbwn that lime is an antidote to this gas, and if a lawn were watered once or twice a year with milk of lime it would be possible to have a very decent looking green sward, even round the Manchester Infirmary. The drip- pings from trees and shrubs in a large town are always acid, and these, falling in a circle described within the branches, prevent the grass growing near, but if the ground be well manured (a process often forgotten in towns) and well limed or treated with milk of chalk, the grass can be made to grow up to the very tree trunks." Vegetation can only be kept thriving by the manures which are rendered necessary by the conditions under which it is called upon to exist, whether of soil or climate, and the chemist can always find a counter agent to maintain the balance of nature. It is merely a question of cost. _

SELLING FAT CATTLE PRIVATELY BY LIVE WEIGHT.— The agricultural correspondent of the .Dumfries Courier, alluding to the derangement of the cattle trade in conse- quence of the restrictions, says :—One result of the present interruption of the ordinary media of disposing of fat stock should be the extension, and, indeed, the general adoption of private sale of such beasts according to live weight. It is the fairest way between buyer and seller, making the fluc- tuation in the returns received by sellers less, and, more- over, curtailing the profit pocketed by the middleman, who acts as.the agent between buyer and seller. An enterprising farmer in the south of Scotland recently sold half a dozen fat cattle to a Liverpool butcher, the particulars of which we take the liberty of quoting for the benefit of our readers. The bargain made between buyer and seller was that the animals were to be weighed at the farm before a meal, and that the feeder was to be paid on the assumption that every 1001bs. weight would yield 531bs. of dressed beef. The rate fixed was 10s. 6d. per stone—that is, 9d. per lb.—for beef, which, according to the abo-Ve" proportion between live and dead weight, is equivalent to 41d. per lb. live weight. The following is the result of the experiment. We may explain that the live weight is the gross weight of each before a meal, that the estimated weight is calculated according to the above proportion of 531bs dressed meat for 1001bs. live weight, and that the actual carcase weight was ascertained in the scales after they had been killed in Liverpool : • Estimated Actual . Live carcase carcase • weight, weight. weight. No. lbs. lbs. lbs. 1. a. • 4. 6. 2,357 2,410 Nos. 2 and 5 were not killed for three or four days later. The _figures in their cases were:—
No: lbs. lbs. lbs. 2. 5. 1,151 1,141 The following is a summary of the lot : -

• - 6,605 - 3,498 3,551 This gives a proportion of 5311b5. dead weight to 1001bs. live weight, but it will be seen that the actual carcase weight in the four beasts killed soon after they came off their journey was in every case decidedly above the esti- mated weight, whereas in the other two, which had been partially starved for a time, the ascertained weight was slightly under the estimate. Thus the strong presumption is that had every beast been slaughtered without delay the result would have been even more satisfactory. Now, these figures illustrate very well what the practical working of such a system would be. The butcher who bought the beasts had no reason to be dissatisfied with his bargain, for it Wiled out better than the estimate on which it was con- cluded.. The seller had no cause to complain for he got value for his beefers ; and there was • this further ,valuable feature in the transaction to him, that there was no un- certainty in the amount he was to receive, as there always is when animals are sold by pure guesswork in an auction mart, or in any market where the scales are not made use of. The cost of conveying the cattle to Liverpool amounted only to Bs. per head, and the butcher lost none of his own tinaea.nd incurred no-ekpense in effecting the purchase. Why cannot other farmers, espeoially in these times of restriction on the movement of cattle, go and do likewise? STocx TENDEUS.—" If one decides hastily with any beast in trouble one decides wrong," should be one maxim of force, in all cases dealing with herds and flocks; and "never take a beast by surprise" should be another, i.e., let every animal see and have time to recognise what one is going to do. A certain slow, tentative way of moving, even down to forming an opinion, Was characteristic of the old stamp of sarm-folk. They arrived at conclusions more from sympathy with their charge than through any consciously reasoning process. They never were in a hurry, therefore they had little to undo. What they did was wisely done, and this slow, almost dawdling, way of proceeding is, of all others, that which suits the better stamp of neat stock best. No living thing does so badly under hurry and worry as does a cow; and no living thing makes a better return for quiet and patient help than the same animal. To be good cattle-tenders one must begin at the beginning, and learn the elementary part of one's training at the side of a mach animal. We have known really clever, active, industrious !men to fail as cattle attendants; but never sone of the quaint, staid type of humanity which, to this hour, goes by the name of "old-fashioned.". Is it that these men know less? is it not rather that they feel more? Certainly want of knowledge is not—let any anti-school men say what they like—any assistant; but want of sympathetic insight almost amounts to a disqualification, and so does constitutional irritability. In a considerable experience we have never known, even"with the fiercest bull, one of the slow-moving, regular, attendants hurt. It is the quick, jerky conceit of the biped which makes the huge quadruped occasionally re- member that, after all, he is the stronger. The very best cattle tender we ever saw was an old man, who would pro- bably have been called an idiot. He couln't even count ten. There were 20 cows under his charge, and his only way of finding whether they were all right in the field was going over the herd "you and your partner" (they stood in 'Sails, two to a stall), and so checking each pair by a finger or, a thumb till he had made on his nomber. His old master was the talk of the district for his wonderful luck with his cows. He had more and bettebcalves, and more and better butter than any ono round .the country-side. He never failed to give the crealt to the right quarter, i.e., to the old herds- man, and used to say of him,," He was brought up with the cows; he is almost an animal himself, and he knows cattle talk.' " It really seemed so. No change occurred in the cattle that this old fellow did not detect at once; no beast so sick but would lie down and rest when he had waited on it. One of the earliest things remembered by us is an eager discussion how a certain wild brute of a bull should be in- duced to leave a pasture, through which a public road ran, into which he had broken, and return back to his stall. All kinds of plans were suggested, even to sending for the yeomanry (they were on drill in the next parish) to come and shoot the bull. Someone, wiser than the rest, said "Tel/- old Sam to do it." The difficulty was to get the old man to understand what was wanted. All that he did grasp was that, for some reason, milking time was come sooner than usual. He called the cows in his usual way; the bull came with them to the homestead. When in the ruck with them the bull was followed and easily got into the yard, but not his own keeper dare try to separate the bull from the cows and tie him up in his place. Sam without being told took up the pail with which this bull had used to be watered) into the yard, into the box, and the bull followed him at once. The soundest and widest reasonin,, could not have dictated a better plan. Sam arrived at the same conclusion without any reasoning at all. What was the qualification of this man for his calling? Was it not his complete sympathy with his charge his recognition that they had individual peculiarities ? It is the tendency of all modern training to take for granted that beasts—and men—are all alike • and, if they be not, to try. and force them to behave as if they were. Except to a very limited extent this assumption is not true, and this endeavour is not wise. That leader of men (and tender of live stock) succeeds best who is not only tolerant, but is ready to encourage individuality. Cattle soon get to know that thefel a difference in men, if men will,not notice that there are peculiarities in .each beast.— .4gricultU7'al Gazette.

David Williams (the celebrated " Pablieola"), being on one occasion at an assembly, observed that whenever he ap- proached a group of people, they were all seized with violent fits of sneezing, and to such an extent that he speedily left for home in dudgeon. On- relating the case to his sister, she laughed, and pointing to his dress-hat, made of beaver, said, "Therein lies the explanation. To avoid any danger from moth, I peppered the hat well." Publicola remem- bered he had, in the course of conversation, waved his hat About, and also struck his person with it, and so caused the peppery particles to escape. _

Veitrenix Don.---ir Edwin Landseer is accredited with the following jeu d'esprit: The sagacity of several retriever dogs was being discussed in his presence. "Not one yet mentioned to come up to mine," said he, "and as thus: Upon a certain occasion I showed him a five-pound note of a well-known county-town bank, near to which I Was residing. I rolled up the note, putt into my pocket, walked into the woods, hid it in the trunk of a tree, then strolled on for a mile or so, the dog at my heels. 'Back, find, and bring, Troyer,' I said; and the dog was off like a shot. I waited, and waited, and waited for a considerable time but no Troyer. Presently, however, he came—but without the note' "Hi back, find, and bring,' I repeated, or you shall know what stick means.' But instead of doing my bidding the animal came quite close to me, and dropped from his mouth, at my feet, one after the ,other, five brand-new golden sovereigns. He had not only found the note, airs, but had gone to thetank and changed it. The intelligence of my retriever eclipses even that of the cele- brated pointed Mr. Jingle of Pickwickian renown once pos- sessed.'

HOUSEHOLD PETS.

DOGS,-,—THE GREYHOUND.—Greyhounds are much more sought after from a sporting point of vie-w than an orna- mental one, but as a good greyhound is generally good- looking, there is no reason why they should net be favour- ites as pets. To make a really good dog, there are several chief requisites, namely, a deep chest, sloping shoulders, muscular quarters, and well-made hind legs, with well-bent stifles, and without these speed and stamina are not to be obtained. The legs must not be fleshy, or the dogs will soon be found to tire in a long.course. The neck should be light, but long and round; the head rather large—riot very high, between the highs and ears, for intelligence does not need to be .very highly developed, but there should be a good width behind the ears; the jaws should be clean cut and lean, the upper jaw fitting into the lower one, for a pig jaw is deemed objectionable; the eyes need to be bright and animated in their expression; the ears small and neat, and the teeth large, strong, and white; the shoulders, as already stated', sloping, also amscular, but not at all loaded or thick. The toe nails are required short and strong, and the points are generally cut off with a sharp pair of scis- sors when the animal is about three weeks old. The back should be strong with a ridge of muscle on each side the back bone, the length extending from shoulder to last rib; 'the loins should be strong and muscular; the hind quarters wide and thick, and, in action, the hocks not approaching , each other; the stifles need to be strong and neatly arched 'or bent ; the toes close together, flat feet being deemed very , objectionable; and the tail fine and strong. For colour, any ' kind will do, but blacks, reds, and fawns are the favourites. The weights vary greatly, dogs ranging from 50 to nearly 80 lbs.; bitches 36 to 60 lbs., 60 lbs. in dogs and a little over 50 in bitches being average weights. Greyhounds need careful training, and on this account they are generally placed under the care of professional trainers, a very neces- sary thing to do. SNAICES.—BUILDING A CAGE.—We have known snakes kept in an ordinary drawer, but it N much safer and better to have a proper cage, in which the habits and movements of the reptiles can be watched. For general purposes one 3ft. 6in. long, 2ft. Bin. wide, and height inside from gravel to cover 2ft. 4in. will be found enough. It should be made entirely of glass and metal. The ends, front and back should be of thick plate glass, and the top of perforated zinc. The ends can be each in one piece, but the front and back should be in two pieces to give the necessary strength. ,The edges or framework should be of metal, sufficiently strong to Te- sist a large amount of pressure, and the top, which should be made with half a dozen strong hinges or screw fasteners at the back, and two or three staples at the front, should fit closely over the top of the sides like the lid of a biscuit box. These staples are most necessary, or the snakes will be able to force their way out by prizing up the lid. One end of the cage should be made to elide up to facilitate cleaning, but it is most necessary to see that every movable portion of the cage fits closely and does not offer an opening for the reptiles. The floor is best made of perforated zinc, but it should be covered to the depth of an inch with gravel. Be- low the floor there must be a cistern for holding hot water, which either may be a portion of the structure or separate from it. This tank is a most important part of the whole, and is necessary to maintain th'e temperature of the cage. The larger the size of this cistern the better, as the greater the body of water the longer will it maintain the heat, and in an ordinary room one holding about 30 gallons of water can be kept up by a kettleful of boiling water being added thereto once a day, of course as much being taken out. This tank must be embedded all but the top in some nonconduct- ing material such as felt or sawdust packed tightly in, and have two taps in,front, one as an inlet near the top, and the other as an outlet at the bottom. Between the top of this tank and the bottom of the cage a space of an inch and a half should be left, in which a tray filled with coarse dry earth or sand must be placed, and closed by a door in front. This tray will drain and purify the cage, regulate the heat, and prevent the accumulation of moisture, and will need replenishing once a week. That doneAe cage will be corn- plete.

RABBITS —FATTENiNG.—Just now a most important thing is to get rid of all surplus stock, so as to leave the hutches free for the young one as they come on. As this is the case with nearly all rabbit keepers, animals are difficult to sell, and the best thing is to fatten them up and kill off for table purposes. As a rule it will in found that fattening the smaller varieties does not pay, but in the case of the larger ones they can be fed up to a very great size. Six or eight of the animals can be put together in a large hatch. For food it will be found that barley meal is the cheapest and most rapid fattener of all, but to it should be added boiled potatoes or tea leaves. This may be regarded as the staple food, yet as much variety as is possible should be, introduced. It mast be remembered that rabbits cannot be crammed with food as can fowls, and, therefore, it is all the more needful that they should be tempted to eat it by offer- ing to them as great a variety of food as possible. As soon as a rabbit is fat or begins to regard the food placed before it with any degree of aversion, it had better be killed. Variations from the barley meal may be found in boiled peas, oatmeal, and a little Indian meal, and now and again a little spice, as well as the tea leaves, should be mixed with the same. Green food must on no account be omitted. In winter, when it is scarce, boiled roots can be given in place of it.

MICE.—FBEDING.—The food of mice when at libetty con- sists of grain, nuts, and seeds for those• who live out of doors, but when indoors bread, meat, cheese, and; in fact, anything that can be picked up. The great thing neces- sary is to see that their food is clean, and not calculated to make them gross and fat. As a staple food stale bread soaked in milk, and oats and bran, with an occasional change to canary seed or millet, are the best. 'Wheat should not be given, nor yet hemp, linseed, rape, mustard, or any very oily seeds. In preparing the milk and bread crumble the bread, which should be at least three days old, into a cup or basin, and pour scalding hot milk over it just sufficient to soak it well without being sloppy, Feed regularly once a day with this, and when the mice cease eating remove the tin, and throw in some oats or canary seed. During the winter a small portion of suet, chopped fine, or lean meat well boiled and chopped up, should be given once or twice a week, with canary or millet seed instead of oats. Water will not be needed where the milk and bread is the food, but .if dry food is provided instead, the!i it should be sup Pied. When flowering grass can rre had,lhen a few blades should be given, but if not then a piece or two of carrot will be relished. One most important matter in the feeding of these pets is to see that the tins are properly scalded out, so as to prevent all sourness.

"Mrs. Miiiin," said a visitor, "Emma has your features, but I think she has got her father's hair." "Oh, now I see," said the dear little Emma ; "it's because I have father's hair that he has to wear a wig." "ENFANT TERRlBLE."—Grandmamma (maternal) : What a fidget you are, George! What are you looking about for now? Grandson: Grarema, where's that—l was looking for that "miserable table" pa' says you keep.—Punch. A Philadelphia girl refused to marry a young man until she accidentally discovered that his hair and moustache were dyed. Then she blushingly cousented. She knew she could throw that up to him if he ever found out that she had a glass eye.

"Your future husband seems very exacting; he has been stipulating for all sorts of things," said a mother to her daughter, who was on the point of being married. "Never mind, mamma," said the affectionate girl, who was already dressed for the wedding, " these are his last wishes." Fred Flasher and Miss Florentine Flounce were discussing the mental power of controlling thought. Said Flasher, "I will give you a pair of gloves if you think of positively nothing for fire minutes, and still be awake." "Done," she responded. Five minutes passed. "I won the gloves !" she exclaimed. "How did you manage to. think of nothing for the whole five minutes ?" he asked eagerly. "I fastened my mind firmly on your moustache, and kept it there," she replied triumphantly. The referee awarded her the gloves. /lOW DO You KEEP Youn Room P—A look into the chamber of a boy or girl will give one an idea of what kind of a man or woman he or she will prctbably become. A boy who keeps his clothes hung up neatly, or a girl whose room is neat always, will be apt to make a successful man or woman. Order and neatness are essential to our comiort as well as that of others about us. A boy who throws down his cap or boots anywhere will never keep his accounts in shape, will do things in a slovenly, careless way, and not be long wanted in any position. A girl who does not make her bed until after dinner—and she should always make it herself rather than have a servant do it—and throws her dress or bonnet down on a chair, will make a poor wife in nine cases out of ten. If the world could see how a girl keeps her dressing-room, some unhappy marriages would be saved.—Congregationalist.

THE BORDESLEY RITUAL CASE.—The church at Bordes- ley in which, until'his inhibition a few days ago, Mr. En- raght officiated, was on Sunday morning the scene of a dis- graceful disturbance,on the occasion of the newly-appointed. vicar, the Rev. H. Allan Watts, reading himself in. On Mr Watts entering the vestry a protest acmias6 his administra- tions was handed to him, on behalf of the old vicar's ritual- istic sympathisers, and when he passed from the vestry into the church he was greeted with a storm of hisses and cries of "Traitor." The old choir having resigned, a new set of singers had to be organised, and when the Litany came to be sung the choral malcontents made a counter demonstra- tion, with the object of drowning the voices of their suc- cessors. From this point to the end of the service the pro- ceedings were of the most disorderly nature, the ritualists breaking out in derisive laughter and shouts, interspersed with pieces of " gag " from a local pantomime, and also some profane language. .The greater part of the " readin e in" was so much dumb show. When the Vicar left the building the disturbance was renewed even more violently in the churchyard, and, but for the protection of the police, Mr. Watts would no doubt have been severely maltreated. It was deemed necessary to place a number of constables on guard at the rev, gentleman's residence in order to protect the house from damage. At the evening service there were again distureances of a scandalous character. There were several free fights, and a number of brawlers were ex- pelled from the church by the police. Several men left the place with blackened eyes and bleeding noses. From 50 to 60 police officers were on duty in and about the church:

Two Bengalee ladies have successfully passed the B.A. degree examination at the Calcutta University. Madame Christine Nilsson is singing in Canada. She will be the Marquis of Lorne's guest at Qttawa. The strength of the British army of occupation in Egypt will shortly be reduced to 0,000 men. Two line regiments, a battery, and a company of engineers have received orders to return.
An OttGiVit telegram sties that Mr. W. E. Falter, M.P., will, in October next, succeed the Marquis of Lorne as Governor-General of Canada.
Several persons have been killed by the falling of the roof of one of the wings of the Payret Theatre at Havana during a heavy fall of rain..

Commercial advice' s just received at Liverpool report that a very extensive fire is raging at Iquique, the great nitre port on the coast of South America. There is reason to believe that the Porte will shortly pro- nounce on the question of the passage through the Darda- n alles of yachts flying the British flag. A registered letter carrier was murdered at Berlin on Tuesday, and a sum of about five thousand marks which he had in his possession was stolen. His body was found on Wednesday, but at present there is no clue to the assassin. It appears from information received in Athens that the Porte insists that the exclusive right to carry on the coast- ing trade in the Sea of Marmora belongs to vessels flying the Ottoman flag. Our Foreige Office has, of coarse, repudiated this pretension.

It is stated that to providesfor the concentration of 50,000 troops at Moscow during the coronation, the Ministry of War will allow a credit of 2,500,000 roubles; and for the extra accommodation for staff officers and military representatives from Russia's Asiatic dominions another 100,000.roubles. A member of the Auscrian Reichsrath is to be prosecuted for having taken part in a students' demonstration in favour of the incorporation of the German subjects of Austria in the Germanic Empire. The penalty for "disturbing 'public order" is severe.

• The Vienna Town Council on Tuesday resolved to hold an international exhibition there next year of articles ap- pertaining to city improvements, and have voted a sum of 100,000 florins for that purpose. The municipalities of all the towns of Europe, Americ.i, and Australia will be invited to take part in the exhibition,

The result of the inquiry into the charges made against Signor Amid, an interpreter of the British Vice-Consul at Castblanca, who recently superintended the public flogging of a number of girls at that place, has resulted in the facts as stated being established. Amid l has been dismissed from the office of interpreter to the Vice-Consulate, by order of he British Minister, Sir John Hat. .

.Maitre Lachaud, the famous advocate, who was retained to defend Prince Napoleon, has published a pamphlet in which the origin of the manifesto is explained, and an ac- count given of the treatment to which the Prince was sub- jected in prison. The pamphlet, says a Paris correspondent, is written throughout in a tone of contemptuous hostility to the Government.

SUICIDE OF A RUSSIAN MilasTsu.—Details are published at St. Petersburg concerning the suicide of M. Makoff, ex- Minister of the Interior. They state that on the evening of the 11th inst. the deceased received a visit, and when after- wards left alone he wrote some letters before committing the act of self-destruction. On the room of the deceased being entered, a Bible was found on his writing table. The suicide was apparently premeditated,every arrangement having been made and all private affairs put in order beforehand. Death appears to have been instantaneous, the bullet remaining lodged in the skull. M. Makoff leaves a widow, two daugh- ters. and a son. •

• MURDER OF AN OFFICER IN INDIA.—A. despatch from Al- lahabad, dated February 19, says :—Lieutenant Coode, act- ing adjutant, 2nd Lincolnshire Regiment, was shot dead by a soldier named C3ghlan, of the same regiment, at Benares, on the 17th inst. The murderer, with his rifle and ball amunition, deliberately opened fire upon some companies drawn up on the parade ground. A soldier was wounded in the leg. Lieutenant Coode then rode at the man, who stood his ground and. fired two shots, the first killing lieutenant Coode's horse and the second killing the officer. He was afterwards disarmed and arrested by a comraae. The mur- derer said he had been suffering from delirium tremens. Lieutenant Coode was the only officer at evening parade. Private Tilly was shot in' the legs, and is not yet out of danger. Coghlan was regarded as a man generally steady. THE NAVIGATION OF THH Dearrne.—The agreement at, rived at on the question of the Danube has been embodied in a treaty, which was signed by all the plenipotentaries on Saturday. The mandate of the European Commission has been extended for 21 years, with a power of perpetual re- newal; the jurisdiction of the Commission has been extended un to Braila, and the river from that point to the Iron. Gate has been placed under the control of a Mixed or Rivirain Commission, consisting of the representatives of Austria- Hungary, Roumania, Servia, and Bulgaria, with one mem- ber appointed by the European Commission. The Mixed Commission will administer the riglernext drawn up by the European Commission for that purpose under the terms of the Berlin treaty. Concessions in regard to those branches_ of the stream which are on Russian or Roumanian territory have been made, but entirely subject to the approval of the Powers as to the works and tolls. The articles of the treaties of 1815, of 1856, and of 1878 have been confirmed. DBATH OF PRINCB GORTSCHAKOFF.—Prince Gortschakoff died at Baden-Baden at four o'clock on Sunday morning. The deceased statesman was born in 1798, and educated at the Lyceum of Zarskoe-Selo. According to 'Men of the Time" he commenced his diplomatic life at the Congresses of Laybach and Verona, in the capacity of attacho to Count Nesselrode ; was secretary to the Russian embassy in Lon- don in 1824, charged' affaires to the court of Tuscany in 1830, and was attached for the first time, in 1832, to the legation at Vienna, where the death of his superior, the Russian ambassador, gave him great influence. In 1841 he was sent on a mission to Stuttgard, where he negotiated the marriage of the Grand ' Duchess Olga of Russia with the Prince Royal of Wurtemburg. During the events of 1848-9 Prince Gortchakoff maintained a dignified neutrality, but it is rumoured that in .1850 he exercised some influence in procuring the abdication of the Emperor Ferlinand I. in favour of his nephew, Francis Joseph. During the dispute respecting the Eastern ques- tion, the prince was ambassador at Vienna; at his instance the Russian Government accepted the four points which formed the basis of the Conference of Paris in 1856, and he was recalled to St. Petersburg in that year, to replace Nes- selrode as Minister for Foreign Affairs. A proclamation of hie, very hostile to the Western Powers, during the Sicilian and Neapolitan revolution, excited much attention, and his policy during the Polish insurrection tif 1863 has been freely Commented upon. In October, 1870, while Paris was being besieged by the Germans, Prince Gortschakoff issued a circular to the representatives of Russia abroad, an- nouncing the resolution of the Emperor to be no longer con- trolled by the treaty of 1856 so far- as it limited his rights of severeignity in the Black Sea. This led to the Confer- ence held in London in 1871, when the treaty was modified so as to satisfy the demands of Russia. In recognition of his services on this occasion Prince Gortschakoff was ac- credited with the rank of Highness. He was one of the Russian Plenipotentiaries at the Congress of Berlin in 1878.

Soon after, Johnson, after a fine run, got over near the corner .flag: he was, however, rolled in play. Nothing save minor points were furtker added. ZiA.TDOCK TEMPERANCE V. ST. THOMAS'S (Sr. HELENS )—TIIB return match between the Ist teams of the above clubs was played on the ground of tha former on Saturday last. The captain of the home team having won choice of ends deoided to play with the ground slightly sloping down hill in theirfavour. After commereing pay in seven minutes time the home team assured their firsts goal, wit:eh was shortly followed by the visitors, making the score equal. As t lay went on the super- iority of the home team soon manifested itself ft om the fact that most of the play was carried on in the visitors quarters. How- ever, owing to the good play of Tvrer in goat the home team were prevented from adding more than one more goal before ends were changed. At the call of half time the se ,re Was for the home team two goals against one. On resuming play, the visitots having changed their goalkeeper. the home team set to work in earnest and soon became complete masters of the posi- tion, and sun faceted in adding six more goals to the score. At the call of time the Tempetance team were victors by eight goals to one.

div.p: SCOTCH SAYINGS—Some interesting information is to be found in the returns just issued in connection with the Post- office Savings Banks is Scotland. It would appear from these returns that, during the past ten years, notwithstand- ing periods of considerable depression in trade, the amount of the deposit savings in almost every county has nearly doubled. In some cases the total amount was more than doubled. In Argyllshire, for example, the amount at the close of last year stood at £20,637 in round numbers, as against £11,975 in 1873 ; Aberdeen, £51,541, against £27,569; Ayr, £55,498, against £37,262; Berwick, £16,115, against £7,399; Bute, £5,306, against £1,709; Caitkness, £5.990, against £2,808; Clackmannon £7,991, against £4,604; Cromarty, £1,050, against Z 263 ; Edinburgh, £70,597, against £37,872; Kincardine, £6,950, against £2,783; Kirkcudbright, £10,856, against £4,959; Moray, £17,010, against £8,210; Nairn, £2,260, against £872; Ross, £19,301, against £7,560; Sutherland, £5,991, against £2,894; and Wigtown, £11,402, against £5,493. There was also a large increase in the counties of Dumbarton, Dum- fries Inverness, Kinross, Linlithgoe, Perth, Renfrgw, Rox- burgh, Selkirk, Stirling, and even in the counties so far north as Shetland and Orkney. Lanark (including Glas- gow) was the county in which the least increase was registered, but there the deposits rose from £75,087 in 1873 to £99,609 in 1882,

div.head: IRISH MURDERS.
div.p: THE IRISH MURDERS.
ARREST OF A CRIMINAL IN ST. HELENS.

It appears that the rumours which have from time to time been in circulation that Irish detectives were prosecu- ting inquiries in St. Helens, have not been without founda- tion, and it now transpires that a man, who, by his own confession, has been implicated in one Irish murder, has been living for some time in this locality. John Walsh, who, as reported within the last few days, had been con- cerned in the murder of the young woman Esther Croughan, at Dist .town, near Mullingar, on the 31st December, 1881, and in connection with which it is stated he has turned in- former, has up till quite recently been employed at Mesars. Kurtz' s chemical works in this town. On the sth Jan., it is stated, a member of the Royal Trish Constabulary,stationed at Mullingar, accompanied by a detective from Liverpool, came over to St. Helens and placed themselves in communication with Superintendent Johnston, chief of the local division of the county constabulary, their object being to ascertain the whereabouts of a person named John Walsh, who, it was believed, could give valuable information concerning the murder of Esther Croughan, at Irishtown, near Mullingar, on the 31st December, 1881. The local authorities took the matter in band, Inspector Wood being instructed to make inquiries. The inspector, who has been in the division 15 or 16 years, and has a thorough knowledge both of, the„town and its inhabitants, very quietly and .discreetly proceeded with his work, and eventually ascertained that a man bearing the name and answering the description of Walsh was working at Messrs. Kurtz's chemical works as a labourer, and residing with his I wife and three children, and several lodgers, at 71, Bolton- street, Parr. This intelligence was at once foruarded by Superintendent Johnston to the Irish Detective Department, and the officer, whose name was Fitzgerald, again came over to St. Helens, and had an interview with Walsh. It is believed that at that interview Walsh confessed to being in possession of some knowledge that would throw light upon ' the tragedy, and consented to go back to Ireland as a wit- ness, it being arranged that the journey should be under- taken ir. about a fortnight's time. This was done presumably to allow him to leave his situation in the ordinary manner, and get him away without attraceing undue attention to the circumstance, he having, it is said, "borne a good charac- ter," and had presented testimonials which he had obtained in Ireland when he applied for work. On the 9th ult, the officers came again, and Walsh, accom- panied by his wife and three children, proceeded to Liverpool, and crossed to Ireland. Very few pecple knew of the circumstance, the house being kept on by one of the lodgers, who was given to understand that Walsh would be back in about a fortnight or a few weeks at the latest. Last week, however, the few " effects" left behind were packed up and forwarded by the St. Helens police to Ireland and the house turned over to the landlotd. Walsh, who had the appearance of a decent, hardworking man, came over to St. Helens at the beginning of January, immediately after the murder of the unfortunate girl, and soon found employ- ment, no one suspecting that he had played any part in the terrible crime. The facts of the crime as they are reported to have been confessed by Walsh himself, are that he was employed by the murdered girl's sister, Jane Croughan, who promised to "pay him well" if he would do away with her sister Esther. Walsh undertook the job, , but did dot commit the actual murder himself. He employed a man named Lawrence Kenny (who is at present under a sentence of penal servitude for life for shooting at a soldier) and Michael Kane (who is in custody) for tLat purpose. On the morning of the mutder Kenny and Kane went to Croughan's house, and, whilst Kane watched outside, Kenny I went in and shot the murdered girl, afterwards throwing the revolver into a pond near by. ' According to Walsh's statement he lent the revolver with which the murder was committed to Kenny, and he further stated that he had lent the same weapon on a previous occasion to another man named Turrissy for the purpose, he believed, of com- mitting a similar act.

Mr. Enraght, it is said, has decided to obey the Bishop's inhibition, and not again to enter the church at Bordesley. Mr. Bradlaugh, M.P., has signified his intention of writing a public letter to Mr. Justice North on the manner in which the Freethinker prosecution was conducted. The sea wall at Salthurn was almost washed away to the foundations on Sunday night, and the promenade pier was damaged. There are now 11 breaches in the bank of the haven of the liver Witham, and quite 2,000 acres, most of which were lOwn with wheat, under water. There was an unusually high tide at Yarmouth on Sun- 'Y night, but it was small compared with the one which visited the town last week. Nine of the cars of the Glasgow Tramway Company 'Were, on Sunday, destroyed 'by fire which broke out on the ,t;IP story of the eastern district depot, and did darr.age to Me extent of £lO,OOO. Several members Of Parliament have each taken £5,000 worth of shares.
