The estimates for the civil service and revenue depart- ments show a net increase of £268,125. A cotton mill at Smallbridge, Rochdale, belonging to Mr. Edward Healey was burned down on Tuesday. The loss of property is estimated at £B,OOO. Judgment was on Tuesday given at Alfreton County Court for Ll' 50 against the Blackwell Colliery Company by a collier who sought compensation for injuries caused by a a cage breaking. A lady named Bullock has obtained a verdict for £1,300 against the South-Eastern Railway Company as compensa- tion for personal injuries. The train in which she was travelling to Dover drew up short of the platform, and in alighting she was seriously hurt. The Exchequer returns from the Ist April, 1882, to 10th March show Receipts, £82,270,221; expenditure, £80,858.745; balances, £8,233,017. Corresponding period last year—Receipts, £80,474,762; expenditure, £77,808,987; balances, £8,041,223. In the Queen's Bench, on Tuesday, the Judges quashed the decision of a Swansea police magistrate that under the Welsh Sunday Closing Act Christmas Day and Good Friday were included. Their lordships held that Sunday could mean no other day than Sunday. The Morning Post is informed that the Charter-house is unable to fill up the vacancies made by recent deaths among the "poor brethren" in consequence of deficiencies of income caused by the reduction of the rents of farms owned by the institution, and in many cases by the inability to let the property. A woman nanea Hibbert was committed for trial by the Liverpool coroner, on 'Tuesday, for the manslaughter of her husband, a carter. During a quarrel she struck him with a paraffin lamp, which broke, and, the oil becoming ignited, the unfortnate man was so severely burnt,that death ensued. The divers report regarding the wreck of the Cimbria that one large fireboat is in its place on the deck, where also parts of human bodies are found jammed in amongst the gear, while the entrances to the cabins are closed by a com- pact mass of bodies. It would be impossible to save the cargo. On the motion of the Prince of Wales' it was resolved, on Monday, at a meeting of the committee for erecting a suit- able memorial to the late Mr. Street, R.A. to approve of the design submitted by Mr. Armstead, R.A., and the commit- tee were authorised to carry it out, subject to such medifi- citions in the pedestal as may be deemed advisable. ROYAL NATIONAL LIFEBOAT INSTITUTION. The Duke of Northumberland presided, on Tuesday, over the annual general meeting of the Royal National Lifeboat Institution, field at Willis's Rooms. The report stated that nine new lifeboats had been placed on the British coasts during the past year, there being now 273 lifeboats under the manage- ment of the society. During the year they had saved 741 lives, and assisted in rescuing 23 vessels from destruction. The receipts during the year were £43,117, and the expen- diture £36,746. • FROZEN TO DEATH ON THE MOUNTAINS.-At Blaenavon, Monmouthshire on Monday evening, an inquest was held on the body of Ralph Deaken, who was found dead on a mountain in the vicinity. It was stated that whenthe de- ceased was found his hair was frozen to the ground, and his head was bleeding. By his side was a broken Whisky bottle. Two men who had seen Deaken lying drunk on the mountain and left him there were severely reprimanded by the coroner, who said they had narrowly escaped being charged with manslaughter. A verdict of death from ex- posure was returned. The number of failures in Englund and Wales gazetted during the week ending Saturday, March 10, was 249. The number in the corresponding week of last year was 242, showing an increase of 7, being a net increase in 1883, to date, of 37. The number of bills of sale published in Eng- land and Wales for the week ending March 10 was 279. The number in the corresponding week of last year was 1,041, showing a decrease of 762, being a net decrease in 1883, to date, of 7,686. The number published in Ireland for the /same week was 34. The number in the corresponding week of last year was 27, showing an increase of 7, being a net increase in 1883, to date, of 68.—Kenip's Mercantile Gazette. I DISCOVERY OF A SKELETON ON CHAT MOSS.—OR SMUT- day, as a workman in the employ of Mr. William Kirkham, Jun., of Chat Moss, Irlam, was cutting a drain he struck upon a human leg. On further search being made the whole of a human skeleton except the head was found. The body was evidently that of a man over six feet in height. Three or four years ago a human head was found not far from where this body was found, and it is conjectured that head and body belonged to the same individual. The body was laid under an old drain, and over it was placed a piece of the trunk of a mountain ash which had been cut with a sharp instrument. From these circumstances it is thought that the body exhumed from the peat is that of the victim of some murder. • DEATH UNDER CHLOROFORIL-At an inquest held in London on Tuesday on the body of a boy who had died in St. Mary's Hospital for failure of the heart's action whilst under the influence of chloroform Dr. Pepper, assistant sur- geon at the hospital, stated that Chloroform was given about 40 times a week at the hospital, and the last death was over two years ago. Permission was not asked for the giving of chloroform, because if it bad to be gained from ielatives, much delay would be ciused and the lives of patients placed in danger. The Coroner said that the death rate in such cases as these was about one in 5,000 cases; and if chloro- form was not given, many operations which were performed with success, and life saved, could not be done. ALLEGED ADVERTISING SWINDLE AT SEAFORTIL—A num- ber of people have, it is reported, been cleverly duped by an individual who formerly lived in the neighbourhood of Sea- forth. For some time past advertisements have appeared in various newspapers stating that a gentleman living in the above locality was desirous of becoming possessed of collec- tions of foreign stamps. A large number of people sent their stamp-books to the advertiser. Receiving neither a remit- tance nor an acknowledgement, they became suspicious, and both the Bootle and Seaforth police have been beset with letters anxiously inquiring about the "stamp swindler." Some of the dupes have come long distances to see the individual, but all they could learn .was that he had left the neighbourhood of Seaforth and had gone to live somewhere in Toxteth Park.

MANCHESTER AND LIVERPOOL AGRICULTURAL Snow.— In Beptember next the Royal Manchester and Liverpool and North Lancashire Agricultural Society is to hotel its annual meeting in Liverpool, and it has been arranged that the show shall be held in Newsham Park. It is twelve years ago since the Manchester and Liverpool Society visited Liverpool, and then it bad only 600 members. It has since been strengthened by amalgamation with the North Lancashire Society, and now numbers about a thousand members. It is anticipated that.the show will be an important one, and at a meeting at the Town Hall, Liver- pool, on Tuesday, under the presidency of the Mayor, it was decided to form a local committee to assist the committee of the society in making arrangements for the show, and especially to raise a fund to augment the £2,000 which the society itself provides for distribution in the form of prizes. A GENTLEMAN THREATENING TO SHOOT HIS COACH- MAN.—At Warwick, on Tuesday, Mr. Thomas Bradley Dickenson, a gentleman of independent means, was brought UP in custody charged with presenting a loaded revolver at his coachman, William Richard Ashwin. About 11 o'clock on Monday night the prisoner called the coachman into a smokeroom and asked him for his hat, as he wanted to go out. Seeing that hie master. was under the influence of drink, and in a very excited state, he advised him to go to bed instead. The prisoner refused to do this, and on going into the hall he, without the least provocation, deliberately presented a revolver at the coachman aid threatened to shoot him. It was stated that on a previous occasion he had used similar threats towards Ashwin, and also the nurse, because she had declined to supply him with champagne. The prisoner was bound over to keep the peace for six months, in his own recognisance of £lOO, and those of two sureties for £5O each. He was removed in custody. AN " INFANT " AND HIS NECESSARIES.—In the Canter- bury County Court, on Monday, Annie, Lady Honywood, was sued by a local tradesman for £9 10s. for goods supplied to one of her ladyship's Bens, who at the time was under age. Plaintiff said he supplied the goods upon the faith of the young man's statement that he was sent by his mother to obtain them. The defence was that Lady Honywood was not responsible for her ison's necessaries, and she denied having given him authority to pledge her credit.—The Judge asked the plaintiff's solicitor upon what principle he sought to make Lady Honywood liable ?—Mr. Minter : That the son was in infant.—His Honour: If he was an infant and pledged* her credit without her authority she would be no more liable than his sister, or his cousin, or his aunt. (Laughter.) His Honour, giving judgment for the defendant with costs, said plaintiff had every opportunity before supplying the goods of ascertain- ing whether the young man had his mother's authority to pledge her credit. •

. THE LANCASHIRE IRON AND COAL TRADB.—The iron market continues firm so far as prices are concerned, but if anything there was a falling off in the amount of business doing- on 'Change on Tuesday. Makers hold for an advance on late low rates,and in some cases leper ton more is asked. The actual advance realized does not average more than eid per ton upon the lowest prices, bnt buyers have to pay this to place out orders. Lancashire makers are holding for 46s fit, less 2& as their miuimum figure for forge and foundry qualities delivered equal to Manchester, and as they have sold largely during the week are indifferent about booking further orders. For district brards delivered the lowest 6fures are 45s 6d to 475, less 27--; for Lincolnshire forge and foundry. Some of the finished iron makers are rather better off for.wo,k. Prices show more steadiness, and makers are not anxious to commit themselves lar zely at £6 ss, which is the minimum figure for bars delivered into the Manches- ter district. A steady tone is maintained throughout the coal trade of this district. The cold weather has kept up the demand for the better classes of round coal for house- fire purposes, and during the past week orders have been coming in pretty freely. In the Manchester disrict, where the men have not made any general attempt at restricting the get, the pits have been kept going about full time, and in other Lancashire districte about five nays a week, with the whole of the output going away, and in many cases stocks being ~reduced. Prices are firm at late rates, the average qu, tations at the pit mouth remaining at about 93. 6d. to 101 fa- best coal, 7s. 6d. to Bs. for seconds, Gs. 6d. to 7s. for common house-fire coals, ss. 9d. to 6s. 3d. for steam and forge coals. ss. for burgy, with slack, which has a ten- dency to harden, ranging from about 3s. 6d. to 4s. for or- dinary We.‘t Lancashire qualities, to about 4s. 3d. to 4s. 6d. per ton for the best sorts in the neighbourhood of Man- chester. and at these figures colliery proprietors are not disposed to entertain forward sales. For shipping there is a fairly good demand. Steam coal delivered at the high level, Liverpool, and the Garston docks ranges from 7s. 6d. to Ss. per tie.

div.head: EXAMINER, SA TURDAY, MARCH 17,1883
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SA TURDAY, MARCH 17,1883

The bodies of two sailors have been washed ashore at Chapel, Mid-Lincolnshire. They have not yet been identified. Grave fears are entertained of the safety of the steamer Craigton, bound from Greenock to New York, which sailed on February 20th, and has not since been heard of. Mr. Cheaters, of Norbury. Cheshire, a well-known agri- culturist, and a prominent Wesleyan, fell down dead while 'walking in his stockyard on Thursday morning. The last stage of the city of kilasgow Bank liquidation was reached on Wednesday, when the Scotch cot= of ses- sion pronounced an order formally dissolving the bank. Lord Derby, replying on Thursday to a deputation on the subject of the Boer atrocities, aid it was improbable that any military expedition would be undertaken. The Govern- ment were giving the subject their earnest attention. In consequence of the various quarter sessions being held the first week in, April, the ensuing spring assizes will be postponed for a week, and they will not, therefore, begin be- fore the 10th or 11th of next month. Mr. Wheeler, who edited the Freethinker upon Foote's conviction for blasphemy, having become through serious illness incapable of continuing the work, Dr. Aveling, of the London School Board, has become the editor. At Londonderry, on Thursday, a number of newsboys were summoned for selling a Dublin evening paper on Sunday, contrary to the Lord's Day Act. The papers were ordered to be forfeited. Lord Catlingford, Lord Bramwell, and Mr. Mundella, the arbitrators oppointed to settle whether the mw College for South Wales should be at Cardiff or Swansea met on Wed- nesday at.the- Privy Council Office, and decided in favour of the claims of Cardiff. .

_ George William Thomas, late town clerk of Boston, Lincolnshire, was on Tuesday committed for trial charged with obtaining by false pretences the sum of £7OO from Mr. John Foreman, of Lincoln. A warrant was issued for the arrest of John F. Brewster, Thomas's clerk, against whom a charge of conspiracy is to be brought. The wife of a Glasgow compositor, named Hugh M'Crindle, leaped, on Thursday forenoon, from the window on a third storey of a house in a central street in Glasgow, and was caught on the iron spikes of a railing in the court below. Some workmen close by took her off, but she was frightfully injured, and died a short time afterwards. A letter from the Prince of Wales to the manager of the Louisville Cotton Exhibition, dated Berlin, February 27th, is published in New York, in which his Royal _Higness contradicts the Tumour that he is about to visit America, and therefore declines the invitation to the exhibition, which he would otherwise certainly have accepted. Da. WHITMARSH.—A deputation of his parish patients waited upon Dr. Whitmarsh, at Hounslow, on Wednesday and presented him with a testimonial consisting of a silver pencil case, a claret jug, and an album, together with an address expressing appreciation on the part of the poor of the parish of his kindness and attention. A man named Ernest Collridge net with a frightful death late on Thursday night while working at Wycen Colliery, near Coventry. He was effecting some repairs in the shaft, and while so engaged he by some means or other ' fell from the cage to the bottom, a distance of 9.0 feet. His skull was smashed, and death was instantaneous. The de- deased was to have been married at Easter. The Chester Custom House officers, on Thursday morn- ing,received a slip of paper picked up by their agent at Sale Bank, a dangerous reef near the Point of Ayre on the Dee shore. It bears the following inscription in a bold, legible hand in pencil :—" March 9. R. Bason and James Nixon got wrecked this day. Try and find our bodies." The Custom House officials think it quite possible the note was written by distressed fishermen. An exciting scene was witnessed on the Dee sands, on Wednesday. Mr. Joseph Broster was driving his horse and cart along the shore, when the horse and cart gradually sank, until the horse's head only was visible. Mr. Broster, who was also rapidly disappearing, cried for help to some Neston fishermen, who eventually. rescued him and the horse and cart with great difficulty. Brestor describes the sensa- tion of sinking as if his legs were being dragged away front' the body. The Blackburn magistrates, on Wednesday, committed to prison for six months a labourer named William Tunstall, who had suspended his young son from the ceiling, heal downwards, and then beaten him about the body and face with a belt having a buckle at the end. The story of bar- barity told is almost incredible and there will be little wonder that the Chairman of the Bench expressed regret that they could not order that the prisoner should be flogged under the same donditions.

James Wood, lime merchant, of respectable position at Hanky, was on Thursday charged with assault under singu- lar circumstances. On Wednesday evening he and two other "gentlemen " attended a meeting of the Salvation Army, all being drunk, one being so helpless that he bad to crawl into his seat on his hands and feet. While the service was pro- ceeding they lit their cigars and commenced to smoke, and subsequently the defendant assaulted the officer in charge of the meeting. A fine of 40a. and costs was inflicted. The marriage of Mr. Leonard Courtney. M.P., Financial Secretary to the Treasury, with Miss Catherine Potter, daughter of Mr. Richard Potter, of Stonehouse, Gloucester- shire, and Prince's Gate, Kensington' was solemnised on Thursday. at St. Jude's, Whitechapel, London, this church being selected owing to the recent connection of the bride with charitable work in the parish. The sacred edifice was crowded, a large party of relatives and friends being in the chancel. The ceremony, which was fully choral, was per- formed by the Rev. S. A. Barnett._ _

• ACCIDENT ON AN IRONCLAD: TWENTY MEN INJURED.— An alarming accident occurred on Wednesday morning on board H.M.S. Defence, now lying in the Mersey. The vessel had been on a cruise for firing practice, and, while the anchor was being heaved, in order to move her to her regular moorings, the capstan gear broke and reversed at great speed, and 20 men were more or less injured, two of them—Samuel Riley and Thomas Sertin—baying to be re- moved to Birkenhead Hospital with broken legs, the latter also having a shocking wound in the head. THE NEW PRIMATE.-The official programme to be ob- served at the entbronisation of the new Primate in Canter- bury Cathedral on the 29th inst. has been finally approved. The ceremony will commence at eleven o'clock, and will probably last about two hours and a half. The procession will include about 600 persons, and will move twice around the aisles of the nave. The committee appointed by the Chapter to make arrangements for the occasion have recommended the Cathedral authorities to reserve the en- tire space in the choir for the clergy and representative laity, leaving the transepts and the nave for the general MINISTER Ftbre,p FOR IrcroxicATiorr.—At Newport, Isle of Wight, on Saturday, a minister of the Presbyterian Church, named the Rev. John Robinson, of St. John's House, near Rvde, was charged with drunkenness. A police officer stata that on the previous Monday evening the de- fendant was in the road outside his residence in a very intoxicated state and using violent language. It was urged in defence that ;he defendant was labouring under excite- ment, due not to drink, but to disease and provocation. The bench said no doubt the defendant was drunk, and as he had been convicted twice before of a similar offence, they fined him £1 and costs.

William Rutherford Benn, who lies in Derby Infirm ary in custody of the police, on the charge of murdering his father, the Rev. Julius Berm. of London, made a despotate attempt to escape or commit suicide on Wednesday. Con- stable Alexander left the head of the bed to put on his boots previous to being relieved. As he was doing so Benn, who had been quiet during the day and who was recovering from the self-inflicted wound in his throat, suddenly jumped up, rushed to the window and threw himself through. Alexander caught him by the night-shirt, but it gave way, and Benn fell to the ground, a distance of over 20. feet He fell on his back, and does not appear to have been seriously in- jured, though he was much cut by the glass. He sprained his ankle by the fall, and was easily recaptured.

EDUCATIONAL GRANTS yo Scuons.—A return issued on Thursday, shows that the expenditure for educational grants was divided as follows :—On schools connected with Church of England, £1,317,803; on British, undenomina- tional and other schools, £221,933; on Wesleyan schools, £lll, 956; on Roman Catholic schools, £137,244; on Beard schools, £813,408; on parochial union schools, £120; administration, £196929; organisation of districts, £283; grants to school boards, £2,325; total, £2,802,005. The increase on .Church of England schools amounted to £65,786; Wesleyan schools, £932; Roman Catholic schools, £11,642; and Board schools' £106,978; while there was a decrease of £2,813 to British and undenominational schools.

THREE MEN BURIED ALIVE.— About noon on Wednesday a serious accident occurred at number four pit, Stank Mines, Furness. A great amount of rock fell in the geueral working and crashed through the 50 fathom level to the 75 fathom, being followed by many smaller falls. The haft was ren- dered quite useless and many of the men narrowly escaped with their lives. The strong current of wind which was occasioned took a number of 'men off their feet and upset some waggons. Great fear prevailed that many men were buried, but it was found that only three only were missing, Isaac Hartley, of Roose, and John Richards an-I Thomas Rosea, of Dalton, all married men, who were working in the 73 father,' level. Forty fathoms from the great fall the picks and spades of the missing men were found. The pre- sumption is that alarmed by. the noise the men rushed to number four shaft and were caught by the falling debris. Searching parties were on Wednesday evening making ex- plorations of the mines and large numbers of men were rapidly clearing away the debris, which represents tens of thousands of tons. EMPLOYMENT IN THE ENGINEERING TRADES.—The re- turns just issued by the leading trade union societies con- nected with the engineering branches of industry show a general improvement in the state of employment. After the Jose of last year there was a tendency to increase, although not to a large extent,in the number of out of work members, but during the past month there has been a decided decrease all round. In the Manchester and Sslford district the Amal- gamated Society of Engineers have no less than 2 per cent of their members in receipt of out of work donation, and the returns received by the Steam Engine Makers' Society, which are the most satisfactory for some time past, show that throughout all their branches, numbering 4,600 mem- bers, there are not 40, or less than 1 per cent, of the members receiving out of work suppol t, whilst the Boiler Makers' So- ciety is practically paying no out of work donation. To a large extent the present good demand for labour is due to the great activity throughout the shipbuilding yards of the country, which is absorbing surplus labour from the en- gineering trades of the inland districts. 11./Di4sasTlON.—The main cauge of nervousness is indigestion, and that is caused by weakness of the stomach. /to one can have sound nerves and good health without using Hop Bitters to strengthen the stomach, purify the blood, and keep the liver and kidneys active, to carry off all the poisonous arid waste matter of the system. THE MID-CHESHIRE ELECTION.
LIBERAL MEETING AT MOW COPE.

A meeting in furtherance of the Candidature of Mr. Lat- ham was held at Mow Cope on Saturday bight. The candi- date, who was well received, dealt with the question of the extension of the franchise, expressing himself in favour of giving every ratepayer a vote. In 1474 the Conservatives went into power by far fewer votes than the Liberals polled, who were in a minority. Such a system was manifestly wrong. They must redistribute the seats in such a way that Parliament may properly represent the feeling of the country. He condemned minority representation. They must get rid, under the reform Bill, of those small boroughs which were mere nests of immorality and corruption, and have equal constituencies, too large to be bribed or cor- rupted, with plenty of vigour and health in thetn.—Mr. CRAIG, M.P., advocating the claims of Mr. Latham, re- ferred to several measures before Parliament affecting the agricultural interest. He spoke favourably of the Bank- ruptcy Bill; which would indirectly benefit the labouring classes. The Rivers Conservancy Bill would not only pre- vent flooding, but increase agricultural production, bene- fiting both the owners of land and the general community. The Conservatives had prevented these Bills from being passed by wasting the time of the House with fruitless in— quiries and persistent obstruction. The Oppositioa had hitherto done all in their power to obstruct useful :measures in order to proclaim to the country that the Government made promises which they never fulfiled. A motion of confidence in the candidate was was passed.

IMr. W. HANDLEY, in a speech which was very appropril ate to the time and the audience, moved "That thiS meeting has full c3nfidence in the present Government, and I trusts that Mid-Cheshire will show its appreciation of the 1 benefits it has already conferred upon the country by returning Mr. G. W. LathaM at the head of the poll to- , morrow." I

Mr. B. KNIVETON, who was warmly received,-seconded the resolution in a racy and energetic speech, which elicited much laughter and cheering. Mr. W. OULTON, of Liverpool, after paying a compliment to Mr. Kniveton for his abilities as a speaker, alluded to the important influence Mr. Latham would have upon politics if returned, and threw ridicule upon the public utterances of his opponent, eharacterising them as a chaolic mass of con- fusion. Referring to the Bradlaugh incident, he observed that religion would lose nothing by the exercise of charity, while its influence would never be lessened by the mainten- ance of justice. (Cheers.) Mr. D. DUNCAN also supported the resolution. He said while he abhorred the opinions of Mr. Bradlaugh, whose' sentiments struck at the foundation of the greatness of any nation, for no nation could be great without God, he main- tained that the interests of religion were better safeguarded by the Liberals than by those who used Mr. Bradiaugh's position as a political stalking horse. It had been stated at the Conservative meeting on the previous Friday that the present Government was extravagant, and Mr. Duncan. in reply, observed that the last Tory Government spent £20,000,000 in the war in Afghanistan, and about six or eight more millions upon the war in South Africa. Yet the Tories were saying the expenditure was increasing. Yes, because the present Government was not only paying its just debts, but also repaying that money which the last Government had so wantonly and sinfully thrown away. (Cheers.) Mr. ALAN JONES, in supporting the resolution, brought forward several weighty reasons why Mr. Latham should be supported. Mr. JAMES TOMEINSONc who was received with enthu- siastic cheering, referred at length to the state of Ireland in past centuries, and the absolute need which had existed for Mr. Gladstone's legislation in respect to the sister isle. He de- fended the Premier's conduct as to supplementary estimates, which had been criticised by Sir Henry Holland in that hall at a meeting a few nights ago. The speaker ridiculed the statement of the vicar of t•andbach as to the cost of the Egyptian campainga, and showed that it was grossly inaccurate. Duing the existence of the present Govern- ment the national debt had been reduced eleven millions; and by the end of the financial year the total reduction of that debt would be no less than sixteen millions. He urged them to remember that the contest would not be won by mere enthusiasm in a public meeting, but by influencing the various voters to use their influence on the side of Mr. Latham. Then they would place the Liberal candidate at the head of the poll. (Loud cheers.) The resolution was then put to the meeting, and carried without a dissentient voice

Mr. ROBERT SHAW moved a vote of thanks to the Chair- man, touching in a neat speech upon the anomalies Of the present franchise. Mr. TOMICINSON seconded the motion, which was carried with acclamation, and Mr. Rigby having replied, the meet- ing broke up.

div.head: LIBERAL MEETING AT LYMM.
div.p: LIBERAL MEETING AT LYMM.

A crowded meeting of electors and non-electors was held on Monday evening, at the Plough Hotel Assembly-room, in support of Mr. G. W. Latham's candidature. Mr. Wm. Long presided, and the gentlemen on the platform included Mr. Samuel Smith, M.P. (the recently-elected member for Liverpool), Messrs. C. Broadbent, J. A. Swanwick, J. Hud- son, D. Boyd, A. Bickley, D. Stewart, John Swanwick, B. Armitage, 'I. Draper, W. Derbyshire, H. Camgron, W. Pierpoint, The CHAIRMAN felt that he owed those present an apology for not answering the call of his name at the meeting on the previous Friday evening. The fact was he was a long way from home, and was not able to get back in time. Still he thought they would believe him when he said his heart was entirely with them—(cheers)—and that his loss was their gain, for he was glad to see from the reports the chairman they bad was more than a substitute, and that they had one of the most enthusiastic meetings Lymm had ever seen. (Cheers.) He was a long way from home when he heard of the death of Lord Egerton. He thought they might all of them pay this testimony to his character, that they regret- ted that a good, conscientious public servant had been taken away. However little tirey might agree with his political principle still they must not withhold that testimony to his character. (Hear, hear.) They were to fight the battle they had often fought before for Liberal principles in that division of the county of Chester. (Hear, hear.) They did so without any bad feel- ing towards their opponents. He was only sorry to see that so much personal feeling had been brought into the contest this time—he was afraid there was rather more than they had had in previous contests. Let them hope that kind of feeling would die away. Englishmen were a fair dealing nation, and surely they could be contrnt to argue without descending to vulgar personalities. (Hear, hear.) He had to welcome in the name of the meeting. and to propose a vote of thanks to a gentleman who was present that night, at very great personal inconvenience to help them. He was a gentleman who took Lancashire and Cheshire, if not the whole of England, by storm (cheers) by the victory he won for the Liberal cause in that very Tory city of Liver- pool. (Cheers.) He very well remembered the delight that was expressed amongst his own people at G-rappenhall when they got .the morning papers with the news that Mr. Smith was • returned as the member for Liverpool. (Cheers.) He should say that by the weight of his own personal character Mr.-Smith won the day in Liverpool, and good as he believed Mr. Smith to Ibe he did not believe him to be one whit better that their candidate for Mid-Cheshire. (Cheers.) Mr. Latham was a man who bad done more for his native county than a great many people gave him credit for, and there were many people who were anxious to hide his light under a bushel for men who had not done one tithe of the work that he had done. .(Hear, hear.) He had the pleasure of seeing Mr. Smith at his duties in Parliament on Friday evening, and he was rather astonished to see him in Lymm that night. He therefore proposed this resolution :—"That this meeting desires to express to Mr. S. Smith, M.P., its cordial satisfac- tion at seeing him in Mid-Cheshire at the present conjunc- ture; that while thanking him heartily for coming down to Lymm at so much trouble to himself, it is glad to have the opportunity of warmly congratulating him on his great victory in the last election at Liverpool; further, that it looks upon his presence as a happy omen of the success of the Liberal party in Mid-Cheshire at the poll on Wednesday next." (Cheers.) Mr. S. SMITH, M.P., who was loudly cheered, thanked the meeting for its hearty greeting, and said he had come amongst them, at no little inconvenience, to support them in a battle upon which the eyes of all England were fixed. In Mr. Latham they had an excellent candidate, who possessed a politically educated mind, was capable of expressing his thoughts in very clear language, and had very definite views on the important questions that were before the country at the present time. (Cheers.) In attending that meeting, he (Mr. Smith) was.prompted not only by his desire for their 'success, but by a feeling that they ought to give their earnest support to the Government presided over by Mr. Gladstone. (Cheers.) It was not so much a question as to which par- ticular individual should be returned, as of whether Eng- land, speaking through the electors of Mid-Cheshire, would testify its adhesion to the .policy of Mr. Gladstone or not. He was confidently of opinion that the country never pos- sessed a more able Government than it did to-day, or a Government more capable of carrying forward great and use- ful reforms, and he thought it was the duty of all patriotic Englishmen to give their strenuous support to the govern- ment of their noble Premier. He had, during his brief experience of parliament, been driven to the conclusion that the government of England was paralysed by a system of deliberate obstruction. There was a system in force the object of which was apparently to hinder all useful legistation—(hear, hear)—and unless the country spoke mit strongly, and expressed its disapprobation of these tactics, they might expect ancther barren session and a con- tinuance of fruitless government for the next two or three years. It was high time that a stop should be put to this habit of incessant interruption, of making aimless and use- less personal speeches, and of attacking, in every conceiv- able manner, the character of our great men. (Hear, hear.) He did not see in what way a stop could be most effectually put to that habit except by the great constituencies sending up men who were determined to give a hearty support to the Government of Mr. Gladstone. (Cheers.) That ob-, struction and interruption proceeded from a a:nail number of the Irish members, who were totally irrecon- cilable, lived on agitation, and intended to keep it up as long as they could (applause) and also from a 'number of irresponsible Tory politicians, chiefly Bitting below the gangway. These latter knew what fate was in store for them if the Government could only get their-measures through Parliament, and they appeared to be desirous of making the Government of Mr. Gladstone as barren as possible of wholesome legislation. They wished to say at the end of the session that the Government had not fulfilled its promises, but they would forget to tell the country that they had been the chief cause of it. (Laughter and cheers.) The Government had a large number of important and beneficial measures in store, and if the country wished them to be passed they must send up men willing to assist in the tax, and he hoped Mid-Cheshire would, on Wednesday next, return a man who would bear an able part in furthering the great measures at present under consideration. (Cheers.) Mr. H. E. PREST moved a resolution declaring the eminent fitness of Mr. Latham to represent Mid-Cheshire, and pledging the meeting to leave no stone unturned to secure his return. Mr. Anams seconded the resolution. The resolution was carried unanimously, and the meeting soon afterwards terminated. ENTHUSIASTIC MEETING AT RUNCORN.

The Liberals of Runcorn brought a vigorous election campaign to a conclusion on Tuesday evening, when a crowned and most enthusiastic meeting was held in the Public Hall. Half an hour before the time announced for the commencement of the proceedings, the room was almost filled, but Mr. Richard Morris beguiled the weary interval by an able rendering of the popular patriotic song "The Pilot of the State." Mr. T. Rigby, of Sutton, presided, and occupying seats on the platform were the Revs. Hack, John Billington, J. D. Thomas, S. Mees ; Messrs. R. Shaw (chairman of the Runcorn Liberal Association), J. Tomkiu- son, J.P., and David Dtmcan (Liberal candidates for West Cheshire), J. A. Jones, W. Oultou' J.P., Thomas Hadfield, R. N. Davies, James Handley, P. Speakman, Thomas Nor- man, Robert Norman, F. J. Norman, William Handley, J. Yapp, Samuel Taylor, J. N. Lello, J. R. Frith,'R. Wright, F. Fairhurst, J. Tomlinson, J. Bridgewater, J. Littler, J. Hunt, F. J. Adams, R. Morrie, J. Unswortb, S. C. Beckett, W. H. Chadwick, J. 0. Jackson, S. Pope, J. Sproston, F. McDougall, J. W. F. Pankhurst (London), W. Townes, T. Handley, J. Kirkham, F. H. Pankhurst (Widnes), R. Web- ster, S. Sadler, J. Midwood, C. Littler, B. Kniveton, G. Bellamy, W. Marsh, Joseph Williams, J. Beveridge, 0. Leak (Liberal agent), tic. The CHAIRMAN, in his opening remarks, said he had come forward at the present crisis because he regarded it as his duty, considering the positions he had held in connection with agricultural societies, and the inefficiency of those so- cieties to do what they wanted; and it was the duty of every man who wished his country well to adopt those views which would be most for the benefit of the country. Speaking of the necessity for a reform in the land laws, he said the difficul- ties in the way of successful agriculture bed been experi- enced so long, and were of such a character, that it as im- possible to remove them except by legislation. The farmers required greater security for their capital and labour in the soil; and if they had confidence that these would not be confiscated to others they would produce four-fold, aye, 40 fold more from the land than they did at the present time. (Cheers.) That being so, he thought they had a legitimate right to agitate and to express their opinion at the present time that Legislature should be called upon to provide for this crying want. He was there that night to bear his testimony to the necessity of such a measure, and because he saw in Mr. Latham a candidate of the right sort— (cheers)—a man who had a clear and comprehensive know- ledge of the whole question. (Hear, bear, and cheers.) Thc chairman concluded by referring to the utility of the Agricultural Holdings Act, and to aye beneficial measures passed by the Liberal Government.

div.head: CONSERVATIVE MEETING AT KNUTSFORD.
div.p: CONSERVATIVE MEETING AT KNUTSFORD.

Sir H. H. T. Holland, M.P. and Mr. J. C. La7rance, M.P., addressed a meeting at lenutsford on Saturday even- ing in support of the candidature of the Hon. Alan Egerton. —Sir H. Holland remarked that the Liberal Government, unlike the poor farmers, had good weather, but how wretched was the crop they had produced They had heard so much of peace, retrenchment, and reform, that they must have become almost nauseated with it. As to the first named, they had had a most disgraceful peace in the Transvaal. Hardly was the ink dry on the paper on which the conditions of that peace were written than the Boers, at first covertly and-new openly, attacked the natives with the distinct intention of annexing their land, con- trary to the conditions of the. convention. The matter was the subject of a Cabinet Coincil,and would again come up in the House of Commons. As to retrenchment and re- form, nothing practically had been accomplished.—A vote of confidence in Mr. Egerton was carried.

div.head: CONSERVATIVE MEETING AT ALTRINCHAM.
div.p: CONSERVATIVE MEETING AT ALTRINCHAM.

The Conservatives held a crowded meeting in the Assem- bly Room of t'e Conservative Club, at kltrincham, on Monday evening. Sir Richard Cross was expected, but was detained by his Parliamentary duties. Amongst those present were Sir Henry Drummond Wolff, M.P., Lord Folk- stone, M.P., Mr. Cunliffe Brookes, M.P., and Mr. J. C. Law- rence, the tenant farmers' representative for South Lincoln- shire. Lord Brabone, in the course of a letter to Mr. Candelet, Parliamentary agent of the Manchester Licensed Victuallers' Association, expresses his approval of the course taken by the association in recommending the trade in Mid-Cheshire to support the Conservative candidate, the Hon. Alan Egerton. "The leaders of the Liberal party," his lordship writes, "seem to have done their utmost to change the old principles of theparty." •

div.head: POLLING.
div.p: THE POLLING.

Wednesday, which was the polling day in the election, was opened with weather that was anything but favourable, considering the straggling nature of the divisien—rain, sleet, and fog prevailing until mid-day, when there was a slight Improvement. The absence of excitement, which has characterised the contest from the commencement, was again noticeable even on Wednesday, as during the polling hours —eight a.m. until five p.m.—there was little to indicate that a momentous struggle was taking place to decide whether the important division of Mid-Cheshire should he repre- sented by a gentleman whose oily recommendation was that he belonged to an old aristocratic family, or Fy a gentle- man who based his claims to the suffrages of the electors upon the principles he bele! and the measures which he was prepared to support. Because, although the fight was nominally between Liberal and Tory, it has been evident all through the election that the Conser- vatives relied for success upon the fact that their champion was the representative of the Egerton family. None knew better or felt it more than the Conservatives that there was really no comparison between the candidates, so far as experience, ability, and sagacity went, for the Hon. Alan Egerton, at the commencement of the contest, was not only comparatively unknown, bat a perfect infant in politics, and as time wore on it became painfully evident that he had scarcely an idea of his own, and was lamentably unfit to re- present an important constituency in Parliament. But this was no great drawback in the eyes of the Conservatives, who could only see in him an Egerton and an opponent of Mr. Gladstone—two features which were the best passports ob- tainable to the good opinions of the Conservatives of Mid- Cheshire. Ott the other hand, the Liberals, encouraged by diminishing Tory majorities in the past, were not willing— without a good fight, at any rate—to allow it to be supposed that the representation of the division was the exclusive privilege of an aristocratic family, and especially determined were they that the seat should not pass over undisputed into the possession of an opponent of Mr. Gladstone. In Mr. Latham they found a man who was more than a landlord and neighbour, and more than a mere supporter of Mr. Gladstone—a man who, dnring many years of public life, bad proved himself a sound thinker, a practical politician, and a good speaker; and who had displayed many other qualities which rendered him a most desirable representative. To him the Liberals turned, and Mr. Latham readily accepted the invitation and entered upon the contest with a determination to wrest the seat from the Tot ies who had monopolised it so long. The prospects of the Liberal candidate at the outset were singularly bright, for not only was the Conservative candi- date little known, and less popular than his brother, now Lori Egerton, but there was the strongest indication that the tenant-farmers were "coming round," afforded in the greatly reduced Tory malority at the last election. The first time a contest took pram, I n Mid-Cheshire since the division was formed was in the general election of 1868, when the Hon. J. B Leicenter Warren, son of Lord de Tabley, was the Liberal candidate, and the Hon. Wilbraham Egerton (now Lord Egerton) and Colonel Cornwall Legh were the Conservative candidates. The declaration of the poll showed—Egerton (C), 3,080; Legh (C), 3,056; Warren (L), 2,449. so that both Conservatives were returned. In March, 1873, a vacancy was causal by the resignation of Col. Cornwall Legb, when Mr. G. W. Latham (the present Liberal candidate) contested the seat in the Liberal interest against Col. Egerton Leigh, of Jeddrell Hall, Holme. The contest was watched with all the more interest inasmuch as it was the first county election after the passing of the Ballot Act, but the Conservative was again successful, the figures being—Leigh (C), 3,508; Latham (L), 2,118; majority for Leigh, 1,390. There was no opposition to the Conservative members on their seeking re-election in 1874, and in 187.6, upon the death of Col. Egerton Leigh the. Liberals permitted Mr. Piers Egerton Warburton, of Arley Hall, Northwich, to have a walk over. At the last general election, however, Mr. Latham and Mr. V. K. Armitage, of Bakewell, DerbV- shire, both Liberals, made a gallant attempt to oust the Hon. Wilbraham Egerton and Mr. P. E. Warburton but once more success attended the Consetvative cause, though their majority showed a remarkable falling off, as will be seen by the following figures :—Egerton (C), 3,808; War- burton (C), 3,700; Latham (L), 3,374; Armitage (L), 3,247. The advance made by Mr. Latham was a significant one, as, while the Conservative candidate polled in, the pre- vious contest as many as 1,390 votes more than -Mr. Latham, the difference between the latter and Mr. Warburton in IEBO was only 326, while Mr. Egerton himself only polled 429 more than Mr. Latham. The Liberals, therefore, had every reason to be confident of success on the present occa- sion.

The contest decided on Wednesday was conducted throughout in excellent spirit, and personalities and offen- sive epithets were very rare. As before stated, there was a remarkable absence of excitement during the polling hours. Some of the enthusiastic supporters of the candidates sported their colours in the form of rosettes, dtc., the Liberal colours being blue and yellow, and the Conservative red and white. Cabs were in great requisition throughout the division, and there were not a few omnibuses and four-in-hands. At Sale, where many -merchants and other gentlemen having business in Manchester reside, the polling was heaviest during the first two hours, after which there was a lull until the after- noon, when there was another rush. There was as many as 1,424 voters in this polling district, and it was confidently believed that Mr. Latham had received by far the greater portion of that number. Altrincham presented a more lively appearance, there being crowds around the polling booths, as well as in the vicinity of the Liberal central committee rooms and the Liberal and Conservative clubs. Here also there was an undoubted majority for Mr. Latham. At orth- wich, the contrast between the present and the pre- vious struggle was most marked, as the outward indications of excitement were few. Mr. Egerton, in passing through the town, was greeted with, several volleys of groans, but

beyond this there was nothing dug the earlier part of the ! day to deservp comment. ,Mr. .L.i."ham's prospects here were beld to be far brighter than hh% opponent's, hut at Knutsford the majority was evidently on the Conserv.,tive side—or rather in favour of Mr. Egerton' ae Salton Park, the seat of Lord Egerton, is close by. The a:vision con- tains 3 population of 120,289, and there are 9,91 w eleotols on the rcgistet, distributed as follows :—Altrincham 2,790, Congleton 849, Grappenhall 475, Holmes Chapel 371, Knutsford -748. Lymm 546, Middlewich 360, North wich 1,072, Odd Rode 391, Runcorn 875, Sale 1,424, Sandbach -526, Lower Wharton 215, Whitley 260. The polling stations were situated as follows :—Atrincham: Market Hall, Market- street. Congleton : Town Hall. Grappenhall : National School. Holmes Chapel.: National School: Knutsford : County Sessions Court. Lymm : National School. Middle- wich : Infant Schoolroom. Northwich: Market Hall. Odd Rode: Boys' National Schools Runcorn: Volunteer Drill I Hall. Sale : Infant Schoolroom. Sandbach : Surveyor's ! Office, Town Hall. Wharton: National School. Lower Whitley: The Schoolroom. CLOSE OF THE POLL.

The poll closed at five o'clock, and the ballot boxes were quickly conveyed to Knutsford from all parts of the divi- sion, those from Mowcop and Runcorn being the last to arrive. The arrangements for conveyin the boxes to Knutsford were on an extensive scale. Those from distant parts of the division arrived with remarkably little delay. Both candidates visited several of the polling districts. At Nerthwich, Mr. Egerton had anything but a flattering recep- tion, whilst Mr. Latham was loudly cheered—at the railway station, where he was rweived by Mr. R. Verdin, a pro- minent Liberal, and on his way to the polling station. The voting was brisk up to about mid-day, no less than 500 having recorded their votes by that time out of a possible 890. It was generally believed that the Irish vote was divided between absentors and the Con- servative candidate, but presuming this to be true, the loss to Mr. Latham could not be great, as the nuni. ber of Irish voters is notlarge. There were additional police precautions in anticipation of a repetition of the rioting which prevailed at the last contest, but these were found to be unnecessgy. The Tories rvorted to the card trick, and issued a series of returns showing how the poll went on in all parts of the devision—a decided majority in all cases, of course, going to Mr. Egerton. It is needless to say that these returns served nivtlier purpose than to amuse those who found time to read them.
At 10 o'clock, Mr. Egerton Leigh, the returning officer, declared the result to be— Egerton Latham

Conservative majority ... 622 The announcement was received with cheers. The Hon. ALAN EGERTON, M.P., then stepped forward to propose a 'cote of thanks to the High Sheriff for the admir- able manner in which he had discharged the dutiesof return- ing officer. He also wished to add a vote of thanks to Mr. Latham. (Cheers.) He would most cordially shake hands with Mr. Latham, and only hoped that on the next occasion he (Mr. Egerton) might have the pleasure of meeting him on the same platform. (Cheers.) He concluded by formally proposing a vote of thanks to the High Sheriff, and also to Mr. Latham. (Cheers.) Mr. LATHem, in seconding the motion, said—Electors of Mid-Cheshire, I have great pleasure in seconding the vote of thanks to the high sheriff of this county. I am very sorry he has come so far with so very little profit to me. (Laughter and cheers.) lam none the less obliged to him for the trouble and care he has taken. lam none the less thankful to my supporters who. though I am in a minority, have done their very best for me. (Cheers.). If ever this division is contested again, I trust the contest will bef ought as good humouredly, as good naturedly, and as free from violence and riot as this last one has been—(cheers)—and I hope the only difference between the next contest and this one will be that the Liberal candidate will have his name read first instead of the Conservative. (Cheers, and cries of "Never.")

The vote of thanks was unanimously accorded. There was much cheering when the result was made known. THE POLLING IN RUNCORN. There was little in the aspect of the town on Wednesday morning to indicate that an election, which was exciting universal interest throughout the country, was to be decided that day. On the numerous hoardiegs the yellow and blue Placards of the Liberal condidate and the glaring red ones of the Tory aspirant for Parliamentary honours met the gaze of the passer-bye, cabs bearing the general invitation to" vote for Lathani," or "vote for Egerton," as the case might be, rattled over the stony streets, while industrious partisans, wearing party favours, could be seen hurrying along in couples, hunting up laggard or doubtful voters. Otherwise the town was quiet—the work people were toiling at their daily labour' and the trademen's shops were open for the transaction of business. Many of the voters having to come from a considerable distance—Daresbury, Moore, Norton, was hoped that the weather, on the election day, would be fine like the week which preceded it, but during the night there was a slight fall of snow, and the sky in the early morning portended still dirtier weather. Nevertheless, a large group of men took up a position opposite the Volunteer Hall, Greenway-road, the polling station. Soon after the poll was opened, voters arrived in quick succession, and as they were recognised, their supporters in the crowd sent forth a cheer. About half-past ten a drizzling rain set in, and continued for about two hours' but the voting went briskly forward, and after two o'clock very few electors recorded their votes. Aware of the tumultous state of the town at the last general elec- tion, Superintendent Williamson took the precaution of ob- taining an extra force of policemen, but we are glad to say their services were not required. The day was particularly barren of the incidents which formerly char- acterised elections, and there was little excite- ment. The morning had npt far advanced when a clergyman, who has been described as of narrow views and Orange peculiarities, was seen wending his way towards the polling booth. Turning aside, he walked leisurely to several well-known politicians wearing the rib- bons of yellow and blue. On reaching them he produced a card printed in blue, and in a mysterious manner, as if he would imply "I'm voting blue, but don't tell my friends," asked: Which booth shall I enter? He was politely told that his query would be answered if he walked further on, and he stepped stealthily away. We have our doubts, but it is to be hoped he followed the directions on the blue card. He was either an astonishing convert to Liberal principles, or making a very bad attempt at humour. As we have stated, the polling station was at the Volunteer Hall. Inside there were two booths, Mr. F. A. Lake pre- siding over No. I, and Mr. T. Beasley over No. 2. In the former Mr. J. D. Jones acted as personation agent for the Liberals, Mr. William Sutton performing a similar office for the Conservatives. In the second booth Mr. James Hand- ley was personation agent for the Liberals, and Mr. William Fisher for the Conservatives. Although Runcom polling district contains a population of about 20,000, a mere fraction of this number—only 875—are voters, and at the meetings held during, the three weeks campaign, the Liberals laid especial stress upon this anomaly. The Liberals, with a good organisation,.worked with much enthusiasm and determina- tion under the buoyant hope that this time their labours were to be crowned with success, while the Tories worked with equal energy under a fear, which they began to enter- tain, that defeat awaited them. Canvassers were employed by Liberal and Tory, and every nerve was strained to poll each voter. Partisans of each party did not scruple to travel long distances in order to exercise their elective rights, and several journeyed from the outskirts of the country. The result was that the highest poll ever held in Runcorn took place, 733 out of 875 votes being recorded, being 84 per cent. of the whole. The average throughout the division was 80 per cent., so that Runcorn compares very favourabl.y. The Liberals claimed to have a majority of 130 in Rencorn, and this estimate agrees with the political proclivities of the place, which is intensely Liberal. Immediately the poll was closed, at five o'clock, the ballot boxes were conveyed to Knutsford by the two presiding officers, who journed by train to Northwich. Towards night the streets became somewhat thronged by workingmen, wlio gathered at street corners, and speculated upon the result of the contest. It was thought that, though it was probable that Egerton would win the fight would be a hard one, and the majority on either side very small. Youths and children of all ages, to the number of. several hundreds, commenced parading the streets, waving ragged banners, and giving voice to some popular refrain in a manner which testified to the soundness of their lungs. Occasionally they would meet a fem. policemen, who with stout sticks soon dispersed the noisy youngsters, but not before they had smashed a few windows. Arrangements had been made to keep open the 'Post Office telegraph, and the receipt of the telegram announcing the declaration of the poll was anxiously awaited. When it arrived about a quarter-past ten there were crowds of people in the streets, and cheers for Egerton, or counter cheers for Latham, were heartily given. Although much disappointed, the Liberals pore not disheartened. They expressed them- selves determined to continue storming the "Tory citadel," and as the County Franchise will have probably been reduced to the level of the Borough Franchise when the next election is fought, there will be every chance of success. It was generally considered that the Bradlaugh question, which the Tories "on the stump" seemed greatly to rely upon, had exercised an adverse influence on the Liberal votes, and there is no doubt it is so. The Liberals. of Runcorn can, however, triumph in the fact that in their own neighbour- hood their arduous labours were not in vain. A substantial majority rewarded their efforts.

COAGITINE.—Cement for Broken Articles, 6d, Is, 23; p ostage Id. Soideverywhere. Kay Bros, Stockport.—Advt. It is stated that William Rutherford Bean, accused of murdering his father at Matlock, is progressing favourably, and will shortly be brought before the magistrates. A man alleged to be the treasurer to the Keighlev Salva- tion Army has el eped with a married woman, and taken with him £6O belonging to the Salvation Army. Mr. Gladstone informs a correspondent at Burnley, who had forwarded to him a memorial "in connection with the appointment of Nonconformists to high offices, and especi- ally in connection with the heads of colleges at the Univer- sities," that Her Majesty's Government will at all times be ready to do full justice to the claims of Nonconformists when I engaged in making selections for vacant offices.

At West Bromwich, on Monday, a summons was partly heard in which Fanny Herbert, domestic servant, sought to show that the Rev. F. R. Andrews, Stanley-street circuit, Sheffield, was the father of her illegitimate child. The case lasted a considerable time, and the court rose before he evidence in chief had been taken, and it was then adjonrne for a month.

"THE STUDY OF BOTANY." LECTURE AT WARRINGTON. The Rev. J. Freeston, of Staly bridge, delivered alecture in the Co-operative Hall, on Monday ev e enin, entitle "The pleasures and advantages of the study of botany." Mr. R. D :vies presided, and there was a fair attendance.—The CHAIRMAN, in a very few words, introduced the lecturer.— The LECTURER said it was his intention to put the subject before the audience in such a manner as to persuade as many as he could to commence the study of botany. It was a subject out of which he had derived a very large amorent of pleasure, and it would increase his pleasure very much if be could do anything to cause anyone to get the same amount, or a greater amoLint, of pleasure out of this beautiful, subject. The science of botany meant a knowledge of the etrucaure and classification of plants, but taken in its widest sense it meant more than that. Some- times it Wl, divided into five divisions— struetural, systematical, economical, geographical, and geological. Economical botany, which meant a know- ledge of the various uses of plants, was a very interesting part of botany, and one which, in Lie opinion, was need- lissly neglected by botanists. Every large town ought to have a museum, in which should be collected together spe- cimens of as many of the useful plants of the world as could possibly be got. And in Warrington, being so near to Liver- pool, if gentlemen were to set about the task, they could have in a few years a very good collection of vegetable substances that could be used by man. But he would con- fine his remarks to two of the divisions—structural and systematicel. In commencing the sttely of botany, the first thing to tee done was to take up a Went and find out the chief parts of it. There aere five chief parts—the root, stem, leaf, flower, and fruit (or seed). Then came the study of the function of each part; that was to say, the work it had to do, or the office it had to perform in plant life. The root had fiist of all to fix the plant in the soil and hold it in its position, but its main function was to absorb the moisture and gas frem the earth. At the end of the very small fibrils of the root was a little porous sponge, and this sponge absorbed the moisture. It was very interesting to study the root and make observations of its behaviour. Some botanists said that plants had instinct. If , it were ever proved that any part of a plant had instinct, the lecturer thought it would he the root. If, for instance, a tree wanted water and there was water on one side of it . and not on the other, it would shoot out its roots in the direction of the water. The lecturer gave other instances of , a similar character. Passing from the root he came to the' stem, the first function of which was to hold up the flowers into the sunshine and light, and the leaves into the fresh ' air. The stem had another purpose—that of circulating the sap. Some stems were weak and others strong. Those that I wore not strong enough to support the weight of their own flowers and leaves had means of clinging to other plants stronger than themselves, and he always found great pleasure in watching the weak plants clinging to the stronger ones. The lecturer then remarked upon the various ways in which plants climb, after which he passed OD to the sub- ject of leaves. How much we owed to leaves! If we were just to strip the earth of leaves, what a barren-looking wilderness we should have! The function of the leaves was to elaborate the sap, that was to digest and purify it. , Leaves had pores through which they breathed. ' The roots, after abeorbing the moisture from the soil sent it up to the leaves, and what the plant did not want the leaves threw out. The sap thus became thicker. . After the sap had ascended from the roots to the leaves and . become purified, it began to descend, and in descending it fed and supported the tree. Passing en to flowers, the lecturer said that however beautiful they mighe _toile/and however they might attract the insects, their ereaj- hien4tion was to produce the fruit or seed. The lecturer,--wittaiand a number of flowers on the t ible, here toolterp-a.tnlizie,and gave the botanical names of the various perls of 111E-t'rer, and explained the uses of each part; and he dtict, eiemiame thing with several other flowers. Passing - glee to the fruits, he said that many of them Were fit to eat, but by skill and attention man could greatly enlarge those fruits and turn them to his own advantage. He could not, however, dwell upon this but ; must pass on and say that the function of the fruits was to reproduce the plants so that there might be a succession of plants for ages and ages to come. He would tell them one great advantage of the study of botany; it was very healthy. They could not have a study more favourable to health than the study of botany, because if they wished to study they must go out into the lanes, down the hill aides, and • perhaps on to mountain tops, and there they were exercising themselves in the fresh air. He knew individuals who had lengthened their lives through getting into tome field naturalist society, and he thought he had lengthened his own life in the same way. A study of botany also exercised the observing faculties, and the best way to develope the faculties of the young was to learn them to take notice of things. It also developed the power of at- tending to little things. In astronomy they were grasping things on a large scale, but in botany they were dealing with little things. He had known men who had failed in life because they were unable to attend to details. There was alto the advantage of being able to distinguish between wholesome and poisonous plants, but above all the study of botany tended to elevate man. (Applause.) A vote of thanks was accorded the lecturer, on the motion of Mr. E. GREEN, seconded by Mr. BIRCHALL.—A similar compliment was paid the chairman, and the meeting concluded.
