div.head: EXAMINER.
div.p: THE EXAMINER.
SATURDAY, MARCH 17, 1883.

THE state of affairs in the Transvaal formed the subject of debate in the House of LORDS on Tuesday, and the same question is at the present time occupying the attention of the House of Commons. It had been evident from the inquiries made to Ministers from time to time these inquiries following of course upon the cruelties recently perpetrated upon the native tribes in South Africa—that a debate would be raised in due course; and it is a matter for regret to find that, though the question is one which ought to be treated from a non-political point of view, the Opposi- tion are doing their utmost to make as much capital out of it as possible. We are not sure, however, that their efforts to damagethe Government will be successful. If a retro- spect be taken it will not be difficult to dis- cover that most, if not all our troubles in the Transvaal, date from the foolish annexation of that Territory in 1877, by the late Adminis- tration. This was done much against the will of the Boers, but with the view, as was stated, of preventing a general war be- tween the natives and the Cape colonists. It had not the desired effect, we all know, and when the present !Government came into power they found the Boers in open revolt against the annexation and the otherwise ag- gressive action of the Cape Government. The revolt resulted in victory, and as a conse- quer ce in 1881 the Boers had their territory restored to them under the Suzerainty of the Crcs,vn. At that time a Convention was en- tered into with the 1 ransvaal Republic which secured to England the right to interfere on behalf of the natives, if necessary, and it is that arrangement and nothing else which the Opposition now seek to denounce and dis- credit as being a failure. They profess that their humanitarian feelings alone impel them on, and we have no desire to question the virtue of their motives, but we cannot close our eyes to the fact that their speeches betray their inward desires. There appears to be a difference of opinion as to the nature and extent of the interference provided for by the Convention. There are those who hold strongly to the opinion that it was only to be of a moral character; others, again, contend - quite as tenaciously that it meant an inter- ence by force of arms should occasion arise. The question has also been raised whether our interference shozld include the interests of the natives beyond the Transvaal frontier, or be confined only to the natives within the territory of the Republic. On this, however, there need be no difference of opinton, for Mr. GLADSTONE explicitly stated, in recom- - mending the Convention, that the whole of the interests of the natives beyond the fron- tier of the Transvaal would be retained in the hands of the British Government by the Suzerainty, and we believe they are so re- tained. Let it then be conceded that all the Many persons were attracted to the h banks ofdithe.Mersey cruelties said to have been perpetrated on the atitdeW:,rhriientftfloono,doend Sunday last, laivstibgbygttoehnl toaoa cnonarsiilgrerhaiellel $ natives have actually taken place, though we depth.

THE election in Mid-Cheshire has resulted in the return of the Conservative candidate, and there is no disguising the fact that it is a very sore disappointment to the Liberal , party. They had every reason to hope that on this occasion they would be successful, and this was shown as much by the fear of defeat manifested in Conservative circles as by the enthusiasm displayed at Liberal gatherings. The contest in 1880 proved that the Conservatives were losing ground. This must have nerved them tO greater exertion, for on Wednesday they polled to a man, and elected Mr. Egerton by a majority of 622. The constituency remains true to its past tra- ditions. It has always been a Tory strong- hold, and Tory it remains. It has always been a pocket constituency for the Egertons, and the seat may be said to be in the gift of that noble family still. Yet it is some satisfaction ,to know that the cause of Liberalism is not slumbering in the constituency. In 1880 Mr. LA.THA At polled 3,37+ votes, on Wednesday , he had 3,592 supporters; so that the Liberal strength has increased by 218 votes, a fact which is not without hope for the future. The Cheshire tenant-farmers are not yet, it appears, sufficiently educated to throw off the territorial influence, but, if slow, their en- lightenment is sure, and a time must come, and that sooner or later, when they will assert themselves and break loose from their j political bondage.

div.head: EA.AMINER, SATURDAY, MARCH 17, 1883.
div.p: THE EA.AMINER, SATURDAY, MARCH 17, 1883.

should think that they are to a very great ex- tent exaggerated, also that the Transvaal Go- vernment are, as Sir HERCULES ROBINSON has reported, morally responsible for these cruel- ties, and let it be conceded further that our interference is to include the interests of the natives not onl with:n but without the fron- tier, the question still remains, what is to beithe nature of that interfe enee ? We are afraid that the debate in the House of Lords, or even that in the House of Commons, so far as it has proceeded, throws very little light on the subject. It is admitted on all hands that something must be done, but what that something is to be is not defined. The Opposition speakers are clearly in favour of our undertaking another military expedition, though they are evidently afraid to openly advocate it, possibly because they know that the country would not be at all disposed to favour another South African war. But even Tupposing the country was disposed to coun- tenance such an adventure, we have not the right to undertake it, for Mr. GLADSTONE has positively asserted that our interference is to be of a moral character only.. It is a mistake to suppose that these internicene strifes, of which we hear so much complaint, are at all rare; they are only the outcome of the "chronic condition of conflict in which the African aborigines live amongst themselves." This was clearly shown on Tuesday, if it was not already known, by Mr. E. ASHLEY in the House of Commons, and by Lord Derby in the House of Lords. The spe,ch of the noble lord, which is characteristic of his caution and sound statesmanship, is remark- ably instructive, not only as to the continual warfare between these African tribes, but also with reference to the actual condition of affairs .at the present time, and our policy with regard to it. After pointing out that the: cruelties which have been practised by the Bechuanas on the one side and the Boers on the other are by no means uncommon in semi-savage war, his lordship points out that on the west and south-west of the Transvaal are a number of tribes which have never been united under one head. In 187 z or 1873, the South African Republic claimed a portion of their territory, and prevailed upon one of the tribes to cede it to them. This cession was not recognised by the British Government, and at the time of the Pretorian Convention the boundary line was drawn between the Transvaal and the independent territories, excluding from the former the territory so ceded. Before the annexation of the Transvaal by the late Government, and, indeed, for many years previously, the chiefs had been divided amongst them- selves into parties, and when war broke out some took sides with the British aind some with that of the Boers. Further hostilities betweert these chiefs took place in May, 1881, and though peace was restored for a time, war broke out again in October of the same year. Our agent, Mr. HUDSON, called upon the Boer Government to preserve neutrality, and to a certain extent they did so; but a mission from Mr. HUDSON to negotiate peace with the tribes was not successful. Then Boer volun- teers began to crowd over into the Bechuana country to take part in the war; and although an agreement was arrived at between the Transvaal, the Orange Free State, and the British Government, neither of the former would aid in clearing the country of these marauding parties. Ultimately, two chiefs. Montsiva and Mankoroane, who had sided together, were compelled to grant a large portion of their territory to the white men who had aided the chiefs acting against them. The Transvaal Government accepted the cession, but this is not valid without the con- sent of the Suzerain Power, aud this our Government has never given. The Cape Government were subsequently asked if they would give facilities for the organising of a police force to protect British subjects, and the answer was that in the opinion of the Government the proposal would not be effectual. The case then, Lord DERBY says, stands thus that Bechuana land has been resorted to by adventurers, some of whom come from the Orange Free State, and some from the Transvaal, and a few from our own colonies. They have not the direct support of the Transvaal Government, but they have the sympathy, which is an important element in the consideration of this question, not only of the Dutch population, but of all South Africa. From these facts it will be gathered that the very root of our troubles is the annexa- tion, and it seems almost a pity that the present Government did not, as Mr. MORLEY suggested. immediately on taking office turn out of the Transvaal bag and baggage. There can be no two opinions that it is a great mis- fortune we ever entered into any Convention, for we appear to have incurred a responsibility which may drift us we know not whither. The natives are relying on our support and we cannot abandon them. Moral suasion is good enough in its way, but with a semi- barbarous Government it is not likely to have much effect. We may rest assured, however, that all will be done that it is possible for our Government to do short of drawing the sword, which, spite of Tory impatience to involve this country in another war, will never be unsheathed unless it cannot be avoided. To us it appears a war would rather increase than mitigate our troubles in South African regions.

RAILWAY SERVANTS' BALL AT WIDNES.—A reference to our advertising columns will show that this event takes place on Good Friday, in the Volunteer Hall. Mr. Powell's band will supply the music. The sum of £l3 has been handed to the widow of the late J. J. Garrett, who was drowned in Ramsay Bay through the wreck 3f the George and Sarah, being the proceeds of the recent football match between the clubs of Runcorn and Sale. THE LATE J. J. GARNETT, OF RUNCORN.—As a result of the football match between Runcorn and Sale, held a week ago, £l3 has been handed over to the widow of thelate J. J. Garnett, who was drowned in Ramsey Bay through the wreck of the George and Sarah. FARNWORTH TEMPERANCE AND TOTAL ABSTINENCE SOCIETY.—In connection with the juvenile se.ction of this society, a magic lantern entertainatent, entitled "Little Joey's mission," was given by Mr. J. McDonald Bell. Mr. J. W. Davies presided, and there was a large audience. DISREPUTABLE CHARACTERS AT WIDNES.—On Monday, at Widnes Police Court, a tramp, named Thomas Smith, was charged with being drunk and begging at Widnes, on Saturday, and he was sentenced to 14 days' bard labour.— For begging in Milton-road, Patrick Heyes was similarly dealt with.—Thomas Higgins was sent to gaol for seven (lays for sleeping in the Widnes Alkali Company's works on S'unday night. SUDDEN DEATH AT RUNCORN.—Mr. J. E. Worsley, the deputy coroner, on Tuesday, held an inquest on the body of Mary Hagen, who was found dead on Monday. It ap- peared that on Sunday night the deceased, who lodged with Mrs. Mary Rowley, Mill-street, was at a wake, and although she appeared in her usual health on Monday, on the even- ing of that day, at six o'clock, she was found lying helot e the fire. Life was extinct. The jury returned a verdict of " Found dead." YOUNG MEN'S CHRISTIAN ASSOCIATION HISTORICAL :30CIETY.—On Thursday night a meeting of this society was held in the rooms, High-street, Runcorn. Mr. W. Handley, the president, occupied the chair, and there was a fair audi- eece. Captain Le Coutier delivered his lecture, "The iden- tification of the lost tribes of Israel with the British nation." A discussion followed, and Messrs. Meredith, Fitton, C. Nicksen, Cunningham, and Heal took part. The proceed- ings concluded with the usual vote of thanks. CHURCH OF ENGLAND TEMPERANCE SOCIETY.—Under the auspices of Widnes branch of this society. a lecture was delivered in the National Schools, on Thursday evening, by the Rev. T. Allen Still, of Liverpool. There was a good audience and the Rev. W. H. Duggan presided. The lecturer laid down the axioms that strong drink made men fools, lowered them to mere brutes, and was the means of making thousands lose their eternal souls, for it was writ "No drunkard shall inherit the kingdom of heay.gi." I e usual votes of thanks were passed. ATTACK UPON A MARRIED WOMAN.—Yesterday, at Run- corn Police Court, Samuel Gregory was brought up in custody charged with assaulting Ann Gibson, a married woman.—P.S. Whalley said shortly before 11 o'clock on the previous night he saw the prisoner come out of the Blue Ball Inn, Friar's-street. strike the prosecutrix, and knock her to the ground. He savagely kicked her several times, and P.S. Whalley then reaching the spot, took the prisoner into custody.—The prisoner pleaded that he had received provo- catiou.—He was fined £l, and costs 8s GI. Wepteas LOQAT, BOARD ELECTION has been fixed for the 7th April, the last day for the nominations being Thurs- day, the 22nd inst., but it is unlikely that a contest will fake place. The two rival ratepayers associatiofle have agreed upon the candidates to be nominated, and even if any other candidate is put forward his chance of success will be small. At a meeting of the Owners and Occupiers' Associa- tion a few weeks ago, Dr. O'Keefe did threaten to lead an opposition, but we hear that the Catholic party, which is very strong numerically, discountenance any such attempt. WIDNES POLICE COURT.—On Monday, before Mr. Geo. Pilkington and Mr. Jiro. Brock, the following persons were fined ss. for drunkenness: Thomas Nolan, Patrick Knock- ton, John MacMahon, and George Saxe.—Thomas Gregson was fined 10s. and costs, or, in default, 14 days' imprison- ment, for being drunk in the West Bank Hotel, on Saturday. —Thomas Doyle, Michael Smith, and John Riley were charged with committing a breach of the peace by fighting in Wellington-street, on Saturday, and they were each bound over for their good behaviour for two months. WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD AT WORK —On Wednesday, at Widnes Petty Sessions, before Mr. W. D. Holt and Mr. Holbrook Gaskell, Mr. G. H. Denby, prosecuted the follow- ing persons, on behalf of the Widnes School Board, for ne- glecting to send their children regularly to school ;--ac Sankey, Michael Molloy, James Sullivan, Thiutas Melia, John Martin, Patrick Duffy, Patrick Hyland, John Hindley, Edward Scrutton, Elize Jones, William Brookes' Rechael Tuffe, Bernard Campbell, Bridget Byrne, Richard Traynor, Peter Ford, 'Primes Atkinson, Stephen White, Thomas Gren- mtn, PattFurie, Thomas WEenna, William Burns, Cornelius Higgins Denis Clancy, and Thomas Brown. The usual fine ot is including costs was imposed in each case. A NEW THEATRE EO4 WIDNES.—At Widnes Petty Ses- sions on Wednesday, Mr. Thomas Russell, late of the Pa- vilion Theatre, Widnes, and now manager of the Theatre Royal, Hyde, applied for a theatrical license for a new building which he has erected in Wellingtcn-street, off Hutchinson-street, Widnes.—Superintendent Barker said he had a letter from the surveyor to the Widnes Local Board, which stated that that gentleman had examined the theatre, and in his opinion the gallery had been erected in a satis- factory manner. The license was granted.—Mr. John Smith and Mr. Thomas Edwards became the sureties of the applicant, each in the sum of £5O. SILVER STAR BRIGADE: FIRST DIVIsION: WIDNES BRANcII.—On Tuesday, the monthly entertainment was given by the members. Captain Davies occupied the chair, and the following programme was goneAlerough :—Reading, "In memoriam," Captain John Taylor; recitation," Spare the little birds," S. J. Taylor; recitation, "A dinner and a kiss," S. J. Taylor ; song, "Remember the poor," Alice Whitby; reading, "Pilgrims and the peas," Captain John Taylor; song, " Little acts of kindness," Alice Whitby; reading, "Duke of Brunswick's diamonds," Captain Taylor; song, "A charge to keep I have," Captain Davies and Cap- tain Mason. The customary vote of thanks closed the pro- ceedings. PRIMITIVE METHODIST MISSION : MEETING AT RUNCORN. —On Sunday, the annual sermons in behalf of the Primitive Methodist Home and Foreign Missions were preached at Greenway-road Chapel, in the morning by the Rev. D. Schofield, and in the evening by the Rev. J. Leece' of Crewe. There was a good congregation at each service. On Monday evening the annual missionary meeting was held under the chairmanship of Mr. Joseph Ashley, who was supported by the Revs. J. Pickwell, D. Schofield, J. Leece, and Mr. T. Stringfellow. The report, read by the Rev. D. Schofield, showed that the society was in a progressing and flourishing condition. Appropriate addresses were delivered, and a collection was taken at the close. LAUNCH OF AN IRON TUG AT WESTON. The Weston Point Towing Company have added another iron tug to their fleet of river steamers. The new tug, which was launched from the side of the Church Gut on Saturday last in the Presence of a large number of spectators, has Ceen built from the designs of Mr. W. Ritchie, engineer, and is about 90 feet in length. It has been built under the personal superinten- dence of Captain Clark, and is estimated to cost £4,000 when finished. The ironwork was entrusted to Mr. Parker, of Northwich, and Messrs. Stubbs and Son, of Runcorn, have done all the woodwork. The engines will be provided by Mr. E. Foden, of Sandbach, and are to be of good towing pewer. The boat will be chartered to carry passengers as far as the north-west lightship. As the vessel left the stays i was named "Celebrator" by Miss Lizzie Clark. JUVENILE THIEVES AT WIDNES.—At Widnes Police Court, on Monday, John Robert Martin, 12 years of age, was charged with stealing a can of salmon frorn the shop of Mr. J. E. Johnson, provision dealer. About nine o'clock on Friday morning the prisoner entered the shop, and purchased a quarter of a pound of butter. As the prisoner was leaving, Abraham Parkinson, the assistant, noticed that he had some- thing bulky under his coat, called him back, and, found the tin of salmon produced in his possession. The prisoner pleaded guilty, and he was ordered to receive six strokes with the birch rod.—A. similar sentence was passed upon another boy named Michael Burns, who was convicted of stealing a quantity of coal, of the value of lid, the property of the London and North-Western Railway Co. Inspector Barnett observed that the boy's mother ought really to be standing in the dock in place of her son. RUNCORN BURIAL BOARD.—This Board met on Thursday afternoon, at the Cemetery Offices, Greenway-read. Ia the absence of Mr. Whittaker, Mr. Coleburn presided; and there.were also present—Messrs. G. Most, W. Mellor, Wm. Littler, and W. F. Salkeld (secretary).—The secretary's statement showed that during the eleven months ending February 35th, there had been 374 interments, or an in- crease over the corresponding period of the previous year of 143.. The amount received in fees during the same period was £346 16s. 7d., or an increase of £llB 6e. sd.—Mr. Moss stated that the Finance Committee had passed accounts amounting to £65 6s. 7d., and owing to the increased re- venue from funerals during the year, there would be no necessity to make a precept on the overseers for the six months ending September 30th.—A notice was ordered to be served on the overseers calling a meeting of ratepayers to appoint two persons to audit the Beard's accounts.—The overseers having demanded payment of a poor's rate for the gardener's lodge, Ford, the occupier, questioned his liability to pay the amount, as it was stated when he Was appointed that all rates should be paid by the Board. The resolution appointing the gardener was found, but as no mention was made of any such agreement, the Board decided that the rate must be paid by Ford. FATAL ACCIDENT AT RUNCORN DOCKS.—Yesterday morn- leg, at the Devonshire Hotel, Runcorn, Mr. J. E. Worsley, the deputy coroner, held an inquest on the body of a dock labourer, named Thomas Feeney, who died on Wednesday night from injuries received on the previous day. From the evidence it appeared that the deceased, with several other men, was helping to unload the flat Alice and Mary, which was carrying sulphur ore. The ore was placed in a bucket, which was then attached to the chain of the crane, which was in charge of a boy named Edward Hughes, of 8, Wellington-street. About five o'clock a bucketful of the ore was being wound up when a piece of the material fell off into the hold of the fiat, striking the deceased on the head. He was conveyed to Dr. lalouritz's surgery, where his head was dressed. Afterwards he was corweyed to his lodgings at 32, Handley-street, Runcorn, where he died at eight o'clock the following evening.—A juryman asked if there was no regulation as to filling the buckets.—The Coroner expressed the opinion that it was very desirable that men who were employed in the work of unloading flats should be careful in the first place not lo fill the buckets which had to be wound over their heads too full, and in the second place to stand clear while the bucket was being wound up.—The jury returned a verdict of " Accident il death."—Mr. Meadowcroft watched the proceedings on ha- half of the Navigation Company.

RUNCORN FREE PUBLIC LIBRARY.—The Library Com- mittee met on Thursday, at the Public Offices, Runcorn. In the absence of Dr. Steele, the Vice-Chairman presided, and there were also present Messrs. P. Briscoe, J. R. Frith, G. Rhodes, W. Handley, and W. Brookes (secretary).—The librarian's report showed that during the month of Feb- ruary, 1,469 books had been borrowed from the library.—A vote of thanks was accorded to Sir James A. Picton and Mr. John Clarke for gifts of books during the month, on the motion of Mr. Handley, seconded by Mr. Frith.—Mr. Handley remarked that the books presented by Sir James Picton would really be the commencement of a reference library, which was very much needed in connection with the lending department.—On the motion of Mr. Handley, seconded by Mr. Simpson, it was decided that application be made to the Commissioners for the residue of the library rate.—There was no other business.

ENGLISH CONGREGATIONAL CHAPEL BUILDING SOCIETY. —The thirtieth annual meeting of the English Congrega- tional Chapel Building Society, was held at Derby, on Wednesday evening, the Mayor of Derby presiding. The society was founded in Derby in March, 1853, and since its formation has assisted in the erection of 616 chapels and 38 manses. The total aid by the society, paid and promised, has.amounted to £150,000. The loan fund amounts to £41,000, and the total grants advanced have been £62,000, of which £12,000 has been returned. £3,000 has been ex- pended in Ireland. Aid is also given to colonial churches. The total income last year was £13,491, being an advance of £2,974 on the previous year. The number of chapels con- tributing and individual contributors is larger than ever be- fore. The report containing the above facts was read by the Rev. J. C. Galloway, Birmingham, secretary. All the officers were re-elected, including Messrs. R. S. Hudson (Chester), president; Thomas Simpson (Caton, Lancashire), chief of committee; L. J. Crossley (Halifax), and Josiah Alexander (London), treasurers; the Rev J. C. Galloway, secretary; Mr. Conder (London), asgistant secretary; and the Rev. H. J. Heathcote (Birmingham), travelling repre- sentative.

THE PRUDENTIAL ASSURANCE COMPANY, LIMITED.—In our advertising columns will be found the annual report of this company, which shows that its business is still on the increase. The invested funds, including the paid-up capital, now exceed three millions, viz, ordinary branch £928,176, and industrial branch £2,119,223. The new business of the ordinary branch for the year consists of 7,067 pllicfes, as- suring the sum of £856,148, and producing a new annual premium income of £32,777. The claims of the year amount to £73,621, representing 455 deaths and 24 endowment assurances matured. The annual premium income at the end of the year is £164,949, being an increase of £22,216 over the year 1881. The premiums actually received during the year in the industrial branch are £2,126,022 3s 11d, as compared with the sum of £1,849,494 18e 5d received dur- ino 1881, being an increase of premium receipts of £276,527 ss'6(l. The claims of the year amounted to £773,813. and the total amount of claims paid in this branch is £4,955, 925. The total expenses of this branch as compared with those of the previous years show a reduction of nearly 21 per cent. on the premium income. The company, it is gra- +. 'know. is now represented in every part o the United Kingdom, and the charges for extension expenses no longer appear in the account. Some conception of the amaz- ing amount of business done by this company may be gathered from the lid that last year there was spent in policy stamps, postage and receipt stamps, no less than £30,760 at the head office only. The Prudential undoubtedly occupies the premier position among the insurance societies; more than one-seventh cf the entire population of Great Britain and Ireland is insured in it, and its operations are being very rapidly extended and increased. The claims paid in the Chester and Runcorn districts amounted last year to no less a sum than £3,500.

div.head: ACCOMPLISHED YOUNG THIEVES AT
div.p: ACCOMPLISHED YOUNG THIEVES AT
RUNCORN,

At Runcorn Pollee Court, on Monday, before Mr. W Bankes sod Mr. S. B. Chadwick, three boys named Jdseph Green (9), Thomas Woodfine (11), and Owen MacDonald (10) were brought up in custody charged with having, on Saturday. stolen a purse containing 53. from the person of Annie Elizabeth Hillidge, wife of John Hillidge, of Coliens- street ; and also with receiving the same knowing it to be stolen.—Froin the statement of Mr. Superintendent Wil- liamson, it appeared that between four and five o'clock the prosecutrix went into Messrs. Tunna and Hunt's shop to mike some purchases. Before doing so she counted from her purse the money she would require replacing in her ulster pocket, the purse containing ss. two half-crowns' At that time the prisoners were standing at the window, and prosecutrix, after transacting her business, discovered that her purse had been stolen. Information was given to the police, and subsequently Green was apprehended. The boy stated that MacDonald had pushed his (Green's) hand into ; the prosecuttix's pocket, and told him to take the money. , The other prisoners were then apprehended. They stated they had spent a portion of the money in potato pie at a shop in Church-street. MacDonald offered to show where the other portion of the money was hidden, and he took P.C. Bossons to a field opposite the Green- way Vaults, where the purse, containing 4s. 2A-1., was found concealed in the soil. The receipt which the purse contained was missing, but one of the prisoners afterwards stated that it would be found at the Belvedere. P.C. Bossons went there and found the receipt torn into 13 pieces. Mr. Williamson said from the way the prisoners had gone about the robbery, he thought it was not the first time they had been guilty of such conduct. The state the prisoners were in at the time did not speak well for their parents. They were not then clean and attired as they were now, but without shoes and stockings and very dirty, and he was afraid the boys' surroundings at home had been the cause of this case arising.—Evidence having been given by P.Cs. Finney and Bossons, and P.S. Mac Michael, the prisoners were formally charged. Green and MacDonald pleaded guilty, but Woodfine pleaded not guilty, saying be "had only 2V—Mr. Bankes said the 13-mch considered the parents were to blame for the way in which they had brought their children up, and ordered each prisoner to re- ceive six strokes with the birch rod.

PRESCOT UNITED METHODIST MIS- SIONARY SOCIETY. Two sermons were preached on Sunday in Victoria-place chapel, Prescot, on behalf of the United Methodist Free Church Home and Foreign Missions. The sermon in the morning was preached by the Rev. J. Dimond, Birkenhead; and that in the evening by the Rev. J. Sarvent, St. Helens. 'The collections amounted to about £4. On Monday even- ing a missionary meeting was held in the same chapel, Mr. Rigby Jones, of Liverpool, presided, and there were also on the platform the Rev. J. Johnston, Rev. J. Sarvent, and Mr. Richard Lloyd. The proceedings having been opened with a hymn and prayer, the Rev. J. Johnston delivered an interesting athiress, in the course of which he expressed great and increasing confidence in missionary enterprise. It was impossible to read the accounts of travellers without being convinced of the truth that were it not for Christian missionaries and the Christian literature diffused by them many of those lands which had been opened up to emigra- tion and commercial enterprise would be in a pitiable and deplorable condition. The missionary enterprise proper was not yet a century old, baying begun with the Baptist Society in 1702, but when they looked at what had been done in the first twenty or thirty years of the present century, and looked at the present and the advancement which had been made, and the blessings which Christianity had diffused through the instrumentality of mission- aries their hearts were constrained to gratitude to Almighty God that He had so richly ar d abundantly blessed their manifold labours and sacrifices. One hundred and fifty millions of copies of the scriptures had through missionaries been circulated, and the Bible had been translated into 300 languages and dialects. It had been calcul tted that there was not one city on the face of the earth of any position which had not some representative of Jesus Christ. who carried the Gospel and represented his Master just as ambassadors represented the courts of different nations. In China in 1843 there were six converts to the Christian faith, out of a population of 400 millions. In 1881 there were no fewer than 50,000 converts. India boasted of no fewer than 000,000 converts, while in Africa there were 40 different missionary stations and 175,000 members of churches. In Japan in 1872 there were no missionaries, while in 1882 they counted 3,799 converts. In Madagascar, with a popu- lation of five millions, there were 71,000 church members and 250,000 men and women worshipping every Sunday in houses of prayer. In the Fiji Islands, out of a population of 120,000, no fewer than 102,000 were found every Sunday listening to the word of the true God; while in the Sand- wich Islands, the New Hebrides, and Tahiti the people were beginning to be as beautiful in their Christians as their land was beautiful. When they thought of those wondrous results or fifty or ..3xty years, should they not say to their hearts be of good courage, be of great faith, be of fervent hope, for the Lord's work shall prosper. • Having pointed out the magnitude of the work yet to be done, he urged every one to be earnest in supporting Christians.—Th, other gentlemen on the platform also addressed tht. meeting.

div.head: LATEST NEWS.
div.p: LATEST NEWS.

THE LONDON OUTRAGE. LATEST DETAILS. Until a late hour on Thursday night, a considerable crowd loitered near the scene and speculated upon the origin of the affair, or occupied themselves in observing the many signs apparent on all hands of the violence with which the explosion had shaken every building in the locality. It was impossible to walk a single yard in any of the adjoining streets without treading upon broken glass. It is indeed somewhat remarkable that so few persons should have been cut by the glass, which at many places fell in showers-from broken windows, especially from such' windows as were composed of large panes of plate glass. It is probable that dynamite was the agent employed, and the explosion was deliberately designed by some one, who placed the dynamite between the balustrade and the window of the copying clerks room. This view is corroborated by the latest ex- amination of the cellar, where it is seen that some of the nearer portions of the side walls and of the roof which formed the ceiling of the clerks' room have been forced inwards and downwards, although a large mass of masonry has also been blown over into the street. As soon as the outrage became known the authorities at Scotland Yard telegzaphed to all the Metropolitan out di§- 1 1 tricts directing special precautions regarding Government buildings. It is believed that the explosive was certainly placed outside the window, and not in the cellar, as had been rumoured. No arrests had, up to noon yesterday, been male, and some time must elapse before any can be ex- pected. The Daily News states :—At midnight a consultation was held at the King-street police office between the Home Secretary and the director of criminal investigations. Several witnesses were examined, and we understand that the oonclusion arrived at was that the explosion took place from within the room that was wrecked, not from outside, as was at first generally supposed. It was rumoured in the House of Commons that the intention of the persons respon- sible for the outrage was to blow up the Treasury, where Mr. Gladstone was at the time. No credence is attached to this suggestion in official quarters, where it is believed that the comparatively secluded position of the building where the explosive substance was fired pointed it out as the most suitable place. THE AT I'EMPT TO WRECK THE TIMES. Further particulars with reference to the canister which was found on the premises of the Times newspaper leave no doubt that a most diabolical outrage was contemplated. The canister was placed on a window sill in the neighbourhood of the publishing and stereotyping department, where a con- siderable number of men were at work at the time. Owing probably to the slope of the sill the canister slipped and fell, 11(1 thus attention was attracted to it, but on the discovery of the character of the canister, the men who discovered it were so alarmed that no definite account of the condition and circumstances under which it waf3 discovered can be gleaned. It is fortunate that the canister fell in the manner described, as that had the effect of detaching the lighted fuse connected with it. OFFICIAL INVESTIGATION. At nine o'clock yesterday morning Colonel Majendie, the Government Inspector of Explosives, who was accompanied by Mr. T. Taylor, one of the sufveyors of the Department of Works and Public Buildings, was shown over the injured edifice by the officials connected therewith. Mr. Howard Vincent, the Director of Criminal Investigations, who had been early on the spot, also took part in the examination, whieh was begun at the seat of the explosion and its neighbourhood. Photographs will be taken of the position of the debris, so that its inclination, if this can throw light on the exact spot where the explo- sive was situated, may be noted with exactness. The scientific tests usual in such cases with experts will like- wise have to be applied, and the results noted before any steps are taken to clear away the rubbish and repair the damage done. The police of course are very busy over the affair. They are instituting a strict search for any testi- mony that may be available to clear up the mystery which at present exists concerning this alarming occurrence. The constables on duty in:the locality at the time of the ex- plosion have been called upon for a very particular account of what came under their observation just ptevious to it. The persons observed in the locality, the times at which they were seen, and any conduct on their part in any way unusual, are the points regarding which these officers are being interrogated. Nothing, however, has yet been dis- covered, or if discovered, has yet been revealed by the police authorities that can satisfy the natural curiosity of the public. Some time must elapse before the investigations which suggest themselves in connection with such art event will be completed. Up till two o'clock yesterday morning the p dice had an arduone task in keep- ing back the crowds which the report had brought to the spot. After that hour, however, the press of people became much less, and it was found possible to reduce the number of constables on duty. This was very desirable, inasmuch as many of these men had been on special service in con- nection with the boat race during the day, and were hardly in a fit condition to remain standing on fixed point duty throughout a night atf keen frost. As soon as day broke the crowd returned. All who had occasion to pass that way to their business tried to get a view of the place, and once there they were tempted to linger much longer than was aereeable to the police. Daylight revealed more com- pletely the destruction which had taken place in the win- dows of the neighbourhood. What could not be observed in the darkness was now made conspicuosly plain, namely, that the Local Government Board offices had not a whole windew, and that nearly all the offices, shops, and dwellings facing them were in a like plight. At the post-office at the corner of King-street, for instance, the clerks were discharging their functions muffled up to the eyes. They were rather worse off, indeed, than had they been in the open air, for not only had they the full nip of the frosty air, but they had its keenness and danger intensi- Ified by several very thorough draughts. The Government clerks who were deprived of the protection of windows did not venture, it is needless to say, to risk a heavy cold by sticking to their usual desks. What work they have which cannot be deferred will be carried on elsewhere until the glaziers have fixed some plate-glass between them and the outer air. There will be some brisk business all roand for the glaziers in the neighbourhood. Until their services can be secured many of the householders and shopkeepers are getting boarded up the windows which are not provided with shutters. The fire brigade with their engines were with- drawn daring. the night, there being RO .likelihood of any outbreak which would call for their services. LATER. The Central News telegraphs last night :—Very little has transpired to-day calculated to throw light upon the out- rage. The facts remain as telegraphed yesterday. Colonel Majendie, H.M. Inspector of Explosives, who was sum- moned last night, was early to-day in attendance at the spot, and made a most detailed investigation of everything likely to have any bearing upon the means employed to effect the explosion. That dynamite was the substance used there is now no doubt; but still what puzzles the authorities is the manner in which the perpetrators fired-the material. ' There is no trace of Any vessel or fragments thereof in which I 1 the explosive could have been carried, nor any sign of mec- hanism which could have produced concussion necessary to cause an explosion. These may have been blown into the smallest:atoms,but even then some portions should have been I found. Colonel Majendie will:shortly make.his official report, when he will fully deal with the matter. In the meantime the police are pursuing the sirictea and most careful in- quiries with the view of obtaining some clue to the mis- creants who planned and effected the outrage. Very little doubt is enterteined that these belonged to one or other of the associations of disaffected Irishmen, upon whose ex- istence such a lurid light has recently been thrown. It will be remembered that some months ego the authorities received intimation of threats to blow up public buildings in London, and although it is possible that there may be no connection between that matter and the present outrage, the sequence is certainly a curious one. Sir Charles Mice, who presided over the department which carried on its work in the wrecked building, has been on the spot the greater part of the day, making arrangements for enabling business to be proceeded with as far as possible during the time required for the necessary repairs, on which the workmen are already engaged. He has given up his private office for the accommodation of a portion of the staff whose rooms are uninhabitable. Sir Charles has ex- pressed the opinion that the outrage was not intended as an attempt to assassinate himself or any of the other cfficials of the department, but that the perpetrators had in view merely a widespread destruction of property. Crowds remained at the scene of the outrage all last night, despite the inclemency of the weather, and as day broke and the morning advanced ever-increasing streams of spectators were attracted to the spot. The sightseers were of all ranks and conditions in life, from the heir apparent down to the omnipresent London rough and the hatless and shoeless city arab. Many carriages were stopped while .assing through the neighbourhood, their occupants taking the opportunity of gratifying their curiosity by a sight which is fortunately seldom seen in thie country—a

A terrible tragedy was enacted i Liverpool yesterday morning. A bricklayer's labourer, named M'lntyre, had a drunken quarrel with his wife, who refused to give him more money for drink. When the woman declined to give him the money he produced a revolver and fired at her. She fled upstairs, and he, with the poker ia one hand and the revol- ver in the other, followed her. He knocked her down and beat her fearfully over her head with the poker, leaving her for dead. He then seems to have gone downstairs and shot himself through the head with the revolver, death being in- stantaneous. The woman is not expected to recover. In M'lntyre's pockets were found 40 revolver cartridges, but where he obtained them is at present a mystery. M'lntyre was 46 and his wife somewhat younger.—A later telegram says the woman Wlntyre is not expected to recover. lihe has been shot in the breast, and the doctors have extracted the bullet, but the wounds inflicted on her head with the poker ate of a terrible character.
EXTRAORDINARY FATAL ACCIDENT AT WIGAN.

An extraordinary Zoccurrence took place near Ince station, Wigan, late on Thursday night, resulting in the death of one man and in several othets having narrow es- capes. Without any: warning the front of two cottages in Viaduct-street gave way, and disappeared with a loud crash down an old coal pit shaft which suddenly disclosed itself. It appears that many years ago coal was worked from this pit, but the shaft was filled, and cottages erected on the surface. The material must have been forced into the old workings, and arching over the top of the shaft given way. One house was tenanted by an old man, named plunlsett, who escaped, but his son-in-law John Banks, was buried in the falling debris, and his body has not yet been recovered. His wife, who is nearly blind, also narrowly escaped. The accident has caused great constern- tion, other houses in the neighbourhood being vacated by the tenants.

On Thursfiay night, a contingent of the Whitchurch Blue Ribbon Army were boycotted at Marbury, Cheshire. David Paterson, surgeon, residing in a fashionable quarter of Liverpool, was yesterday fined 40s. and costs for using abusive language towards the Rev. T. B. Banner, a local Incumbent.

The London and North-Western Railway authorities have given notice to their employes that the Crewe railway works will be closed from Thursday next to the Tuesday follow- ing, for the Easter holidays. Reports from various points state that on Thursday night the fall of snow in the North of Scotland averaged six to eight inches in depth. Twenty degrees of frost were registered at Kingussie, Invernesshire, and fifty degrses at Birnam, Perthshire. Vegetation has received a severe check, and the intensity of the cold is also telling with severe effe3t on the young lambs.

Northcote, said that with regard to the explosion at the Local Government Board offices he had no further information to give in ad- tion to that already known. Tun TRANSVAAL.—The adjourned debate on Mr. Gorst's motion with regard to affairs in the Transvall, was resumed. —Mr. FORS ma objected to the motion. He differed from the opinions that hait been expressed by Mr. Ashley, and he ine‘.eted that the Bechuana people were alliee of the British and ought not to be deserted because they were black men. Sir 11. Robinson and Sir George Colley had treated them as such, and he did not see why the British Government should allow the cattle and lands of these people to be plundered by the Boers. He insisted that the Convention gave more than the right to remonstrate. It imposed obli- gations, and those obligations ought to be ob- served. It might be said that the Transvaal Government was too weak to protect natives from raids by filibusters; but it appeared it was strong enough to repudiate all its engage- ments with the British Government. Ile contended that the Convention had not only been broken by the Boers, but treated with absolute contempt, and the question now war What's to be done ? " lie did not think appealing to the public feeling of the Boers would do any good. Compensa- tion would not meet the case, but the Government ought to be earnest when the Dutch representatives arrived here, and if that was not sufficient we ought to use on strength to protect our allies. (Loud Opposition cheers.) He preferred the amendment of Sir M. H. Beach to that of Mr. Cartwright. —Mr. GLADSTONE expressed his surprise at the speech of Mr. Forster, who had done his best to make the action of the British Government ridiculous and advocated the commence- ment of another South African war.—Mr. FORSTER said if the British Government was earnest in its remonstrance with the Boer representative the use of strength would become unnecessary.—Mr. GLADSTONE insisted we had hitherto acted up to our obligations, and justified the Government for not taking part in the quarrel in Bechuana land, where one part of the people were in favour of the Boers, and the other part opposed to them, the latter being the weaker. He would not say what might be done, but the Government declined to take military steps to quell disorder made worse by the action of the free booters. Armed occupation meant annexation, and that would only result in another war. The Government would do their best' for justice. They would not renounce a single right they possessed, but they would not go to war until they could enter on a just one. With regard to the motion and amend- ment, the Government would rote against the motion of Mr. Gorst. He suggested Mr. Cartwright should withdraw part of his amendment. Sir M. H. Beach's words could then be added to that amendment. The Government would move an amendment stating that, in the event of the inability of the Transvaal Government to atop incursions inte Becknana Land, the Government would make provision for any of the chiefs that had claims upon them.—Sir M. BEACH rose and said the sum and substance of the speech of the Prime Minister's was that they intended to do nothing, as the amendment he proposed to move to his amendment simply embodied the proposals announced by the Under Secretary for the Colonies, who proposed money compensation to chiefs. His object in bringing forward the subject was not to urge the Government to enter on another war; but what he desired was that the country shou:d know who was responsible for the disgraceful desertion !of British allies in Bechnana Land. He con- demned the Government for entering into the convention, and then allowing it to be set aside and defied by the 80er5.... Lord COLON CAMPBELL also condemned the action of the Government.—Lord It. CHURCHILL said the object of the motion was not to censure the Gevetnneent, bnt to obtain justice for our allies.--. Mr. RATHBONE opposed the motion, and talked it out. —The debate was adjourned until Tuesday fortnight at two, after which the hitting was suepeuded.---e The SPEAKER resumed the chair at five minutes past nines. and the House was counted out immediately afterwards.

The latter was accompanied by Lord Richard Grosvenor, and after viewing the scene he walked from Downing-street to the House of Commons. The right hon. gentleman was loudly cheered as he passed. Several detectives kept the while an unobtrusive guard over his safety, and we learn that his official residence In Downing-street has been placed under extra police super- vision as a matter of precaution. Sir William Harcourt, and the authorities at the loin Office, as well as other officials, believe that the design was to destroy that portion of the Hume Offiste where the busi- ness of the Criminal Investigation Department is transacted. These rooms are on the second floor, and close above that part of the Local Government Board buildings where the explosion occurred. They sustained, however, little dama. beyond the breaking of windows and overturning of fur- niture.

The Home Office intends to offer a reward of £l,OOO for the apprehension and conviction of the person who caustd the explosion. A reward will also be offered for the appre- hension of the authors of thu attempt at Trinity House Square.

WARRINGTON AND THE SHIP CANAL.

am glad to see from your last issue that the Rivers Committee, whose proper business it is to look after the interests of the ratepayers in this matter, have, albeit at the eleventh hour, shown signs of life and a reason for their existence. The magnitude, and the interests involved, render this a subject worthy of the highest consideration and the gravest deliberation. In dealing with the question before us it is best to discard sentiment and enthusiasm, leaving these instable agents for the use of riparian owners on the proposed route and the promoters of the scheme. The pleasures of hope and the golden anticipation of future profit may have prevented them seeing that their interests are not the interests of the great bulk of the Warrington rate- payers. Having no pecuniary interests in this scheme un- shared by the bulkof my fellow townsmen,the ratepayers,l beg to thank the Rivers Committee for the care they are taking in this matter, and to advocate deliberation in dealing with it. Twenty years constant practical experience in the naviga- tion of our noble waterway, and the earnest desire that possesses me not to have it imperilled either as a source of profit or pleasure, must be my excuse for breaking silence on this question. In common with every person of right mind and feeling, I should be glad to rejoice with the 6,000,000.wh0 are said to be anxiously awaiting this boon in the full fruition of their hopes on the establishment and suc- cessful working of this grand scheme. But while we wish the general scheme every success, we must have a care, we people on its track, that its prosperity and progress is not gained at the expense of ours. Let us look a few facts in the face. .I. At present we have a more or less efficient free waterway between Bank Quay and Liverpool. 11. It is capable of great improvement, and could be made to accom- modate the whole of the traffic between the twe towns. 111. It suffers at present from having so little depth at low water—i.e., from tidal silting and the want of fresh water scour. Now the making of a tidal canal would imperil these advantages and increase these evils. I. The present free navigation would be bat and be subject to toll. 11. The canal must necessarily take its stream water from the Mersey basin, thus lessening the present deficient scour. HI. Its influence at the Runcorn end of the canal would be, by the increased capacity for tidal influx, to increase the speed of the inflowing tide, and, in like ratio, its silting effects. The effect of the proposed half-tide training walls in the estuary would be to plant sunken reefs to add to the dangers of the present navigation. As to the river as a source of pleasant recreation, no one says a word in defence of rights which the poorest at present enjoy, but which then will be a thing of the past.—l am, sir, Litc., JOHN PEERS. Liverpool, March, 1883.
