div.head: EMIGRANT LIFE IN WINNIPEG.
div.p: EMIGRANT LIFE IN WINNIPEG.

LETTER FROM A LANCASHIRE MAN. Mr. James Suinrnersgill, of Sankey Bridges, has forwarded to us for publication a letter from a relative of his, a labouring man, who emigrated from Manchester some 12 months ago Co Winnipeg, Canada, in which the writer gives the following interesting particulars of his adopted city :—Winnipeg, says the writer, is a city on the Red River, with a population of about 25,000; and perhaps it may in- terest you to know that Winnipeg is an Indian name which means "muddy water." It has grown very rapidly, and, as yet, there are to be seen everywhere traces of a ruder , existence; but the rude shanties which suited the Winni- I peggers of ten years ago are fast disappearing before grand and stately buildings. Buildings rise like mushrooms. It scarcely looks the same city it did nine months ago. One large block of stores (and Canadians call shops stores) have been built last summer, which are the grandest I have seen anywhere. They are brick buildings, five storeys high. The first storey is supported by huge iron columns, andlthe whole building is then veneered over with ornamental zinc, having a beautiful deep cornice overhanging the top:storey. These grand buildings are called the " Cuachon Blocks," and are admitted to be the finest in the whole Dominion. Then the Hudson Bay.CompanY'have 80me fine stores just opposite, which are built of splendid red brick; and I am told that every brick in these stores cost 8 cents (4d. in English money) to lay them. And besides these, there is not a bank in Canada but what is represented here, aud most of them have very large buildings, especially the banks of Montreal and Ontario. The Canadian Pacific Railway Sindicate have now a large station in course of building, and also a large machine shop which will employ over a thousand hands when completed. At the west end of the city dwell the gentry, and I observe a great deal of artistic taste in the style of their houses. Along many of the streets ae this end of the city are planted maple trees, which present a charming appearance. But I also observe that work, taken on the whole, is not nearly so well done as in England, although it may surpass it in artistic taste. The principal street in the city is Main-street, which is a handsome street indeed. It is one hundred feet wide, and will be five miles long when completed. It has now a line of buildings extending a dis- tance of over two miles, and buildings, too, which would be a credit to any city in the world. Next spring they are going to build a very large college just off Main-street at a cost of $50,000 (or about ten thousand pounds, speaking in round numbers), which will certainly be a benefit to the city in more ways than one. We have churches of every denomination here. The Methodist I consider to be the strongest. I may just say that Methodism has conferred a very high honour on Winnipeg. One of our ministers, Rev. Dr. Rice, has been made president of the Methodist Chlirch of Canada. He is an old man, and an excellent preacher; but we are shortly going to lose him, for he is appointed to go to Toronto. We have little variety of scenery here, it being all prairie. In whichever direction we look we see nothing but the bending sky touching the beautiful prairie land. Along the banks of the rivers it is nicely wooded, and pre- sents a picturesque appearance; but taken on the whole we see little variety of scenery. There is a great trade done in every department, and Winnipeg from its very position must of necessity continue to be the great trading centre of the North-West. Vow, as to the prospects for a man here, I may just say that they are not so good as might at first appear. For it is mostly outdoor work, and the winters are co long and severe that the building trade almost comes ta a standstill. There are hundreds of workingmen at this moment walking the streets who cannot get work; but there are few signs of poverty, for men as a rule, if they be careful, earn as much as keeps them through the winter. Now, I think a man makes a sad mistake if he comes out here with no other object than working as an artisan, for this part of Canada has not yet passed through its experi- mental period, and things have a fictitious value; few specu- late to hold as a permanent investment; and there is a great want of capital, which to a great extent cripples enterprise. I think the best thing a man can do is take up land and be- come a farmer, and then be has a living in the soil, no matter what else may betide. That is what I intend to do when I see my way clear. However, I consider a working- man better off by far here than he is in England. There is a great deal of money to be made during the summer, and men do make hay while the sun shines. I will just give you a few examples of the wages earned here during the summer :—Carpenters earned three dollars (12s 6d) per day, and some even earned three and a half dollars per day through the months of July, August, and September. Brick- layers during those months earned six dollars (D. ss) per day, and in a few cases seven dollars; but bricklayers were not able to work as long through the summer as carpenters, which must be taken into consideration. Masons earned from three to four dollars per day. Of course wages come down during the winter and spring. I commenced last spring to work a sawing machine at two dollars (8s 4d) per day; then I got advanced 25 cents per day, making my wages Os 41d per day. Towards the end of July I left that job and went to help the plasterers at a wage of three dol- lars (123 6d) per day, where I continued to work until I broke down ill. lam now working at an iron works at two dollars (8s 4d) per day. Board is from five dollars (£1 Os 10d) to six dollars (£1 ss) per week. 1 pay five dollars. But men, especially if their wives be with them, get tents to live in during the summer, and build shanties for winter. It al- most looks as if an army were encamped round Winnipeg to see these tents in the summer. As for our Manitoba winter, I think that to say they are exceedingly doid would scarcely give you an idea of what they are like. The thermometer often registers 25 below zero, and some days it even falls to 48 below zero. But 48 does not feel so cold as 25 when the wind prevails. When the thermometer gets to 40 wind ceases; but it is more stealthy for all that. For instance, you may just walk down the street at 40, thinking it is not so cold as yesterday at 25 with a wind; but you soon find out the fact, for somebody meeting you calls out, "Eh, your nose is frozen," and putting your hand to your nose you find it as hard as a stone. We have to be very careful, for we lose all feeling when we are frozen, and it becomes a serious matter if we allow it to keep going on. The part frozen becomes as white as milk, and if it be any part of your face you may be told of it; but if it be your feet or hands, they being covered, you rarely find it out until night, and then you are made to smart. If we go out our beards become filled with icicles, giving us the appearance of Father Christmas. Many times I have found my beard full of icicles as I lay in bed, and the timber in the house has been cracking all night like the shot of a gun, and the cold , beating upon my face like a hammer filled with needles I so that sleep has been impossible. All this may sound dread- ful, but on the whole I am rather enjoying it, and would rather have a Canadian winter by far than an English one. In fact, winter seems to be the most enjoyable season. The sun shines brilliantly all day long, so that if we did not feel the effects of the cold we might mistake it for summer, and the nights, when the moon is shining, are simply lovely. It is a delight- ful sight to see the sleighs gliding through snow, and to hear the ringing bells on the horses, just as you see them in pictures of Canadian winter life. E. A. Poe gives a nice description of this in his "Bells." And it is very amusing to see the children who have small sleighs driven by dogs —with bells on of course. We dress in furs, which give us , the appearance of grizzly bears, when we go about our daily business, or to spend an evening on the ice. I rather like Manitoba winters, and only wish that many dear ones were here to share them with me.

EDUCATIONAL .GRANTS TO SCILOOLS.—A return issued bn Wednesday shows that the expenditure for educational grants was divided as follows :—On schools connected with Church of England, £1,317,803; on British, undenomina- tional, and other schools £221,933; on Wesleyan, schools, £111,956; on Roman Catholic schools, £137,244; on board schools, £813,408; on. parochial union schools, £120; administration, £196,929; organisation of districts, £283; grants to school boards, £2,325; total, £2,802,005. The increase on Church of England schools amounted to £65,786; Wesleyan schools, £932; Roman Catholic schools, £11,642; and board schools, £106,978; while there was a decrease of £2,813 to British and undeneminational 'shoo's.

A SCOTCH BREACH or Puomrsz.—An action for breach of promise of marriage was heard at Inverness Sheriff Court, on Tuesday. It was raised by Miss Georgina Elphinstone, Strathsteven, neai Brora, Sutherlandshire, against Alex. Forbes, contractor, near Beauly. Damages were laid at £2OO. Miss Elphinstone is 26 years of age, and Forbes about 27. She first made his acquaintance in 1878, when be was employed on the Brora Riilway Works, learning to be a "practical engineer." Miss Elphinstone said Forbes paid his addresses to her, and succeeded in gaining her affections. He left Brora in 1880. Forbes continued to correspond with the pursuer until about October last, when his letters stopped, and although she wrote him repeatedly for an explanation, she received no reply. The following; letter was written by Forbes to his sweetheart in September, 1881 :—I visited the Muir of Ord Market, on Thursday, and very much enjoyed myself. Of course, I walked there, add drove home in a waggonette, the last seat of which was en- tirely occupied by a real rustic beauty and myself. Age of the rustic beauty, 20 years; weight, 14 atone. We two were Plentifully supplied with yellow haddocks by farmers in the front seats, but as I was smoking heavily, and, there- fore s couldight, each enho t eat, the rustic beauty put five haddocks out weighing 241 b. She, the rustic beauty, gave me her address, and invited me to call, but I was trio much frightened by the scene in the waggonette. I am very busy, and all that sort of thing. To-morrow is pay day. It is now, as I look at my watch, two o'clock on Saturday morn- ing, and I have been writing or rather scrawling since eight o'clock tin Friday night--quite too much of a good thing.— After the bearing of a portion of the proof the parties agreed to settle the case, Forbes paying the woman £4O, and £l5 as expenses—total, £55. There is nothing more nourishing and warming in eold weather than a cup of really good Cocoa, but the diffi.ulty has been to obtain it pure. This May be sec wed at a coo: of nne halfpenny fora large breakfast cup by using Cadbury's Cocos, which pea three times as far as the adulterated and sta.-, hy conripoonds ordinarily sold, the smallest packet making four- teen breakfast cups of strong cocoa.—Advt.

div.head: IRE EXAMINER SATTTIR,DAY, MARCH 17, 1883.
div.p: IRE EXAMINER SATTTIR,DAY, MARCH 17, 1883.
IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT
HOUSE OF COMMONS.-SATURDAY.

A sitting of the House was held to-day, lasting from noon till nearly half-past ten at night. The House resumed Com- mittee of Supply, when a long debate took place on the vote of £45,032 for the Irish Land Commission, which was ultimately agreed to without a division. On the vote of £15,410 for county court officers and magistrates in Ireland. and revising barristers in Dublin, the Committee divided, and the vote was agreed to by 88 to 16. A like result attended a division on the vote of £33,020 for the Dublin metropolitan police force. On the vote for the maintenance of prisoners and prisoners in Ireland, Mr. PARNELL made a complaint of the treatment the untried prisoners under the Crimes Act had received, and this brought up the Horan SECRETARY, who defended the course which had been pursued.—Mr. T. P. 0':-.`ONNOR moved to reduce the vote by £5,000 "to give the Chief Secretary an opportunity of assuring the ComMittee that no unnecessary torture would be imposed upon political prisoners in Ireland."—Mr. TREVBLYAN replied that there had been no straining of the law against prisoners, but that the Government would not depart from ttie principle which Parliament evidently meant to lay down in the Prevention Act, namely, that the punishments should not only be pre- ventive but also deterrent, and that men arkested should be imprisoned under such circumstances as would deter others from following their example.—The amendment was with- drawn and the veto agreed to.—A number of supplementary votes were passed, after n.hich the House resumed, and report of supply was agreed to.—The House then adjourned. HOUSE OF LORDS.—MONDAY.

Dr. Benson, the newly appointed Archbishop of Canter- bury, took the oath and his seat on his appointment. His Lordship was introduced by the Bishops of London and Exeter.—Earl CAIRNS moved that a Select Cormnittee be appointed to consider the accommodation of the House and galleries, mote especially in reference to seating, hearinff, and reporting-, and whether any and what improvement therein could be made.—Earl GRANVILLE consented to the appointment of the committee asked for, and the motion was then agreed to. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—MONDAV.

Lord CLAUD HAMILTON moved the second reading of the Great Eastern Railway (High Beech Extension) Bill.—Mr. BuycE moved a resolution against any encroachment by a railway on Epping Forest.—A fter a debate, the amendment was carried by 230 against 80. The bill was therefore re- jected.—Sir RICHARD CROSS gave notice to move on the earliest convenient day, "That the House regrets that the negotiations with respect to the Cuban refugees have not resulted in the release by the Spanish Government of those persons who were political refugees under the protection of the British flag."—Lord E. FITZMAITRICE stated that the Government had no information as to the arrival of a French squadron at Madagascar, but they had no reason to dis- believe it. The policy of the Government would be seen from the papers laid before the House.—Mr. GLADSTONE informed Mr. Monk that, as Earl Spencer was now to be Viceroy of Ireland in the same way as any other Viceroy, it would be the duty of the Government to submit a proposal at the proper time as to the Ministerial control of affairs relating to commerce and agriculture.—Sir S. NORTH- COTE asked if the House was to understand that Earl Spencer would cease to be President of the Council.—Mr. GLADSTONE thought it would be the duty of the Govern- ment to make other arrangements for that office.—ln reply to Sir Stafford Northcote, Mr. GLADSTONE stated that the navy vote would be taken on Thursday. The Government wert anxious to get on with the bills to be referred to the Grand Committees. As to the Easter holidays, he would propose that the House adjourn on Tuesday till the Thurs- day following Easter Sunday.—The House then went into Committe of Supply, and Lord Hartington afterwards submitted the army estimates.

div.head: HOUSE OF LORDS.-TUBSDAY.
div.p: HOUSE OF LORDS.-TUBSDAY.

Tha PAYMENT OF WAGES IN PUBLIC HOUSES BILL.— The House went into Committee on the Payment of Wages in Public Houses Bill.—Earl STANHOPE moved the amend- ment of clause 2, so as to make it permissable to a master or employer of labour who was the boa% fide occupier of a public house to pay his workmen on his own premises.— This was agreed to, and the bill passed through Committee without further amendment. THE TRANSTAAL.—Lord CRANBROOK called attention to the correspondence on the affairs of the Transvaal, and asked what steps the Government proposed to take in fulfil- ment of the Convention to save the natives residing outside and ou the borders of the Transvaal from the calamities in which they were involved by the lawless action of subjects of the Transvaal Republic. The Earl of DERBY acknow- ledged that the question was one of great importance, and one to which tNe noble Lord was quite justified in drawing the attention of the House. To the question what steps Her Majesty's Government intended to take, it was impos- sible to give a general answer, as everything must depend on circumstances. Everything that could be done in the interests of humanity and to prevent tribal wara the Govern- ment would do, and remonstrances would be sent to the Transvaal Government. .HOUSE OF COMMONS.—TUESDAY.

RAILWAY RATES.—Mr. CHAMBERLAIN repeated his state- ment that it was useless to introduce a bill carrying out the recommendations of the Committee on railway rates, as there was no prospect of passing it. MADAGASCAR.—Lord EDMOND FITZMAIIRICE stated that Her Majesty's Government had no information of the inten- tion of the French to blockade the coasts of Madagascar. There had been a consul representing Her Majesty's Government in Madagascar for some years, and he was there still. THE GOVERNMENT AND THE OPPOSITION.—Mr. GLAD- STONE declined to give a day for the discussion of Sir M. H. Beach's motion against the Government's policy in South Africa. He saw no reason why Mr. Gorst's motion on the Boer atrocities should not come on to-night. and the subject could then be discussed. Mr. Gorst was willing to with- draw his motion if the Government would give a day to Sir M. Hicks-Beach. _

LORD SPENCER.—Mr. SEXTON expressed his anxiety to know whether the resignation by Lord Spencer of the office of President of the Council would involve his retirement from the Cabinet, and was told by Mr. GLADsvotis that the Viceroy of Ireland had no intention of retiring from the Cabinet. HARBOUR ACCOMMODATION.—Mr. MARJORIBANKS called attention to the want of harbour accommodation on the east coast of Great Britain, and moved for a select committee to consider the subject.—Mr. CHAMBERLAIN insisted that sta- tistics show. that the loss of life on our coasts was mainly caused by the misconduct of shipowners, carelessness in the navigation and furnishing of ships, and shameful overload- ing. As the motion only asked for a committee of inquiry he had no objection to offer to it.—The motion was agreed to. THE TRANSTAAL.—Mr. GORST proceeded to call attention to the position i 2 the Transvaal of British subjects and per- sons of, the native race, and moved that energetic steps should, in the opinion of the House, be immediately taken to secure the strict observance by the,Transvaal Government of the Convention of 1881. After some discussion, in the course of which Mr. John Morley contributed his maiden speech, the debate was. upon the motion of Mr. Forster. ad- journed. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—IVEDNESDAY.

IRISH LAND ACT AMENDMENT BILL—Mr. PARNELET moved the second reading of the Land Law (Ireland) Act Amend- ment Bill. He explained that it was proposed to bring tenants under the Land Act who were now excluded. It gave power to the Court .to snspend ejectment proceedings pending a fixing-of a fair rent on the payment of rent equal to the poor-law valution. It defined the term "the tenants' improvements as anything done by the tenant that added to the selling value of a holding. It directed the Court that in fixing fair rents all the tenants' improvements should be- long to tenants, and that the landlord should not be permitted to ask anyincrease of rent in respect of the con- sequent increase in letting value' and it enabled the Land Commission to advance the full purchase money to tenants' and to extend the term of repayment to tenants under £3O rental. The chief part of the Bill was that.which protected the tenants' improvements, and upon that the Irish tenants were centred. The next most important part of the Bill was intended to bring leaseholders under the Land Act. There were 100,000 of them occupying from three to four million acres of the most rack-rented land in Ireland. He contended that the Irish question could never be settled till the improvements he had indicated were made. The present tranquility in Ireland was only due to the sternness of the Coercion Act, not to coa- tentment with the Land Act.—Mr. CHAPLIN moved the re- jection of the bill—Mr. GLADSTONE believed the application of the Land Act was far more extensive than Mr. Parnell had represented. Fair • rents were now-being fixed at the rate of 100 a day. The Land Act in the main was effecting the great purposes for which it Was passed. " He could not h ld out any hope Of agreeing to Mr. Parnell's proposals. The Government amid give no encouragement any plan for the disturbance of the main provisions of the Land Act. —After further debate, the second reading of the bill was rejected by 250 against 63 votes.

div.head: HOUSE OF LORDS.—ThunspAy.
div.p: HOUSE OF LORDS.—ThunspAy.

The Lords sat for nearly three hours, and debated one or two subjects of interest. —After Earl Granville had announced that the Easter holidays of their lordships would conamnnce on Tuesday next and continue for a fortnight, a bill to enable the trustees of the National Gallery to lend portions of the collection to provincial galleries was read a second time.—Lord CARLINGFORD moved the second read- ing of a bill to extend and make permanent the Irish Sun. day Closing Act, and the motion was agreed to. The rest of the sitting was devoted to the subject of recruiting for the Militia. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—TIMRSDA.Y.

THE ALABAMA CLAIMS.—Lord E. PITZMAURICE stated that no steps had been taken to recover the £2,000,000 paid to the United States in excess of the requirements of the Alabama claims, and that the Government did not intend to re-open the matter. THE PARCELS PosT.—The POSTMASTER-GENERAL ex- pressed a hope that the parcels post would be in operation by the beginning of July. - THE TRANSVAAL.—In the course of a discussion on the affairs of the Transvaal, Mr. E. ASHLEY announced that it was proposed to give small pensions out of the Imperial Treasury to Monkraone,and Montsioa, and such other chiefs as might appear to have special claims on this country, in consequence of former good service or promises of protec- tion, and to find them locations somewhere on British ter- ritory. THE LOCAL GOVERNMENT &Lt.—Mr. HIBBERT intima- ted that, in. the event of it not being possible to brieg for- ward a Vocal Gevernment Bill this session, an effort Would be made later on to pass a measure for the simplification of areas and the adjustment of the boundaries of local authorities.

TORY OBSTRUCTION.-Mr. R. YORKE. called attention to some criticism by Mr. H. Gladstone on Tory obstruction, which the hon. gentleman made in a speech at the annual meeting of the Highgate Liberal Association. It appeared that Mr. H. Gladstone had spoken of the obstruction in the House as the result of "a dangerous and malicious con- spiracy on the part of the Tory party." The hon. member for Leeds admitted that the words quoted were substantially correct, and said he thought that the words "malicious con- spiracy" were stronger than thp occasion required; he therefore withdrew them, but he adhered to his opinion that on the Opposition side of the House there was a consider- able amount of united action for the purpose of obstructing the measures of the Government. The hon. member for East Gloucestershire was arixious to proceed further with the subject as a question of privilege, but the SPEAKER ruled that it would be dangerous to consider such a question as a breach of privilege. THE ROYAL MARINES, &c.—Upon the motion for going into Committee of supply on the Navy Estimates, Mr. HOP- WOOD raised a debate upon certain irregularities and defects of administration affecting the Royal Marines. The hon. member moved for a select committee to inquire into the subject and report to the House.—After considerable discus- sion the motion was negatived by 60 to 39.—A discussion on the Naval Reserves followed. An official explanation was given by Sir T. BRASSEY, after which in committee on the Navy Estimates, Mr. CAMPBELL-BANNERMAN made the statement on behalf of the Admiralty.
TERRIBLE EXPLOSION IN WEST- MINSTER. ALARM IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.

POSSIBLE PLOT AGAINST THE PRIME MINISTER. A tremendous explosion occured at the Local Government Offices, Westminster, on Thursday night, and caused con- siderable destruction of property. The report was heard in the House of Commons, and caused momentary alarm. A large and anxious crowd quickly gathered, and the police had great difficulty in keeping them back. The report of the explosion was heard about half a minute after nine o'clock, while Mr. Gourley was speaking. So great was the force that the floor of the House, the side galleries, and the reporters' gallery shook. At the time there was but a thin attendance of members, it being the dinner hour. The Duke of Edinburgh was in the peers' gallery, and he turned round at once and spoke to Sir Henry Fletcher, who was sitting near him. There were only three members present on the Opposition side of the House, Mr. W. H. Sinith, Sir Massey Lopes, and Sir John Hay. The Speaker at once rang his•bell, and in- quired the cause of the alarm; To those inside the House it seemed as if the explosion took place in the direction of the House of Lords. Ten minutes after the report was ex- plained as the result of a gas explosion in Parliament-street. It occurred in the basement of the Local Government Board offices, smashing the stone-work into splinters, and breaking into fragments the windows, portions of which lay strewn in all the surrounding streets. Alarmed crowds gathered in the neighbourhood, and were for some time at a loss to know where the explosion had occurred. The wildest rumours were abroad—suggestions of dynamite being freely used, and fears being expressed that an attempt had been made upon the life of the Premier or his relatives in Down- ing-street. It is believed that no one has been injured. The explosion is believed to have been caused by an accumula- tion of gas in the basement; but even this is not yet clear, and much more alarming rumours are still in circulation. Risidenta in the neighbouring streets rushed out of their houses in terror. A later account corroborates the statement that no one has been injured, but there have been several narrow escapes. The porter who has charge of the Local Government Offices was standing at the door at the time, and the female servant was also on the premises, and was also uninjured. This is the more remarkable considering the extent of the damage done to property, and the extreme violence of the explosion. The housekeeper at the ()Ices states that it sounded quite close to him, like the report of an 80-ton gun, and the crash of the front portion of the building was accompanied by the flash of a large body of flame. The explosion occurred in a room on the basement on the ripper side of the entrance, and has resulted in the massive stone work and stone balustrade in front being thrown forwrrd into the street, causing a great gap in the structure as if there had been a doorway. The in- terior of the room has also been completely wrecked, and the stone work torn up into splinters—in fact the appearances, so far as examination has yet gone, are such as to make it extremely doubtful whether either gas or gunpowder could have been the cause. No explosive substance was stowed in either the offices or basement, and the fact that there were people resident within the building to look after its safety makes it very doubtful whether any large quantity of gas could have accumulated without betraying its pre- sence. At present the suspicion is that dynamite must have been used, and that the affair was no accident, but a deli- berate and malicious attempt to blow up the Government offices.

The alarm caused among menibers of Parliament and others as to the suspicion of a design upon the Prime Minister's life was considerably increased by the fact of the eiplosion having occurred in OA street immediately ad- joining Downing-street, and also by the circumstance that the fact might have beccme known that Mr. Gladstone has been detained in his own house by a slight indisposition. A special despatch bays the effects of the explosion are evident in the quantity of broken glass in the whole block of Goverament offices, the Home Office, &c. So violent was the shock that kis said to have nearly overturnad a couple of cabs which were passing at the moment along Parlia- ment street. So startling was the report and so violent the concussion, that many persons residing in the neighbouring streets rushed out, believing that the explosion must have occurred nearer, either in some part of their own dwelling or in the immediately adjoining premises. At the first glance either apprehension might have appeared well founded, judging by the amount of broken glass in almost erery buiiding within 500 or 600 yards Telegraphing at 11-30 a correspondent adds It has now been ascertained beyond any reasonable doubt that the ex- plosion was not caused by gas. The place where it occurred has been examined, not only by firethen and police officers, but alse by the inspectors from the Gas Light and Coke Company, who are experts, and they distinctly declare that they can find no symptoms of gas being the cause. The meter is all right, and no place has been found where any escape was -likely to have occurred, nor does the wrecked room show any of the traees of blackness which might have been expected among the ruins if gunpowder had been the cause. One bystander, a witness of the explosion from the end of , the street, who declared himself to have some experience of explosions said that in this case the report had the hard metallic char- acter which is rather characteristic of gun-cotton, dynamite, or such other explosives as contain nitro-glycerine. It is true that after the expli,sion there was a smell of gas ih the premises, even in the occupied rooms, but this is believed to be explained by the fact that the force of the explosion was such as to extinguish all the lights in the premi,es, and thus necessarily cause an escape of gas until it could be turned off at the meter. This sudden darkness intensified the alarm which the terrible force of the explosion naturally excited on the part of the wife and servant of the office keeper, who were at the time sitting in their/private room. For the moment they were powerless. Upon recover- ing their presence of mind they went out into the passage, and were nearly blinded by the dense choking clouds of lime dust with which the place was kllede Their first en- deavour was to grope about in search of candles, and when they were lit it was possible to form some idea of the actual damage. At the moment of the explosion several policemen were in the neighbourhood. These, including one from the Horse Guards, another from Downing-street, and a third who was standing at the door of the King-street Police Sta- tion, were among the first to arrive at the place." An alarm was immediately raised, and extra policemen were summoned. The various constabulary stations in the neighbourhood turned out their fire escapes and manual engines, several of which were in proaapt attendance. As soon as possible the firemen went over the entire place to see whether any fire had been caused, or was likely to be caused, by the explosion. There was no trace of anything of the kind. As a prec.ution a steam fire engine has been kept at hand with steam up in readiness for any emergency. MYSTERIOUS CANISTER AT THE TIMES OFFICE.

In the early part of last evening a vet suspicions Or- cumstance occurred at the Times office. • A canister, which is believed to contain an explosive, was found at the back of the premises. It was rumoured that it was found lighted No explanation can be given of the purpose for which it was intended, nor is any information obtainable as te the persons by whom it was placed in the position where it was discovered. The coincidence of this circum- stance with the mysterious explosion at the Government offices has given rise to the suggestion that the same cause is at the bottom of both. The police are investigating the matter.

QUESTIONS IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS. In the Howie of Commons, on Thursday, during the course of the sitting, Sir R. CROIS said: Perhaps, sir, I may, with the indulgence of the House, upon this motion ask a question of the Secretary for the Home Department whether he can inform the House of any particulars of the explosion which has taken place at the Local Government Board Office, and whether there is any report of the explosion at the Times office?

Sir W. HARCOURT : The particulars that I have received from the police are, that at five minutes past nine this even- ing an explosion took place on the ground floor of the Local Government Board Office, wrecking the room, and damaging much of the glass in the neighbourhood. No person has ben injured. Of course there are many conjectures as to the cause of this explosion, but, it would not be right to state them until an official inquiry has been made. In reference to the other matters to which the right hon. gentleman has referred, I have seen a gentleman connected with the Times office, and it appears that there was found there previous to this explosion, about half-past seven this evening, a canister containing some explosive material which seems to have produced a slight explosion'. Mr. PULESTON : Are we to understand that there was any- thing to indicate in a similar manner the cause of the ex- plosion at the Local Government Board? Sir WILLIAM HAncounT : At present I have no informa- tion that anything has been found. The explesion was of such a character as to leave no sign. Viscount POLKSTONE : Could the right hon. gentleman say whether the statement that nobody has been injured refers to the Government officers only, because it was re- ported that other people had been injured in the Central Press Office near?
Sir W. HAECOURT : The information I have is from the police that no person was injured.
LAND SUBSIDENCES IN CHESHIRE.

The damage to property caused by the gradual subsidence which is observed to be taking place over nearly the whole of the Cheshire salt tisld, more particularly ire the districts oL Northwich and Winsford, continaas to be very serious. In December, 1880, was recorded the collapse and consequent inundation of the Platt's Hill mine of Messrs. John Thomp- son and Son, the most alarming accident that bad occurred for many years. The mine was completely filled with water, partly from the river Weaver and partly from a stream called Peover Brook. The ground in the surrounding dis- trict subsided ; chasms were formed in several places; and roads were broken up. The sinking which then commenced has extended along the Peover Brook, and the land on both sides of the stream has settled down considerably. The area of submerged land is said to be now double what it WAS prior to 1880. About a year ago the shaft of a pumping station belonging to Mr. Marshall, situated in Witten, collap3ed, and at the present time, owing to the land having settled down in the direction of the hole where the shaft was, the whole field, four acres or more in super- ficial area is rifted and cracked all over. The hill between the old Platt's Hill shaft and the stream is rapidly subsid- ing; holes are constantly forming; and the surface is cracked and fissured. The large fl isla at Marston—com- monly called Nerrinan's flash—has within the last two years extended very greatly bath in area and in depth. The road between Nort-hwioli and Marston is sinking continuously and rapidly, and the subsidence has extended to the land bordering on the Marston and Wincham road. This road is still below its original level, although it has been raised at various times during the last six years about 30 feet. The area now covered by water where ten years ago there was none, is at least ten acres. The flash has within the last few years ex- tended so as to join a largo lake at a place called " the top of the brook," which consists of over 100 acres of sub- merged land. In the town of Northwich itself the sinking is continuous, but gradual, especially in Leicester-street, Tablev-strees and Iligh•street. The area of depression, of II which' Northwich may be considered the centre, is exten- sive and in places thickly populated. The salt works which lie between " the to of the brook" and Wincham are suf- fering severely, and fears are entertained that when pump- ing is commenced for the supply of brine to Runcorn, under the scheme which was successfully floated a year or two ago, the effects above described will be intensified. The pipes for conveying the brine from Northwich to Runcorn are all laid, and the machinery being ready, work may be cotmeeced at any time. It is impossible to disguise the appre- hension which is felt. The quantity of brine expected to be pumped exceeds that which has been taken from any single shaft in the district up to the present time ; and the results of the operation upon the surface land will be closely , watched. Pumping in connection with the various other works in the district continues, and the brine is maintained at a high level in the shafts, owing to the percolation of surface water through the cracked and broken ground. sa long as this can be maintained no sudden sinking, it is be- lieved, can take place; but immediately the surface fissures get choked—should such a thing happen—and access of fresh water be thus prevented, the old inundated mines which have become enormous brine reservoirs, will inevi- tably get pumped out, and subsidences more serious than any which have yet taken place may be looked for. The ' effects of subsidence during the last two years, in the town of Northwich, are very appareat. In Leicester-street four cettages have been taken down, owing .to their dilapidated condition, which previously showed on signs of sinking. Other dwellings in the same neighbourhood are also suffer- ing, and some have already been condemned as insecure. The police station, built about four years ago, it so badly cracked that its occupancy is almost dangerous, and the county justices anticipate an expenditure of about £3,000 in providing a new building, which will certainly soon be necessary. When the station was built, the site was selected from a belief that it was the soundest in the dis- trict. Its present condition shows how impossible it is to forecast the area of damage even in so short a period. There are houses which have stood for 50 years without exhibiting the smallest fracture, but which, within the last two years, have borne signs of damage. The new bridge across the River Weaver, in the centre of Northwich, is subsiding slowly but surely, and it will ultimately have to be taken down. The sanitary arrangements of Northwich are a matter of serious concern. The roadways are con- tinually being taken up through the bursting of gas and , water pipes. As to sewers, the town has not, and indeed cannot be expected to have, anything like a proper system,. Night soil and other solid refuge is carted away, no accumu- lation being permitted, and as this work is carefully and .systematically attended to by the Local Board the public health does not suffer. Liquid refuse from houses, and flood water from the streets, finds its way into the river. A portion of the town sewage is conveyed to a sewage garden in the outskirts, and utilised with, we understand, fairly satisfactory results. At Winsford the effects of subsidence are hardly less serious. Until within the year 1879 the district most effected was that on the east side of the river Weaver; now it is seen to be going more rapidly on the west side, in places which before were ap- parently sound. In 1879 the beautiful stone church, built by the Weaver Trustees, was damaged by subsidence and had to be taken down. In its place there is now a structure , built upon a stone plinth with a framework of wood. The Surveyor to the Local Board (Mr. Waring) has within the past three months condemned four places of business in the town—one of them a beerhouse which had become un- tenable; and several buildings have been taken down by their owners without his intervention. All new buildings are now constructed, in part, of wood. The Local Board has an office built entirely of that material, a permanent structure, on a sinking site, being evidently undesirable. Adjacent to this is a building which has recently been raised sft. The Winsfoid Town Hall, which sank in 1878, has been raised 9f1.; and several other buildings—public- houses and shops—have been raised from two to four feet. One serious effect of the subsidence is the damage to gas and water pipes. The frequent breakages, with the neces- sity they entail of taking up and repairing the streets wherever they occur, impose upon the ratepayers of the district great expense. Householders are under the further disadvantage of having to pay heavily for their gas. This applies to both Northwich and Winsford, but most of all to the latter town, where the charge per 1,000 cubic feet at present is 6s 8. At Northwich it is ss. In both places the gas supply is in the hands of private companies, who find it necessary to charge a high figure in order to cover the loss from leakages and damage to their mains. In the agricul- tural districts around Northwich and Winsford, at consi- derable distances from any salt works, sinking is observed to be taking place. The Winsford Branch of the West Cheshire Railway has already been raised at certain points, and the process is just now being repeated. The entire area from Winsford Bridge for about two miles up the valley of the Weaver, south of the town, is subsiding at a rate which gives well grounded cause for alarm ; and, so far as can be seen, there is no possibility, short of the complete stoppage of t'se staple industry of Cheshire, oh preventing the mischief from extending.

There was an application on Wedneslay in the Court of Appeal for a rule for a new triAl in the Biggar breach of promise case. Lord Justice Brett remarked that Mr. Biggar's evidence was fatal to his own case, as all his actions were conclusive of an engagement to marry. The application was dischaiged with costs.

The Croydon bench have dealt with " off-licenses" in a manner directly opposite to the plan adopted at Dar wen. They gave their decision, on Wednesday, on forty applica- tions for the renewal of off-licenses which had been strongly opposed by the local temperance societies. The justices considered that a vested interest bad been set up which could not justly be interfered with, and granted. all the re- newals except one, ordering the opposition to pay the costs on the thirty-nine cases upon which they had been de- feated.

ARRIVAL OF LORD ALCFSTER IN ENGLAND.—AdmiraI Lord Alcester, who has been succeeded in the command of the Mediterranean station by Lord John Hay, arrived at Portsmouth on Sunday morning at seven o'clock on board the Admiralty yacht Enchantress. His lordship, on landing, 'proceeded to the Admiral's house, where he breakfasted with Admiral Hornby, who was his lordship's predecessor on the Mediterranean station.. Afterwards, in obedience to the Queen's commands, his lordship left by special train for Windsor. A DISORDERLY LIBERATIONIST MEETING. A crowded meeting was held on Wednesdiy night in the Cutlers' Hall, Sheffield, to hear addressee by Mr. JosPph Arch, the Rev. John Fisher, and others on the stibject of Disestablishment The friends of the Church mustered in considerable force, and at one part of Mr. Arch's speech they became so noisy that an attempt was made to eject the ringleaders. A free fight ensued, and order was only obtained by the interference of the police and the ejection of several persons. A reso- lution in favour of disestablishinent and disendowment was adopted. div.p: DISTRICT NEWS.

ASHTON. NARROW ESCAPE PROM DROWNING AT ASHTON. Be. tween eight and nine o'clock, on Saturday night last, Chas. Painter, a young man, residing in Heath-lane, met with an accident which almost resulted in his death. It appears that Painter has been in the habit of visiting a sister resid- ing a short distance away, and when returning has crossed a field near to the works of Mr. Hodgkinson, in Heath-lane. F Owing to the field having been lately ploughed, Painter, on Saturday night last, crossed the next field to the one lie had been accustomed to return by. When he got to the end I —close to the file works of Mr. Hodgkinson—he came to what he supposed to be the gate, and, instead of opening it, climbed- over. But it was not the gate—he had in mistake got over some wooden railings placed round a tank of water several feet deep in the ground. Before he could discover his error,- Painter fell into the flank, the water in which was covered with a thick sheet of ice. He crashed through the ice and immediately cried out for help. f Mr. Charles Hodgkinson heard the screams, and rushing out of the house succeeded, with some difficulty, in rescuing Painter from his perilous position. Fortunately the latter was not much worse for the " ducking " fie had received. THE SERIOUS ACCIDENT AT TEE MAIN'S COLLIERY: A SECOND DEA.TIL—A waek ago we reported a serious acci- dent at the Main's Colliery, Ashton, belonging to Messrs. Cross, Tetley, and Co., by which two men named Joseph Moore, residing at Stubshaw Cross, and John Higginson, of Golborne, were severely injured. These two men were en- gaged in discharged "shots" for the purpose of bringing down:the coal, but instead of one of the "shots" exploding in the usual manner, it blew out towards them, and very severely burnt them about the head and body. It was found necessary to convey them home in vehicles and medical aid was at once provided. Moore, however, died about a week later, and an inquest on the body was opened before Mr. Barker, the county coroner, at the Ram's Head Hotel, Stubshaw Cross. After the circumstances of the case had been gone into it was de- cided that the inquiry should be adjourned until April Bth, so that Higginson (who was then too ill to appear) might be present to give his version of the affair. Since then, how- ever, Higginson rapidly grew worse, and notwithstanding all efforts, expired about 20 minutes to 11 on Tuesday morning last. He was 34 years of age, 'and resided at 4, Railway View, Golborne. The jury were again called together on Wednesday afternoon, at the Ram's Head, and Mr. Barker, the coroner, addressing them, said the only course they could adopt was to adjourn the inquiry until the Bth April, when it would be resumed concerning both the men. The only witness called was Ellen Higginson (wife of the de- ceased), who identified the body as that of her husband.—The inquest was then adjourned until the date mentioned.

div.head: CADISHEAD.
div.p: CADISHEAD.

FATAL ACCIDENT AT A LEVEL CROSSING.—Mr. F. Price, district coroner, on Monday held an inquest at Cadishead upon toe body of Nathaniel Davies, aged 29 years, a labourer, who lived in Moss-lane, Cadishead. The deceased on Friday night was passing over a level crossing at a time when two trains were due to pass. He was cautioned by a signalman that the trains were coming, and answered "All right." No more was seen or heard of him until the fol- lowing morning, when his dead body, terribly mutilated, was found lying on the railway. The jury returned a ver- dict of "Accidental death," and unanimously recommended that the small gates on each side of the level crossing should, when trains were due to pass, be fastened in a simi- lar manner to the large gates.

C;OLBORNE. INTBILYERING WITH SWING BOATS AT GOLBOJINI : A ROUGH FtwEn.—At the Newton Petty Sessions, on Slturday, James Charles, a rough-looking young fellow, was sum- moned by James Cook for damaging a plank to the amount of 3s.—The defendant pleaded guilty.—The complainant said he kept some swing boats, and the defendant came up and commenced bullying, saving he would stop them and throw anybody out if they did not get out. He interfering with them when he smashed a plank.—The Chairman remarked that the defendant had been up before them very often, and he would have to pay 2s Gd as damage, in addi- tion to a fine of 5s and costs. He must take care and behave himself in future.

LECTURE ON AMERICA AT GoLMORNE.—The Congrega- tional school-room, Golborne, was crowded on Tuesday evening, when a lecture, entitled " A peep at America in mid-winter," was delivered by the Rev.. James Wayman, of Blackpool. The proceeds were in aid of the school funds. Mr. J. Davies presided. The lecture consisted of a very pleasing and interesting description of a toar,in America last year; the attractions of New York, Philadelphia, Chicago, Niagara Falls, &c., being eloquently pointed out. The address was illustrated by a number of capital views, shown on a screen with the aid of lime light apparatus. At the close Mr. R. Yates moved a deserving vote of thanks to the lecturer, whieh was seconded by Mr. Naylor, and carried unanimously. A similar compliment to the chair- man concluded the proceedings.

div.p: HAYISOCK.

CAUGHT AT Les-r.—At the Newton Town Hall, on Satur- day last, Martin Noon was charged under a warrant witeh being drunk at Haydock on Sunday, the 3rd February, 1878.—Superintendent Weir remarked that the defendant did not appear in answer to the summons served upon him, and the constable left the district a short time afterwards. He had recently returned, and the defendant was appre- hended under the warrant.—He was fined ss. and costs. NEGLECTING TO SEND CHILDREN TO SCHOOL —At the Newton Town Hall, on Saturday last, John Twist, of Hay- dock, was summoned at the instance of Mr. Cawley, school attendance officer, for neglecting to send him child to school. He was fined 53.—John Lawton was sum- moned for a similar offence, and the case was adjourned for a month, the defendant promising to take care that in future the child should attend school.—Thcfnas Blundell was fined 5s for neglecting to send his child to school. A PASSENGER CARRIER AND HIS CUSTOMERS.—At the Newton Town Hall, on Saturday last, Joseph Lawrenson was charged with leaving his cart a longer period than was necessary on the highway at Havdock, on the 2nd inst.— P.C. Hodgkinson deposed that about a quarter past ten on the night of the day named he saw the defendant's horse and cart standing in front of the R tm's Head, Haydock, for about half an hour without anyone in charge —Defendant was fined ss. and costs.

ALLEGED THEFT OF A Ducx AT HAYDOCK.—At the Newton Petty Sessions, on Saturday last, Win. Winstanley was charged, on remand, with stealing a duck, value 38., the property of George Corley, of Haydock. Mr. Moore, of Warrington, appeared for the . prisoner, who pleaded not guilty.—George Corley, farmer, residing in Kenyon-lane, Haydock, deposed, that he kept poultry, both ducks and hens, on his farm. In consequence of something told to him on the 28th ult. he got on one of the outbuildings of the farm, and he saw the prisoner going down the lane towards the Ram's Head. He had something bulky under his arm, but he (witness) did not know what it was. He got off the building as quickly as he could, and ran down thelane after prisoner. On getting near to him' he called out, and the prisoner threw the duck produced into the ditch. He did not see him take it. He' held the prisoner until the policeman came.—James Henry Sutton, a lad, residing at Park-lane, Ashton, stated that he saw the prisoner with something bulky under his arm, and Mr. Corley was run- ning after him. The prisoner threw a duck into the ditch, and be (witness) picked it up.—P.C. Hodgkinson deposed that he apprehended the prisoner.—Mr. Moore addressed the Bench on behalf of the prisoner, asking them to deal with him under the Summary Jurisdiction Act instead of eommitting him for trial at the sessions.—The Bench com- mitted the prisoner for trial at the next Liverpool Quarter Sessions. THE HAYDOCK CRICKET AND BOWLING CLUE CONCERT. —The choir of St. John's Church, Earlestown (under the efficient leadership of Mr. H. J. Darman), gave a concert in the Haydock Colliery schools (kindly lent for the occasion), on Tuesday evening last, in aid of the funds of the Hay- dock Cricket and Bowling Club. There was a pretty fair attendance, those present being treated to some capital and first-class singing. The programme opened with the glee " May-day " (Muller), by the choir ; after which Mr. G. Wright sang with his accustomed ability "Under the old flag" (Marks), receiving an encore. Miss M. E.' Jackson sang" Come where the moonbeams linger" (Glover), and the glee " Comrades idarms" (Adams), by the male voices, was re-demanded. Mr. J. White . finely sang Cooke's " The Englishmen," after which " She will, she won't," a "Catch," by Messrs. Lewis, Durman, and Willis, created much amusement, and, the trio were ,re-called. "The minstrel boy" was sweetly sung be, Mrs. Dewse ; the duet, "The army and navy," (Cooke), was effectively rendered by Messrs. T. Ashton and G. Wright; and "Tom the tinker," a song by Mr. Daman, was warmly encored.: After a capital "Vocal quadrille on nursery rhymes," by the choir, the first part .of the concert was brought to a close. After a short interval, the choir gave the ever popular "Hail, smiling morn," after which Mr. W. Leather capitally sang "The midsthpmite," and was awarded with an encore. Messrs. Lewis, Wells, Durrnan, and Millard next gave the catch " charms" (Webhe), and the male voices gave the glee "The anvil chorus" (Adams). "The anchor's weighed" was very effectively given by Mr. J. White, who received a merited re-call, and the male voices of the choir afterwards sang " The three chafers." After Miss M. L. Lewis had sung "Laugh while you may," Mr. J. Wright splendidly gave "Jack's reward,' and Messrs. White, Durman, and Leather gave the trio, "The mouse traps." The last selection was, "Here in cool grot," a glee by the choir. Mr. Charles Pilkington, J:P., then moved a hearty vote of thanks to the choir for their services,which he said had been very kindly given. He thought they were much indebted to them, but hoped they could come again in the future. (Applause.)—Mr. Taylor seconded the motion, which was carried with acclamation. Mr. Durman acknowledged the compliment, observing that the choir would be pleased to come again on some future occasion. The programme was not quite as perfect or interesting as be would have liked it to have been, but that was owing to the short notice be had received.—The concert was then brought to a close with the National Anthem.

HUTTON LITERARY AND SCIENTIFIC ASSOCIATION. -- At the last meeting of this association a second paper was read by Mr. Machin on "Sponges and their skeletons," Mr. Machin illustrating his remarks with specimens and the microscope. The yearly increasing demand for non-Intoxicant beverages has compelled Messrs. J. Cammack and Co. to meet it by the infusion of new blood and additiJnal capital into the firm ; hence the formation of the present company. The direct-it's enter on thAr offica with the determination to give every pos- sible satisfaction to their patrons, and to make the company second to no firm in the kingdom, whether in the excellence of its beveragea, the rrioderat;on of its prio.s, Lr the crefui atten- tion of its officers to the wants of customers.

The consumption of Mineral and Aerated Waters has grown so rapidly that a keen competition in their supply has been excited, resulting in the introduction of some very unsound and even poisonous Itverazes,

This degeneracy has arisen partly through the Inealtacits et the old ruie-o'-thumb manufacturers, who still maintiffi- air antiquated apparatus, consisting of copper vessels, whose tin lining, if they ever had any, has lorg since been removed, and common lead piping—sure and fertile sources of poisonous metalic contamination—and partly through the greed and rapacity of the modern but not less ignorant speculators in the business, who, descending to the vilest, because cheapest means of production, use defective seemd-hand machinery; and employ impure and often poisonous ingredients in the composition of the various drinks. Even the bottle in whist) the goods are supplied has not escaped the effects of this cupidity, for the small wooden stopper adopted In the cheapest type of patent bottle in eermnon use, instead of being weighted with pure block tin is frequently found loaded witis lead, the most dangerous metal for such a purpose, as it Is well known to be a virulent and an accumulative poison.

The proper choice and erection of machinery and apparatus; • the adoption of suitable precautionary measures during the process of manufacture, the ability to selest and the power to make or purify the various ingredients, absolutely require the experience and knowledge of a trained Chemist, His attiye and unremitting personal supervhion is also needed to avoid - or destroy the various noxious _ferments whi;l2 are so apt to form, and the myriads of organised germs, cells, bacteria, &c., which are now admitted to be a frequent source of disease, and even death.

The Directors are therefore pleased to hare retained the pre- fessional serriees of Mr. John Cmainack (Fellow of the Insti- tute of Chemistry and of the Society of Chemical Industri), as Managing Director, whose name is so well and honourably known in the district of St. Helens, and whose long and var:ied experience in Scientific and Technical Chemistry will be ss sure guarantee of the purity and excellence of the varlotls beverages.

reover, they have adopted machinery and apparatui of the latest and most improved type. Every portion of it which comes into actual contact with the Aerated Waters and the Syrups is constructed of glass, porcelain, pure block tin, or et real gun metal (not corrodable brass) thickly lined with pure block tin. Lead is entirely discarded, even the solder used In making the varlotts connections being free from that noxionS metal.

For the storage of the Solutions and Syrups, only slate, earthenware, or glass vessels are used, wood being entirely dis- pensed with as too absorbent and retentive of foul Savours aad Energetic ferments.
All the Waters and Ssrups are carefully Snored before being used.
A special apparatus is employed to thoroughly rinse even the last tr. ces of the wash water from the bottles.
The Sweet Drinks are eomposed of none but real fruit essences and extracts and harmless vegetable compounds.

The Mineral Waters contain the purest m4tetials, and are guaranteed strength. The Eon.s. WATaa, which Is UNEXCELL by any other manufacturers, contains tke standard quantity carbonate of soda, and is not, like the rubbish too often an plied, plain water indifferently oarbonated.

div.p: WIDNES LOCAL BOARD.

The monthly meeting was held at the Board-room, Alforde Chambers, on Tuesday. Mr. F. H. Gossage pre- sided, and there were also present Messrs. Forster, Handley, Pankhurst, Sadler, Webster, Johnson, Midwood, Kershaw, Illartley, Carey, Dr. O'Keeffe, D. Wright, J. T. Allen (clerk), Carr (gas manager), W. Higginson (surveyor). THU SILWERAGE QUESTION. At a meeting of the Sewerage Committee on the sth inst., tin resident engineer was instructed to write to the contrac- tor to go on with the sewerage works, and likewise to call his attention to the unsatisfactory progress he is making with the work, and the dangerous state of part of it. The resident engineer's report, dated the 3rd February, was read as follows: "The present stete of affairs in connection 'with these works are, briefly, that the contractor has not carried out the instructions which I have given him, and has made several excuses for not doing co. Up to the 20th nit. the work executed by the contractor amounts to £32 65. lad. This I have not issued a certificate for, as the damage done to the neighbouring property w:11 cost considerably more than this to rectify, and until I receive your instruc- tions to the contrary, I shall not certify until the amount of damage is compensated for by the value of work done, and not paid for, or until the con- tractor satisfactorily makes good the damage. The contractor has made apugcation for permission to proceed with the work in Dinin-road. Under the pre- sent circumstances, I de not consider it will be advisable to give him such permission, as he has two trenches open, and in a dangerous state, and is not proceeding with the work with such diligence as is necessary to avoid accidents, and complete the centract in the given time. I shall be glad of your inetruetions hereon." Letters complaining of interfer- ence with works drainage were read from 7•I r. J. C. Rost- ledge., Messrs, Suape and Co., Messrs. Golding, Davis, and Co., limited, were read. A special meeting of the commit- tee was held on the previous day, when Mr. Stead was ap- pointed clerk of the works ata salary of 3 guineas a week.— tere_gemseraw moved the adoption of the minutes, and the the diversion of the stre im into the wooden sewer wOulTEe' deleterious to the latter. The stream, it was well known, consisted largely of acids, which came from the works along Use marsh, and it would be equally well known that acids had a most corrosive effect upon timber of whatever kind. It was never intended that any acid should go through the sewer. Certain gentlemen who had works along the marsh applied for permission for their waste products to go through the sewer, but the members of the Board declined to accede to the application, because the sewer was con- structed simply for the drainage of the houses and property of the public, and not for the works. Ho considered it ex- ceedingly important that this matter,should be taken into consideration, because if the acid liquid was allowed to con- tinue to run through the sewer, there was every possibility of collapsing in the course of a few years. Was there no way of overtime such a catastrophe as that from the rate- payers of Widnes. Another serious point was the position of the culvert under the London and North-Western Rail- way' viaduct, which, on account of the proper levels not being taken, might be in some danger of falling, and what in the world would that cost? It would cost at least half a million of money, if it did not approach a neurch larger sum. It would be simply ruinous to the township of Widnes if any accident of that kind should occur. These were matters which were not sufficiently studied, and inasmuch as the Board had been mislead once by inaccurate measurements, there was a danger that the catastrophes he had described might take place. He be- lieved that if matters had not been represented as they were at the tithe the Government inquiry was held before Mr. Harrison, of the Local Government Board, that gentleman would not have consented to the construction of the sewer. That was a matter of opinion of course, but he knew that misrepresentations were made to Mr. Harrison, and through those misrepresentations he consented to the sewer being constructed. It was better for them to be wise in time than to have to pay for sad experience afterwards, and he thought precautions ought to be adopted so to carry out the sewerage scheme that there would be no litigation and no further expense to the ratepayers of Widnes. That was what he really desired to place before the Board, and if he had succeeded in enlisting the sympathies of the members, he should be exceedingly glad, and he hoped that the scheme would he to the ailvantage and benefit of them all.—Mr. PIERPOINT said, with respect to the acid water be- ing turned into a wooden sewer, there was no question that if it were allowed to flow through for any considerable time It would materially affect the soundness of the timber; al- though the wood of which the culvert in question was con- istructed was of that description which would resist acids to a greater extent than any other that could be mentioned. It would be better if the water could be turned into its original course, or into some other course, as soon as possible, rather than allowing it to flow into the sewer. The short time, the water had been running, however, would have done no harm. With respect to the London and North-Western via- duct, as far as he could ascertain the butts of the bridge were carried down to very firm growing clay. If that was the case the distance it was intended to carry this sewer under the railway would r.ot be of the slightest danger : it would not affect the bearings of the foundation.—At the re- quest of Mr. Kershaw, the CLERK read a letter from that gentleman to Mr. Higginaon, dated the 28th February. It asked Mr. Higginson to assume the responsibilities imposed upon him, and call upon Mr. Jeffries, the contractor, to pro- ceed with the work.—Mr. KERSHAW observed that he only penned that letter to clear himself as chairman of the sewerage oommittee.—Mr. WEBSTER said the sewerage scheme seemed to have got into a regular muddle. The contractor overrode the specification, started work and knocked off work when he:liked. They had a report from the engineer a short time VS that he was not performing the work as he ought to do, and he (Mr. Webster) thought Mr. Pierpoint, as he was appointed the resident engineer, ought to see that the contractor complied with the agreement and did the work in a proper, workmanlike manner, and not allow him to do as he like(l.—The CHAIRMAN jocularly re- marked that Mr. Pierpoint would perhaps carry out his duty as thus .pointed out.—Mr. PIERPOINT laughingly replied in the affirmative. The CHAIRMAN said there was no doubt that Mr. Jeffries was not following out the specifications at present or he would not have stopped work.—Mr. MIDWOOD wished the Board to understand that he strongly protested against • the appointment of a clerk of works at a salary of three guineas per week. The Board were at present involved in enormous expense, and they were unaware, as Dr. O'Keeffe had stated, what might come in the future. He would like to give a few facts as to their present position. They had Mr. Copeland, as resident engineer, who was doing nothing except writing letters to them on Sunday,—(laughter)— they had Mr. Pierpoint whose charges they did not know, the surveyor, who was losing 'a good deal of his time in looking after the sewer, and they had expensive arbitration proceedings taking place and they had paid for all with the exception of one month's account. He thought the greatest portion of the sewerage committee were of very small use indeed. (Mr. Kershaw : Hear, hear.) He should like to know what was the use of all these persons they had en- gaged, he was thoroughly satisfied as a member of that Board with what Mr. Pierpoint had done. Mr. Pierpoint had given more information about the sewerage scheme than he (Mr. Midwood) had heard during the past 12 months. But with the exception of Mr. Pierpoint's services he de- clared that the Board got nothing for their money. The sewerage works, although not half finished, had cost already £3,ooo.—Mr. MARTLEY concurred in the remark's of Mr. Mid wood, and expressed his satisfaction at the appoint- ment of Mr. Pierpoint, but desired to know the terms.— Mr. KERSHAIV, in reply, said the carrying out of the sewer- age scheme was as easy as cutting a piece of bread and cheese. The misfortune of the Board was in not meeting with contractors willing to proceed with the work with that due care and diligence that they ought to do. The Board would never have been put in its present fix if they had had .a reasonable contractor. The contractor was greatly to blame for his mismanagement of the work, and, unfortu- nately, the engineer had made an error in the line of the sewer. That, nevertheless, did not exonerate the contrac- tor. With reference to the question of acid water, it was the duty of the surveyor to see that the water was diverted and not allowed to run through the sewer. Dr. O'Keeffe made the serious charge that certain persons bad duped Mr. Harrison, the Government inspector. (Dr. O'Keeffe : I said made misrepresentations.) It was almost the same thing. I But it would take a cleverer Board than Widnes Local Board to dupe Mr. Harrison, and no inspector could have examined more carefully into the plans and elicited more information than that gentleman did. There was, however, nothing wrong put before Mr. Harrison—it was not the wish of the Board to state anything wrong. Replying to Mr. Midwood, the speaker said they could not proceed with the work without a clerk of works, and if they had one they must pay. He was very glad to hear Mr. Midwood express himself so decidedly in favour of Mr. Pierpoint, and he hoped he would retain the same views when j Mr. Pierpoint's bill came in. (Hear, hear).—Mr. MIDWOOD: We will leave that until it comes in.— Mr. MAHTLRY: We don't know what terms Mr. Pierpoint was engaged upeela—Mr. KERSHAW : The Board has made j no terms with Mr. Pierpoint, but I suppose he will have ' professional charges, and we shall have to abide by them. —Mr. PIERPOINT : The charges are not anything but what may be made public. My charges will be 21 per cent. on the cost of the work that is done under my supervision. That will include travelling expenses. my investigation proceedings will be charged in addition, but these will be very trifling.-31r. SHUTTLEWORTH remarked that from what he had heard of the specification he considered it un- fair of Mr. Kershaw to ask Mr. Higginson to take the responsibility of ordering the contractor.—The minutes were then put to the vote and carried; Mr. Wright, Mr.Midwood, Mr. Martley, and Mr. Sadler voting against. Mr. Johnson abstained from voting.—Mr. KERSHAW moved, and Dr. O'KEEFE seconded, that Mr. Pierpoint take the necessary steps to divert the acid water from the sewer. GAS AND WATER COMMITTEE. The minutes of this committee stated that 19 tenders ware examined for firs clay goods, and it was recommended that the tender cf the Ellen Royde Brick and Tile Co. be ! accepted, subject to their signing the necessary contract, which according to the schedule of prices and the estimated I requirements, will amount to about £166 17s. In his report the gas engineer, Mr. Carr, stated that between the 3rd and , 9th of February about 300,000 cubic feet of gas was blown away through a 3-inch air valve on the roof of Ditton gas j holder by some malicious person. There being no direct ' evidence as to the culprit, the committee did not recommend any steps to be taken in the matter. It was recommended that thy offer of Mr. Hanckol o1:S6 per annum for the shoot-
