He drew up the proposal for the policy, and Mrs. McDer- mott signed it. Mrs. McNamarra was not present, And he did not inform her that the policy had been taken out. In August, 1879, the payments were in arrears, and he served a notice upon McDermott.—Mr. Massey said this statement supported his contention with regard to the clause—that the policy was void.—Mr. Gaskell : You had no objections to receiving the subscriptions. Mr. Massey said the company was not bound by what its agents did.—Robt. Yates having given evidence that the payments were 2s in arrear at the death of Mrs. McNamara, Mr. J. Scannell, relieving officer, was called. He said Mrs. McNamara received 2s per week from the Guardians for several months before her death. A few days before that time he saw the deceased, who told him she was 80 years of age, or more. She was a very old person, and looked be- tween 70 and 80 years of age.—The Bench retired to cDnsider their decision, and on returning Dr. O'Keeffe repeated his evidence at the request of the chairman.—The Chairman then said the Bench had come to the conclusion to make an order for the amount claimed.—Mr. Massey gave notice of appeal.—Mr. Gaskell said it was a very important case, in- volving a great many others, and the magistrates thought the judgment of a higher court should be obtained. They quite expected an appeal, whatever the decision of the Bench might be, and they would give every facility for doing it on every pGssible ground.
Netherley
Total

EMMANUEL REFORMED CHURCH. ANNUAL TEA MEETING AT WARRINGTON: The opening services at Emmanuel Reformed Church, Warrington, concluded on Sunday, and were followed on Monday by the annual congregational tea meeting. The party was held in the Public Hall, which had been Specially decorated, and there was a large attendance. After tea Alderman Burgess presided, and he was supported by the Revs. W. Mules and E Moore (Baptist), G. Lacell (Hemel Hempstead), Alderman Davies, and Mr. J. Hall and Mr. E. Jewkes (churchwarelens). The CHAIRMAN said he could not look around him at that meeting without seeing on all sides people whom he had up to a very recent period been intimately associated with— people who worshipped at St. James's Church, but who had now formed themselves into a community of their own. He had known them more, perhaps, than the generality of the people who worshipped in the Church of England, and he had known them as people—many of them, at all events— who sat under the ministry of the Rev. Mr. Wright. After Mr. Wright they had a minister who had another canon of teaching, and he could not help thinking that Mr. Wright's teaching was right and correct, and that the teaching which followed it was wrong and incorrect. That being the case, the people who had established a church for themselves had his entire sympathies. In his earlier days he had had to contend with battles similar to these they were fighting, and his sympathies were entirely with them, be- cause he felt that they would have plenty of diffculties to contend with, and that they would be held up before the public almost as heretics. But they had a duty to discharge to their consciences and to their God, and to bear witness for the truth. He congratulated the members of the church on the success that had attended their efforts up to the pre- sent time. From the time they left St. James's Church they had been worshipping in that Hall under great incon- venience, but by an effort which he believed would be the precursor of success in the future, they had succeeded in raising a house in which to worship God. No one in War- rington felt more than he did how much they were indebted to the Emmanuel Reformed Church fel-the effort they had made. One day, they might depend upon it, it Would be ; nri Oa; VehWiesllll auld PrblVusg about, and they would have their reward. (Applause.) • The Rev. W. MULES expressed his personal thanks to the chairman for the encouraging words he had spoken to them, . and to him personally as minister of that church. Without ; speaking words of flattery to those present, or without speaking one word in discouragement of those present who really were-rot belonging to their communion he feltthathe had a congregation which had the rcost pluck in Warring- ton. If he had to follow the bent of his own inclination for • a few moments he should perform an action similar to that ; performed by Samuel, who, when thinking of the goodness , and abounding mercy of God, set down a atone to be a memorial to all generations of God's goodness calling it Ebenezer, and saying, "Hitherto the Lord bath helped us." , (Applause.) . The thought that was uppermost in his mind —and he dared say some of them would think bad been , uppermost in their minds during the last six months was that of the new church and building fund. . They had erected under the blessing of God, and under anything, perhaps, but the blessing of some people, a church in which to worship God; and he could say that the build- ing did credit net only to their architects (Messrs. Pier- point and Adams), but to their contractor and builder (Mr, James Warburton, Wilderspool). (Applause.) Of course, when they thought of a new church they had also to think of a building fund, for the two were twin sisters. During the past six months the sum of about £5OO had been raised . in addition to the sum of £2OO which has been deposited in the Lancashire and Yorkshire Bank the re- sult of previous exertions of the congregation. making a total of about £7OO, or between £7OO and £BOO raised for the paying off of the debt which had been incurred through the building of their church. What- ever they did as a congregation, don't let them say or do anything in a party spirit; don't let them enlist in any work simply because they were opposing that particular party or the other particular party; do not let prejudice be the ruling passion while striving to work for the Master, but let them do the right and their very best for a work that could be raised against wrong. Do not let them spend their time in breaking down other people's walls, but let them built up their own, and do all they could for the glory of God and for the salvation of men. That was an object that would elevate and ennoble any work and command the regard both of men and angels. He appealed to them RS members of the Emmanuel Church and to their friends, the representatives from both churches, to let their great pas- sion, the all-Absorbing motive power of their life be God's glory and the salvation of their fellow-men. (Applause.) Aldermen DAVIES said he wished to testify his approbation of the very liberal manner in which their worthy pastor had spoken to them. It pleased him beyond measure to hear him speak of all other denominations as he did. He was glad to give his support to any good cense, and he did not think there was a single denomination in Warrington to which he had not been very glad indeed to give a little sym- pathy and support. Their worthy pastor spoke to them about a church building fund being inseparable from the erection of a church. He might say that he never knew a church building in his time without a church debt. (t aughtpr ) He did not think it was altogether undesirable not to have a church debt, as those churches that were most in debt, no matter what denomination, seemed to be doing most good. While it did them no hint to have a little debt in connection with their church, at the same time he should say get out of it as quick as they could. (Applause.) The Rev. E. MOORE expressed his sympathy with the members of the Emmanuel Reformed Church of England in their work, and said, like their friend Mr. Davies, he was very much pleased with the generous and manly remarks made by their worthy pastor. He could assure them that, to the best of his belief, they had the hearty sympathy of all the Nonconformist churches in that town; they had sympathy with anyone who tried to bring men and women to a higher and nobler life through faith in the Lord Jesus Christ. There was plenty of room for them all ; there was a great work for them all to do, and if they did all the work they could, and preached the Gospel to every creature with fidelity, they would be rewarded, and not for the success they achieved. He hoped they would prosper both spiritu- ally and temporally. A The Rev. G. LACELL said the Reformed Church of Eng- land existed simply-as a refuge for those people who lead been accustomed to worship God after the manner of their fathers. Twenty or thirty years ago they would have been horrified, the whole of England would have risen as one man, if things were put before them which they now took as a matter of course. Those who introduced those inno- vations in the church were, however, determined, and got hold of the young, and he would say to the good people of Emmanuel Church, " Try to get hold of the young, and if you don't succeed as you wish in this generation, the next generation will be trained up in the prineples you reverence, and they will be the occupants of your sittings' afterwards." Mr. HALL said the members of that church did not think it was a good thing to have any debt, and they were deter- mined not to be in debt, for a scheme had been set on foot already by which they hoped to be out of debt in a couple of years. As to the necessity of getting hold of the children, he said they had not been neglectful on that score, and their Sunday school was never in a better pr more prosperous copdition than at the present time. There was not a better staff of teachers in Warrington than those of the Emmanuel Church Sunday school. There was some talk of extending their borders, and it was probable that there would be a branch of the Emmanuel Church in Warrington. (Applause.) He proposed a vote of thanks to the chairman and to those who had taken part in the meeting. Mr. JEWEES seconded the motion, which was carried with acclamation. The choir, assisted by Mrs. Pearson, Miss Toft, Miss Richardson, and Mr. Pearson, rendered several pieces of music during the evening. The following is a list of those who gave trays :—His Worship the Mayor (Mr. John Crosfleld), Mr. J. G. McMinnies, M.P., (2), Sir Gilbert Greenall, Bart. (2), Mrs. Mackie (2), Messrs. T. and W. Woods (2); Mesdames Adams, T. Al len, W. Allen, Barber, Birchall, Blom', Buckley, Crownwell, Galloway, Gandy, T. Gandy, Garland, Hall, Hesketh, Howard, Knowles, Lees, Lowe, Mules, Page; Miss Sutton, Miss Tetlow, A Friend, Messrs. Crompton, Milling, J. Pierpoint, Rankin, George Warburton, and J. H. Gallo- way. The following gave subscriptions :—Mrs. Brown, Mrs. Burrows, Mrs. Holcroft, Miss Hindley, Mr. Johnson, Mr. Jewkes, Mr. P. Leigh, Mr. R. Roberts, Mrs. J. Scotson, Mrs. Shaw, Mrs. Sutton, Mrs. Bowcock, Mrs. A. Bowcock, Mrs. Fairhurst, Mrs. Hill, Miss Hunter, Mrs. Parsons, Mrs. Spinks, Mr. Jackson, Mrs. Landon, Mrs. Lawless, and Mr. Whittle.

am, and towards which them seem to advance. The victory of the priest would be again, what it always has been, the death-blow of freedom. Unless Christian Eng- lishmen are prepard to surrender, in a not distant future, the liberties, civil and religious, which their forefatheo purchased by conflict and sacrifices, it behoves them to make a speedy and definite stand against a widely and rapidly encroaching ritualism. They must combine to sweep away all that comes between a man and his Maket ; between a sinner and his Saviour. I I3lieve that yet they will so combine. And movements such as yours here will help to arouse and form and swell a public Christian opinion hostile to all that savours of sacerdotalism, favour- able to all that exalts Christ, and promotes His glorious kingdom. May God give you good success.

SERMON BY THE REV. JOHN YONGE. The concluding service in connection with the opening of the above church was concluded by the Rev. J. Yonge on Thursday evening. After preaching a very eloquent ser- mon from Cor.' 3-11, he concluded his discourse as follows: —My friends, I have spoken upon this first and most fundq- mental of truths from this pulpit now because of its manifest •and peculiar fitness to the occasion which has brought me here. This church has been built for the purpose of giving prominence to this first of Gospel truths in an especial manner. Believing that within the pale of the Established Episcopal Church in this town it has become increasingly difficult to find honest advocacy and homage for this doctrine, you have determined to make a religious home for yourselves, where, with those forms of worship which have become endeared to you, you could still continue to serve God. I come here very cheerfully to-night to express my sympathy with your movement, and to wish you God- speed. Preferring very strongly, as I -do, the mode of free and spontaneous worship to which I am accustomed, 1, can understand your strong preferences for this other mode in which you have been trained. And hence it seems to me not unnatural that you should have elected to build this church rather than, as some would have deemed it wiser, to become absorbed with the various Nonconformist churches. , There is room for us all; especially if we all become more earnestly aggressive upon the world still lying outside the border of all the churches. And there is room for you, inas- much as you now are enabled to offer what our Noncon- formist churches are not in a position to do, a simple unadulterated Gospel combined with that liturgical form of service to which members of the Church of England have been used. It is to be hoped that there are not a few in this room to whom Gospel truth is dearer than every other consideration, and who will speedily find in your church that spiritual home which they can hardly any longer dis- cover in churches of developing ritualism and of sacerdotal teaching. It will be, in my opinion, a sad, a disastrous day for this nation if ever ritualism and sacer- dotalisat should win the victory at which they

div.head: TEMPERANCE MISSION AT WIDNES.
div.p: TEMPERANCE MISSION AT WIDNES.

The teetotallers of Widnes, who have previously shown much vigour and enterprise in advocating the cause which they espouse, commenced a week's temperance mission on Sunday last, under the auspices of the Good Templar Lodges of Widnes and Runcorn. The arrangements of the mission have been under the controrof a committee, con- sisting of Bros. P. Rescoral, J. Johnston, A. Parkinson (assistant secretary), and W. Routledge, of the "Star of Widnes ; " P. Faulkner, J. Makin, and Withingten, of the "Hope of Runcorn Lodge • " C. Smith, W. Galilee, J. Jenkins, and W. Higginson, of the "Haste to the Rescue Lodge;" 0. G. Carter, J. Tomlinson, and J. Ireland, of the "Samaritan Lodge;" J. P. Morewood, T. E. Hill (secretary), Joseph Reap (treasurer), and T. Jones, of the ‘• Hope of Appleton Lodge." The inaugural service was held on Sunday afternoon in Lacey-street schoolroom, when the Rev. George Hack, of Runcorn preached a sermon to a large congregation. The service was conducted by Bro. T. Reay. On Monday evening, a tea meeting took place in the same place. About 120 persons sat deem to the repast, which was served by the following sisters :—Reay. Rescorl, Lamb, Carter, Johnston, Ramsey, and Miss Alice Ramey. Subsequently a public meeting was held in the Volunteer Hall, under the presidency of Bro. M. Bebbington, D.C.T., of Runcorn. There was a fair audience, and the members of the order present wore their regalia.— The CIEMBILIN commenced the proceedings with an earnest address. He remarked that they were met to support a movement which called for the countenance of every philanthropist, every good citizen, and every Christian in the country. It was a movement only 50 years old, but during that short period it had overcome obstacles ap- parently insuperable, and had within its ranks to-day almost the whole of the Christian community. (Applause.) The Church of England had at the present time more teetotalers amongst its ministers than ever it had before, and many of them not only professed temperance principles but wore the blue ribbon. He pointed out that the minority of the medical faculty were becoming converts to temperance prin- ciples, and declared that more than half the people of the country never took drink at all. It was the majority that placed public-houses in their midst, to the great inconven- ience, of the majerity who had to suffer. The Good Templar Organisation was the most likely to wean a man from drink, and having done so, to keep him in the paths of sobriety and vittue. In the ranks of good templary there was a larger proportion of men who had been saved from the thraldom of drink, than could be found in any other body, and be urged those present to join the order.—Bro. R.- W. KIRKIIS, hon. secretary to the Good Templars Organisation of South West Lancashire, also addressed the meeting. During the • evening the Baptist choir sang several musical pieces in good style, under the leadership of Mr. David James. Mr. Street presided at the harmoniarn. The Star of Temperance brass band was also present, and played several selections. Bro. Johnson recited "The Sabbath bells are ringing," and in response to a hearty encore gave another, entitled "Would you ?" Miss Bailey sang " Little sister's gone to sleep," for which she was loudly applauded. Bro. Kirkham Evans, of Runcorn, gave a spiritualistic entertainment, for which he is well qualified. The performance was a clever one, and excited great interest.

The mission was continued on Tuesday evening, when a meeting was held in the Volunteer Hall under the presidency of Mr. L. P. Stubbs, of Liverpool. There was only a poor attendance. On the platform were the Rev. J. Holden, M.A. (Farnworth), Bro. M. Jones, D.E.D., of Liverpool, Mr. S. Compston, F R.H.S., of Rawtenstall, and Mr. Taylor, of Liverpool. Several addresses were delivered. On Wednes- day evening another meeting was held, Mr. S. Owen occupying the chair. Addresses were delivered by the Rev. R Harper and Mr. C. H. Murray, of the United Kingdom Alliance, Manchester. On Thursday evening, Mr. T. S. Small occupied the chair, and Mr. D. Crossley, of Bolton, delivered an address. Last evening the fifth meeting of the mission was held, but, like those which preceded it, was very poorly attended. The chair was occupied by the Rev. J. Tessyman, and he wAs sup- ported by the Rev. J. Bond, vicar of Farnworth, And Mr. W. Touchstone, .of Manchester.—The CHAIRMAN referred to the spread of temperance principles throughout the land. Thirty or forty years ago there were veiy few temperance organisations in existence, while to-day the whole temperance firmament was filled with the radiance of their beams, like the sky shone with the radiance of the stars. Froin conquering to conquest the cause moved on lapace, and the drink traffic,with all the gigantic evils which followed in its train, was doomed. (Applause.) He called upon those present, by their individual influence and per- :einel abstinence, to aid in the desired speedy consumma- tion.—Mr. W. ToucHsrouE, speakine, of the Sunday Cies- ing Bill for Ireland, at present before ° the House of Lords, said there was not the slightest doubt tiNat during the opera- tion of the Act, which had just lapsed, crime had not been so extensive as heretofore. (Cheers.) He narrated sev ileal harrowing incidents, eying their origin to drink, observing that be wished the women of England would consider the drink question. Drunkenness was terrible in the man, but it was more terrible to the

div.head: VIOLENT ASSAULT AT RUNCORN,
div.p: VIOLENT ASSAULT AT RUNCORN,

Yesterday, at Runcorn Police Court, before Captain C. W. Hazlehurst and Mr. W. Bankes, a young fellow named Joseph Venal)les was charged with assaulting Agnes Ford. It appeared that Venables and Ford had resided together for some time, the former living off the proceeds of Ford's im- moral conduct. On Tuesday night two sailors visited the house, and prosnutrix left with them. The prisoner fol- lowed them, and a quarrel took place in Back Regent-street, the sailors' striking him. After the sailors had gone away, the prisoner struck Ford a violent blow on the eye, knocked her down, and while she lay on the ground he belaboured herjn a most dreadful manner.—P.S. Whalley said the pri- soner had often assalted Ford, who, on many occasions, had gone to the police office at two and three o'clock in the morning to seek protection. He had often sent an officer to the prisoner's house, but the prisoner had always contrived to get away.—The prisoner. whe had previously served three months' imprisonment for a similar offence, was sen- tenced to six months' hard labour, and at the expiration of that time to be bound over to keep the peace in his own recognisances, for a further period of six months; in de- fault of so doing, on additional month's imprisonment.

With these exceptions the work has I.),±en rightly and thoroughly done, while the answers showed considerable intelligence. The Catechism is fairly under- stood, the singing -good, and the discipline and tone ex- cellent."

The following are specially mentioned :—Group V., Standard 1: F. Roberts, J. Croinpton, Thomas Hackett, J. Daniels, H. WWI., A. Garland, J. Gilbert, Samuel Booth, F. REVISION OF THE REGISTER OF OWNERS AT WARRINGTON.
MR. SUTTON'S DECISION.
The following correspondence has taken place between Mr. James C. Sutton, who recently revised the list of owners and proxies, and the Local Government Board :

"Warrington March 9th, 1883.—My Lords and Gentle- men,—On the 26th ult. I revised the register of owners for the township of Warrington, to over 750 names of which objections had been made. I enclose herewith copies of two local newspapers containing reports of a portion of the first day's proceedings. It will be seen that the parties were represented by counsel and solicitors. The points on which I heard them are involved in the following questions : " When a register of owners is duly headed, certified, and signed by the overseers, and in that condition submitted to the reviser, is he em- powered, and, if he is, is it for him, on objection duly made, to inquire into the made and time of service of the claims of persons whose names are included in the regis- ter ? " If he is, and he finds the service of their claims bad, is it his duty on that ground to expunge their names from the register?' If it is his duty, then, was the service bad?' I reserved my decision on the points named, and the revision was proceeded with, objection also having been made to the qualification of the same persons of whom, subject to the points reserved, T &tided 160 to ha person,' gnalified to vote as owners. At the Board meeting preceding the revision I conferred with the Guardians on the importance of the ob- jection, notice of which had been given, and they concurred with my view of the desirability of a consultation with your honourable Board on the questions reserved. With the con- currence of the advocates in attendance, arrangements to the following effect were made :—‘ That at the close of the revi- sion a formal adjournment be made, that statements in writ- ing of the grounds in support of and against the objections be served on the reviser, and a copy of each delivered by him to the other party, that the statements be forwarded, to the Local Government Board prior to the revisor's con- sultation with them, and that after such consultation the revisor give his decisions on the questions reserved.' The mode of service and the circumstances are given in the papers, and were not in dispute. It was understood that Mr. Tunstall, the person to whom the claims were handed, would be at liberty to submit observations in writing thereon. I enclose all papers, herewith, and request to be favoured with an appointment to meet your honourable Board at Whitehall, at an early day for the purpose ex- plained.—l remain your most obedient servant, JAMES C. SUTTON.—To the Local Government Board, Whitehall." "Local Government Board, Whitehall, 12th March, 1883.—Sir,—I am directed ty the Local Government Board to acknowledge the receipt of your letter of the 9th • instant, and in reply to state that it devolves upon you in the first instance to decide upon the points submitted, and that you must be guided by your own judgment in doing so. The Board could not undertake to advise you on the subject.—l am, sir, your obedient servant, S. B. PROVIS, Assistant Secretary. James Sutton, Eq., Clerk to the Guardians of the Warrington Union." The following letter has been addressed to Messrs. Nicholson, White, and Nicholson, and Messrs. Ridgway and Worsley : "Warrington, 13th March. Register of Owners. Dear sir,—l submitted the cases pro and con. to the Local Government Board, and asked for a conference. They reply that it devolves upon me in the first instance to decide upon the points submitted, and that I must be guided by eery own judgment in doing so, and that the Board could not undertake to advise me on the subject. I have, therefore, in discharge of the duty devolving on me, to decide that the names of the owners not already erased from the register do remain thereon.— Yours faithfully, J. C. SUTTON."

div.head: ISSIULTS ON THE WARRINGrON
div.p: ISSIULTS ON THE WARRINGrON
POLICE.

At Warrington Police Couy, on Monday, John Shields was charged with being drunk and darderly in Dallam-lane,, and with assaulting P.C. CorcliTan.—The prisoner was drunk and creating a disturbance, and as he refused to go away, after being requested to do so three or four times, P.S. Bowen took him into cus,tedy. He would not go quietly and the police had to put the "snaps" on him. A crowd collected, and whilst the sergeant was keeping the people back, the prisoner kicked P.C. Corcoran, and re- sisted all the way to the police station.—The prisoner was committed for three months with hard labour.--John McCormick, labourer, 3, Erwood-street, and John Ford, la- bourer, 16, Portland-street, were charged with being drunk and disorderly in Buckley-street; McCormick, Ford, and Thomas Allen, forge labourer, 3, Erwood street, were charged with violently assaulting P.C. Cheney; and Mary Troy, fustian cutter, 58, Tanner's lane, Eliza Jane Duffy, factory hand, Buckley-street, and Annie Mahar, fustian cutter, 12, Erwood-street, were charged with assaulting P.C.'s Cheney, Paice. and Hitchmough whilst conveying McCortr ick to the police station, by striking them with stones. -.-40:0n Saturday night, at 11.45, P.C. Cheney was in Winwick - street, when he saw a woman named Margaret Delooze, drunk, and standing on the footway. He requested her to go home to Buckley-st, but she refused. Three young men were standing on the footway and he removed them, and the woman black- guarded him for so doing. She eventually got to her own house, the door of which she commenced to kick, and created a noise. The constable went to the house when the husband put his head out of the window, and he asked him to let his wife in. Delooze said "No ; she is drunk ; I wont. She left a sick child in the house to die." Cheney got bold of Mrs. Delooze to take her into custody, when a large crowd collected round them. The crowd endeavoured to separate them,' and about five minutes afterwards the husband came and rescued his wife. Allen and Ford kicked the officer, and McCormick pulled his whistle away, and a girl got hold of it and threw it away. Cheney. went to a youth who had assaulted him, when the crowd got him down, and Ford kicked him on the mouth and loosened his front teeth. His new /*met was also smashed by a kick whilst he was on the ground. The youth he had in custody got away, and he arrested Ford opposite his house. Ford's father and mother asked the constable to summon their son, but he thought it his duty to lock him up. The father and mother and some girls then got Ford into the house, but the police ultimately took him into custody. About twenty young women followed them down to the police station, and threw stones, which fell in a shower around the police. —P.C. Paice proved that the female prisoners threw stones, which hit Cheney and Corcoran. The girls were a terror to the neighbourhood, and were worse than the men.— McCormick was finediloa. and costs, or 14 days' imprison- ment in default ; Allen was discharged; Fora was sent to prison for three months' hard labour; and the girls were each fined 20. s and costs, or one month's hard labour.

STOCK AND SHARE MARKET.

Messrs. Joseph R. and W. P. Baines, share brokers. 13, Queen's Chambers, Market-street, Manchester, write (March 15th) : Only a meagre business is renorted for the past week, the markets throughout lacking ac. ivity. Since the completion of the settlement a somewhat better tone has been manifested, and more has been done, but it does not amount to any great number of transactions Values ~re not moved generally to any extent, only in very few imtances are the alterations of any moment, and the general balance of change is pretty evenly preserved without preponderance either way. Foreign stocks do not exhibit much alteration, E,zyptian Unified have gone better, but most of the others are fractionally easier. Mexican Railways have rallied, and quote a rise of about 2 per cent. Miscellaneous investments dull on the whole, and with- out special feature viewed together.

COAL, IRON, &C., AND In this market there is still very little doing. The tone, however, still keeps fairly steady, what changes In quotations there are being contradic- tory and apparently mo e the outcome of Individual influences than of tendency of market as a whole The transacting re- corded are solitary dealings, ti•ere being no stir manifested in any particular investment. Canadian Coppers and Tharsis Sulphur and Copper, though not dealt in (except one trans- action in the fo. iner), both shew substantial advance. On the other hand Bolekow's fully-paid and Rio Tinto are decidedly lower. ROBY CHURCH CLOCK AND BELL. Ihe tower which supports the spire of Roby Parish Church has just been adorned with a new clock. The clock has been made by Mr. John Smith, a horologer of repute, whose house has been established in Derby for fully a century, 'and who enjoys the honour of being clock maker for the Midland Railway Company. The cost, which will probably he about £l2O, is being raised, by a subscription originated and stimulated some time ago by a contribution of £5O from an unknown hand, and as it is probable the subscription may fall short of he amount needed, whatever i 4 may be—for it has not yet I been precisely ascertained—the deficiency will be sought to be made up by a sale of work in April next. The new time rnetsurer is not furnished with chimes, and for a very suffi- cient reason Mr. Smith has not been called upon to provide it with a bell to strike the hours, the church being already possessed of a hell, to which "hangs a tale," as 'well as a clapper, and which the parishioners who are acquainted with its history as well as familiar with its peculiarly musical tone, would be exceedingly loth to see superseded. This bell weighs 15 cwt., and its claims to respect and reverence are founded upon its having done duty in the church towers and elsewhere for no shorter a period than 600 years. It is of I Spanish workmar.ship, and bears its own evidence of its age land nationality in the form of an inscription in the Spanish tongue, recording the date of its founding and the fact of its having been d(dicated to the Virgin by the religeux of that far-off time, in adcordance with a still prevalent con- tinental custom. In addition to the halo of sanctity by which it is illuminated, it is also—as becomes a bell of such antiquity and venerable parentage—adorned with legendary graces. The tradition bears that after leaving the coast of Spain the ship in which the consecrated bell was to be car- ried to England was beset by storms in the Bay of Biscay and lost with all its crew, but that the bell was miraculously , saved and carried in the hands of angels to its destination. In more modern times its career, so far as it is known, has been more prosaic than that to which so romantic a begin- ning of existence ought perhaps to have been the prelude. For some years it did duty as the tenor bell in a peal of four in Huyton Para Church. The late vicar of Huyton, Mr. Ashton, being desirous of increasing the peal to six, Mr. Meers, the celebrated bell maker of London, was consulted, with a view to his providing two more bells. He found, however, that he could not produce hells whose quality al metal would give forth a tone in harmony with that of the old Spaniard, and accordingly the latter was removed from the belfry, and the peal completed with three new bells. Mr. Meers offered £BO for it, but Mr. Ashton did not feel justified in parting with it, and so it laid mute and inani- mate in the tower of Huyton Church until laso. At that time the new church was built at Roby, rand the old bell was transferred to that church, where, as. bas been said, it is now associated with A new clock.

JLINNEY CAUNCE, DECEASED.—Parsuant CP to the provisions of an Act of Parliament of the 22nd and 23rd Victoria, cap. 35, int Ruled "An Act to further amend the Saw of property and to relieve trustees." NOTICE IS HEREnr GIVEN, that all PERSONS HAVING CLAIMS or DEMANDS against the estate of JAMES LINN EY CALTNCE, late of Wigan, intim county of Lancaster, Wholesale Confectioner (who died on the 25th day of January, 1883, and whose will, with a codicil thereto, were proved in the principal Registry of the Probate Division of Her Majesty's High Court of Justice on the 15th day of March, 1883, by Eta, ah arunce, one of the executors therein named), are hereby required to SEND FULL PARTICU- LARS in writing of their CLAIMS or DEMANDS to me, the under- signed, on or before the 15th day of April next, at the expira- tion of which time the said executrix will proceed to administer the estate and distribute the assets of the deceased amongst the persons entitled thereto, having regal d only to the claims and demands which the said executrix shall then have had notice, and that the said executrix will not be liable for the assets of the said deceased, or any part thereof, so distributed to any person, of whose claims or demands she shall not then have had notice. —Dated this 15th day a March, 1883. THONIAS HEALD, 3, Market-street, Wigan, Solicitor for the Executrix. PPRUDENTIAL ASSURANCE COMPANY, LIMITED, HOLBORN BARS, LONDON. Thirty-fourth Annual Report for theyear ending 31st December, 1882. The Directors have much pleasure in presenting their report and accounts for the year 1882. The reduction in the rate of expenditure in both branches has been continued during the year. The invested funds of the Company, including the paid- upeapital, now exceed three millions, viz., ordinary branch, £328,176; industrial branch, £2,119 222. ORDINARY BRANCH. The new business of this branch for the year consists of 7,987 policies, assuring the sum of £865,148, and producing a new annual premium income of £32,777. The claims of the year amount to £73,621. representing 455 deaths and 24 endowment assurances matured. The annuli premium income at the end of the year is £164,949, being an iscrease of £22,216 over the year 1881. The investments of the year have been made prin- cipally in consols, mortgages upon freehold property in London, and reversions. The rate of expenditure of the branch Is less than ten and a-half percent on the premium income. INDUSTRIAL I3RANCH. The Premiums actually received during the year in this Branch are £2,126,022 3s. 11& as compared with the sum of £1,849,491 18s. od. received during 1881, being an increase of Premium Rec ipts of £276,527 ss. 6.3. The claims of the yehr amount to £773.813, and the total amount of claims paid in this branch is £1,559,925. The investments of the year have been made in New Three par Cents , Loans upon Rates, and Freehold around Rents. The total expenses of Uri, branch, as compared with those of the previous year, show a re- duction in the rate of expenditure of nearly two and a half per cent, on the premium Inc ,me. The Company is now repre- sented in every part of the United Kingdom. and the charges for extension expenses no longer appear in the accounts. LEWI:S'S IN LIVERPOOL, AND THE PROVININGr OF THE BEST TEA TO FAMILIES, HOTELS, AND PUBLIC AND PRIVATE INSTITUTIONS THROUGH- OUT THE UNITED KINGDOM. Who are Lewis's? Well, Lewis's are as well known in Liver- pool as the Bank of England is known im London. Lewis's began business in Liverpool thirty years ago, and Lewis's have at this present time one of the very largest businesses in Eng- land. Lewis's have not always sold Tea, but having a very large number of employes to provide with an afternoon meal, Lewis's I were struck with the difficulty of. procuring a good drinkable and refreshing Tea for them at a moderate price. The ordinary Teas were perfectly abominable. Tired of the constant and not unreasonable complaints, and of the perpetual changing of their Tea Dealers, Lewis's at last resolved to buy their Tea for the use of their establishment direct from the shippers, and to en- gage A qualified person to make the purchase. Lewis's could hardly believe there could be such a ehange for the better in the cost and quality of the tea so bought, but "experience teaches." Lewis's thought what was good enough for the use of all their establishments, public and private, would surely be good enough for the general public. Lewis's then began to sell Teas to their friends, and at last were induced to make the sale public in Lancashire, where they sell 20,000 pounds of Tea per I week. Lewis's now feel they have benefited only a small pro- portion of the population; they intend in future to make their Tea known all over the United Kingdom. Lewis's pure, splendid Tea, is one stated price, 2s a pound. Lewis s have no other price Tea, neither higher nor lower, and this Two Shilling Tea is fit for the Queen to drink. Two shil- lings is a favourite nriee with Lewis's, they having been able to supply the public with many excellent things at the price. Not till after much hard work did Lewis's succeed in blending a splendid and most deliciously-flavoured Tea, which they are giving to the public for 2s a pound. Many tea dealers charge the public 3s and 3s 6d for a similar quality. Lewis's desire to be the universal suppliers of Tea. Tea is drunk in every house- hold in the United Kingdom; it should therefore be sold at a less profit than any other article of consumption, except bread. Lewis's wish particularly to direct the attention of every family and every householder to the great advantage there is in buying Lewis's Two Shilling Tea. The flavour is so good and the strength co very great, that one pound goes further than 18 ounces of most other Teas, providing always the water boils thoroughly. The proof that Lewis's do not exaggerate the appreciation in which their Two Shilling Tea is held lies in the fact that they receive thousands of orders every day from all parts of the United Kingdom. Lewis's would like members of the Press all over the United Kingdom to write for a pound of Lewis's Two Shilling Tut ; they are sure to be satisfied and astonished with the result. Every hotel-keeper, and every public and private institution throughout the country, should write to Lewis's in Liverpool for a pound of Lewis's Two Shilling Tea. The risk is not great; it is only to send 2s in stamps to Lewis's in Liverpool, and in return they will receive a sound of splendid Tea, packed neatly in a hex, carriage paid. to any address in the United Kingdom. —Address Lewis's in Liverpool.

THE STATE OF IRELAND. The authorities believe that they have now a clue to the murderer of Mrs. Smyth, in Westmeath. Forty Civil Service clerks have, it is stated, been sent to Ireland in order to expedite the work of the Land Courts. A Dublin correspondent states that over £70,000 has been paid out of the Arrears Department to landlords under the Arrears Act, and it is calculated that nearly £3,000 per day !viI.II:PC disbursed till the claims are satisfied. The Phonier Park prisoners now awAitiiig trial have been notified that they will be tried in Dublin on April 9th on three separate counts—namely, the Phcenix Park murders, the attack on Mr. Field, and conspiracy to murder. James Carey, it seems, has instructed his solicitor to apply for a warrant as against any person who may be elected for Trinity ward, with the view of testing the legality of the action of the Dublin Corporation in declaring his seat vacant. It is stated that documentary evidence has been received in Paris from London showing that the prisoner John Walsh was not concerned in the Phconix Park murders, and that he was elsewhere at the time of the commission of the crime. The documents in question are to be forwarded to the De- partment of Justice immediately. The strike of bakers at Cork has produced such incon- venience that the military authorities in the city and at Ballincollig have been obliged to make arrangements for the delivery of bread from the military bakery in Dublin to supply the wants of the troops. The bread will thus have to be sent a distance of 150 miles. Last week the dead body of a gentleman unknown was found on the Galtee mountains. Late on Sunday night a young lady was discovered unconscious lying near where the mangled body of the mysterious stranger was found. The patient is in hospital, and is still unconscious and un- identified. A Zulu hat on the lady when discovered had disappeared, so had one boot of the gentleman's. The emigration statistics of Ireland for 1882 were issued on Wednesday night. From these it appears that during last year 89,556 emigrants left Irish ports, being an increase of 10,847 on 1881. The number of males was 47,246 and females 42,320. Over 74 per cent, were between the ages of 15 and 35. Of the total number the United States absorbed 65,902; Canada, 7,268; and Australia. 4,614. A Parliamentary paper was issued on Wednesday night of the number of agrarian outrages in Ireland during the last month. The total number was 54, but 33 of those consisted of threatening fetters, and six of resistance to legal process. Four incendiary fires were reported, and three of killing or maiming cattle. There was only one offence, against the person, and that an assault endangering life in the West Riding of Cork. There were no cases of firing into dwell- ings. The Rev. Isaac Nelson, M.P., has issued an address to his Mayo constituents, condemning the policy of returning Nationalists to Parliament. Ho says that the Irish memhere have rivetted the chains more firmly on Ireland, and should retire from the House of Commons in a body, without say- ing an unchristian word or giving encouragement to an un- christian act; and he adds to pay members of Parliament would create a branch of trade for persons who need support and require a profession. DR. KENNY AND SUPERINTENDENT JENBINSON. Dr. Kenny having written a letter to Mr. Jenkinson, complain- ing of the allusion made in the published statement of that gentleman to Dr. Kenny's professed attendance on Mr. Patrick Egan, which Dr. Kenny says was such as to "lead to the inference that he was using his professional position to aid Mr. Patrick Egan in eluding the detectives," Mr. Jenkinson has caused a reply to be sent to the effect that in his communication with the reporters he never mentioned Dr. Kenny's name. Another proof is given of the decrease of agrarian dis- affection in Ireland. In charging the Tyrone Grand Jury at Armagh, on Tuesday, Mr. Justice Harrison said there were only five new cases for investigation, in addition te two bills from the last assizes. The report of the county in- spector of constabulary was a most satisfactory document, showing only nine serious cases since the last assizes, against 39 for the same period last year. This was owing to the total disappeaaance from the county of the crime of send- ing threatening letters. Mr. Patrick Egan has appeared in New York, and, of course, has been interviewed. He declined to state on what steamer he made the passage, and declared that his business in the States was "partly commercial." One statement is that he has gone over at the invitation of the Land League in America to give them an account of affairs at home, and another is that his visit has been made at the request of Sheridan, and for the purpose of giving testimony if neces- sary, should extradition proceedings be taken against the latter. It is understood that Mr. Egan will remain several months in America. It was stated some days ago that the Duchess of Marl- borough proposed to hand over to the Tuke emigration Fund the balance of the amount collected for the relief of Irish distress which still remained in her hands. This the Duchess has now formally done in a letter to the Duke of Bedford, placing at the disposal of the Tuke Committee the sum of £3,(500. This year the committee propose to assist three to four thousand persons to emigrate from the district of Connemara to America, Canada, or elsewhere, and the substantial balance now oontributed .from the Duchess of Marlborough's Fund will be of material assistance in settling the emigrants in new homes. A deputation from the Dublin Chamber of Commerce waited upon Earl Spencer at Dublin Castle, on Wednesday, to urge the reconsideration of the contract arranged with the London and North-Western Railway Company for the conveyance of mails between England and Ireland, and to 1 deprecate the employment of steamers of less draft and ton- nage than those of the City of Dublin Steam Packet Com- pany. The deputation also opposed the alteration of the port of departure. Earl Spencer said he did not think the Government intended to make any change in the vessels employed, and the port of departure would not be altered. He would submit the representations made to the Govern- ment before the contract was concluded. The man Michael Walsh, who was at one time under arrest on a charge of being concerned in the murder of Esther Croghan, at Mullingar, has turned approver, and gave evidence at the magisterial inquiry held on Saturday. This man stated that one of the prisoners, Anne Croghan, offered to pay him well to get Esther Croghan, her sister, out of the way, and he closed with the offer. He hired a man named Kenny, who was recently convicted of firing at a soldier, and handed to him a revolver which he had lent on former occasions for similar deeds. After the murder Kenny told him how it was committed. He stated that he went into the room and shot the woman; Kane' the second prisoner in custody, remaining outside to watch. A writ of habeas was issued for the production of Kenny, who is un- dergoing penal servitude, and the inquiry was ad- journed.
